text: I've been to Memphis Taproom 3 times, so far. I think the food is great, the service is great (knowledgable staff), and the atmosphere rocks! I love visiting bars and restaurants where everyone seems to be in a great mood. Though it's loud, we'll say boisterous, it's welcoming and lively! The food is consistently great. I try something new each time. I remember the first time, I had the pork sandwich, expecting pork bbq, and it wasn't with bbq, but it was still delicious, and hot! I had the chicken fingers dinner with mac and cheese the second time - equally scrumptious. Then, yesterday, I was there for the no-repeat week (beers on tap). I had the Mams's Little Yellow Pill, I think. Very smooth, yet tasty, light-hearted beer. Started with the cheddar soup with a cider touch, and I haven't had soup that great this entire winter season! I fell in love with the battered dill pickles dipped in Horseradish sauce. Loved. Them. My brisket burger was not too big, as some gastropubs seem to do to me (I am small!!), but not too small, either. Just right. I almost cleaned my plate. Go here.
label: POS

text: After seeing this place featured on the Food Network and Travel Channel I knew that I absolutely HAD to come here the next time I was in Tucson. I usually am not a very big fan of hotdogs... in fact, prior to eating at El Guero Canelo it had been at least five years since the last time I had one. I am not really into bacon either, but I felt it was a necessary experience, since Sonora-style hotdogs are a unique regional snack. ... and I was not disappointed! Who knew that hotdogs wrapped in bacon, in a sweet bun, topped with pinto beans, diced tomato, roast onion, jalapeno sauce and mayonnaise could be so good?!! Not to mention how reasonable the prices are! They also have a lot of other very affordable, delicious items on their menu. The salsa bar is pretty impressive too. I am now a big fan of these hotdogs, and will definitely make El Guero Canelo one of my regular stops whenever I am in Tucson.
label: POS

text: This is my favorite spot to take people in Philadelphia. Mahogany has the best atmosphere in the city to lounge, drink good scotch, and smoke cigars. Imagine sitting in a "smoking room" of a large mansion; it is dimly lit, has a fireplace, and offers huge chairs and leather couches to lounge around on. Food is decent but more of a light fare. While there are two beers on draft, the scotch and brandy is top notch. Any scotch you can imagine is here. As an added bonus, Holt's Cigar Co. is next door (though Mahogany sells cigars). Service is always good and the waitresses are all extremely attractive. There is nothing better than sipping scotch, smoking a cigar, and catching the game here. It's the type of place you take your dad, grandfather, or a client to. It's the type of place to have a classy celebration in or hold a fundraiser. There is also great ventilation so the place smells like cigars without being smokey. However, I do not recommend taking your girlfriend here unless she likes cigars.
label: POS

text: My husband and I always enjoy going to Iron Hill -- either this location of one of their others in the region. Of particular interest is the fact that the seasonal beers are different in every location, so you get quite a variety in that sense. In general, we think that the regular house beers they have on tap are okay, but nothing too exciting. On the other hand, we LOVE the variety and quality of their seasonal selections that change on a regular basis. We generally drink from those only. As far as the food, I have had very few things there I didn't like. I wouldn't say I'm the most picky person ever, but I enjoy good food. Love their burgers (particularly the Turkey Burger), the mesclun greens salad, their wings (good and meaty), pizzas (the goat cheese one is great), and the sweet potato fries among many other things. Iron Hill has become one of our favorite spots and more than just the food and great beer, we really like the friendly, knowledgeable, helpful staff. Downsides? I don't love any of their desserts. And it does get loud in there, particularly in the dining area. Other than that, it keeps me happy.

In order of least-to-most interesting: - red chips - salty - regular chips - fine - tomato mozzarella pizza - fine, thin crust - pigs in a blanket with a mustard on the side - tasty - mushroom dumplings with a truffle sauce - not objectionable Four stars for effort, ignoring their management.

text: I just moved back to Indiana after a few years in California. Everything about Kabuto is what I feared Asian food in Indiana would be. I had the sushi (spicy tuna and rainbow roll), my friend had the steak yakisoba. The price for the spicy tuna was inexpensive ($4.95) but the rainbow roll made up for it registering at an outrageous $10.95. First the spicy tuna, well, wasn't spicy. The rolls were poorly formed, rice was mushy vice sticky and somewhat firm, the "filling" was grainy and bland. I understand Indiana is landlocked so I'm trying not to be overly critical but the sushi was gross. Rainbow roll didn't even have the avocado-topped pieces I'm accustomed to. Frankly the sushi seemed nothing more than a biscuit to sop up soy and wasabi. What a shame. The steak wasabi tasted like rice-a-roni seasoning and the "steak" was cheap chop steak not worthy of the $15 price tag. Stringy and chewy meat, generically seasoned pasta, underwhelming sauces. Dissatisfying. I will also warn you I got a little "digestive fluidity" once got home, and I normally eat quite a but of sushi, so I'm sure it's not just me getting an upset stomach. It's not food poisoning but something in the sushi did not agree with me. On a final note, the service is atrocious, especially for the price tag. Then again, it is behind an abandoned KrispyKreme, so ... There you go. Don't waste your time or money if you have even a marginally discerning Asian pallette.
label: NEG

If you'd like something Asian that's a little more exotic than Chinese in Ballwin, I'd go down the street to Monsoon Vietnamese Bistro, they're usually pretty good. Edit: Oh, and regarding Rachel's comment about the peppers, the way it works is that 1 pepper is sort of like the default level of hotness. Then, if you want it hotter, rather than the waitress trying to interpret what you mean by "Extra hot," you say "3" or "4" or whatever level you think you can tolerate. Related to this, and as a fan of extra hot food, I wouldn't recommend going much over 2 on most dishes because they do make it nice and hot, but as I noted in my review, the flavors aren't that strong to begin with and it's easy to overpower them with the heat. text: I don't normally write reviews, but this event pissed me off so much that I need to warn people. First off, there was no parking. text: Reading the reviews confirmed my personal experience, and I just sent in a request to terminate my membership in Philly Carshare... PCS pitched Business membership to my firm, in a clever effort to get more work out of the fleet during the week, given that the genesis of the nonprofit was residential carsharing on weekends for urban residents. I thought it was clever, convenient and relatively economical, and easier to deal with than getting a car back to a rental shop prior to closing...... Given the condition that the cars are in, using them for a business trip has become challenging, particulary following their reversal of "take it to Shore" for a long weekend!" to "we're jacking the rates up for overnight stays.... my travel involves overnight travel. Also, while I don't expect a nonprofit to bus the cars after every trip, taking the risk as to the cleanliness of the cars was a challenge, and the last business trip I used the car for was one that had soda spilled all over the driver's seat, food trash all over the passenger's seat and a rather compelling stench of dead french fries. Did nothing to help me prep for my client meeting.......if the tradeoff is to have my firm reserve a rental, use my personal car or get a Zipcar, I'll now turn to those more expensive options.... given the tradeoff of quality of service. My last personal use was when a massive accident blocked access to my personal car, and I reserved a PCS at the last minute for an evening appointment. The car (a Prius) would not start, and I spent 30 minutes in the car with a PCS staffer "guiding" me through the startup instructions. When I threatened to abandon the car, which had been parked not in a PCS pod, but on the street, by the previous user, I was informed that I would be responsible for any damage to the car in its (somewhat shady) location on the street.... Eventually, after another 15 minutes of wrangling, I convinced the woman that her instructions, however, pure of heart, were not getting the Prius to fire, and I walked, cancelling my evening in the process. the followup, with a PCS supervisor, resulted in a discussion about my functional incompetence in being able to either follow instructions....... The cars seem to have deteriorated in terms of basic maintenance, frankly, in the last several years.....and contacting the "hotline" with the information that the service light is blinking generally resulted in a "oh, we know that" response, which was not helpful. Contacting them about interior condition is a waste of time, frankly... Given that sense that the service was deteriorating, I was pleasantly surprised to see a team of cleaners with vacuums and window cleaner swabbing down a batch of cars at a PCS pod, and was reflecting on what I hoped was a change of policy.... then I realized that the pod had "flipped" and was now a Zipcar location..... PCS is a great idea! and for about 18 months, I enjoyed the reality. Increased cost coupled with decreased service makes other options preferable............

text: I came here with a friend a couple months back on his suggestion. I love Mexican food, but I didn't want to stuff myself (I had a reservation for Amada later), so I ended up getting a taco platter. It wasn't big, but I don't think it gets better than al pastor that's been slow-cooked and flavored for several hours and chopped cilantro in a tortilla. It's very basic, but you really didn't need anything more for the dish. It was amazing; my only suggestion might have been to throw in a pinch of pico de gallo-like salsa. But for $6 or so, you couldn't get better tacos elsewhere. I was also a fan of the juice selection; they had guava juice in one of those 12-ounce glass bottles. I've been a huge fan of guava juice since my first visit to Hawaii, but it's hard to find the genuine thing on the mainland. The service was straightforward; I would have appreciated a little bit quicker service in terms of getting a refill on my drink (I had to ask for a glass of water after finishing my juice), but all in all it was a very pleasant experience, and I'd definitely recommend it to anyone who wants a quick, authentic bite of Mexican.

text: If you want to experience short, cold and unfriendly customer service, look no further than the Carrabbas on Rt 38 in Maple Shade, NJ. You'll definitely encounter unprofessional and sub-par service from their managerial staff. Scenario: I wanted to purchase a bottle of champagne for a table celebrating a graduation. Naturally, I called the restaurant to see if I can do so and asked to speak with someone who would be able to help. The hostess answered the phone and I relayed what I wanted to do for a party that was currently seated in their restaurant. She put me on hold and a manager (you know who you are) came on the line. This is how the conversation played out. MGR: How are you going to pay for this? (sounding very annoyed) Me: I was going to pay with a credit card. MGR: We don't do that. Me: You can't take credit cards over the phone? MGR: No. Me: Oh do you need me to fill out an authorization form? I can fax it... MGR: I need to see the physical card Me: Ok, I guess not even a faxed copy of the front and back of my card will do? I know other places... MGR: (sighing exasperatedly) I guess I can do that Me: It's ok. Just forget it. If it's too inconvenient MGR: Fine And we both hung up at the same time. Now if this manager's customer service skills is a reflection of what kind of service is being given at the restaurant, then it is certainly a very sad state of things at this Carrabbas on Maple Shade, NJ. Now I understand if you can't take credit cards over the phone but there is, most definitely, another way that conversation could have have been handled. If this "manager" had any inkling what true customer service was, then this person would've have known how to handle that situation in a reserved and polite manner. Needless to say, I won't be going to this Carrabbas anytime soon. Good thing I live out of state!

text: I went to Brennan's for Sunday brunch. Let me preface this review by saying that it isn't based on a comparison to simply any other place for breakfast/brunch: you can expect to drop between $100-$150 for two people, which places it among the most expensive places to have brunch. Expectations are extremely high. I've been to places like Commander's Palace and Dante's Kitchen for brunch on multiple occasions, so they are my baseline. Here's how Brennan's compared: 1) Service: Good, but clearly inferior to Commander's. I got the idea that our server might be responsible for too many tables. Silverware wasn't replaced and it took several minutes to clear extra place settings after we sat down. 2) Menu: The menu wasn't quite varied enough. Too many eggs and benedict meals. For my appetizer, I had the Oyster soup, which was good and well-presented. For my main course, I had the oysters benedict. The oysters were sub par. At least one tasted very rubbery, and another had some hard bits in it (I think they were pieces of shell). For the dessert, I had the cheesecake, which was quite good, although normally I expect more imaginative desert options from Brennan family restaurants. 3) Drinks: I had a Sazarac with my meal. It was very well-prepared, on par with the Sazerac bar and Commander's. Everyone else seemed to enjoy their drinks as well. 4) Atmosphere: The dining area was too crowded. The bar was too crowded. The bathrooms weren't terribly clean. Compared to comparable options, it just wasn't an attractive environment. Bottom line: For the money, you can do a great deal better for brunch in New Orleans. I enjoyed the meal, and many aspects of it were quite good, but there are far better options.

text: Like most people that live in the neighborhood, I am always excited when a new restaurant opens up. Kong is pushing the street food theme, which is visually reinforced by the restaurants décor. Some walls are consciously left unfinished with one wall depicting Chinese letterforms. There are low-glow light bulbs on the ceiling encased by various wooden birdcages, some left empty. The burned wood tabletops are a nice touch. Looking at the menu, I found it hard to make a decision on what I wanted to eat. As some of the other Yelpers pointed out, I think they need some more vegetarian selections. Not that I'm a vegetarian but it's nice have some options other than meat-centered dishes. To start I got the Three Pork Dumplings, I was surprised and then a bit overwhelmed by the smoke flavor in the filling. The dumplings were tender and presented well, but I've had better from take-out joints for 1/3 the price. I followed up with a beef brisket noodle bowl. It was a salt fest. It was salty to the point where my lips started to pucker like I was swimming in the ocean for 2 hours. The brisket was a little chewy and reminded me of hydrated Jack Links beef jerky. The noodles were cooked well, but stuck in clumps in some spots. The broth was savory, but again, really, really salty. For dessert I got the only option on the menu, coconut/jasmine rice pudding. It was served warm and the rice was an interesting texture. As rice puddings go, it was pretty good, but I would have liked something more refreshing, seeing that it is August. I was hoping for some mango or jack fruit ice cream or something more exotic. Our waiter was nice and put some jasmine tea on ice which tasted great. The tea was probably my favorite part of the meal, which was unfortunate. As a side note, it was good to see that they offered Hitachino Nest White Ale even if it was $9 a bottle. In conclusion, going into Kong I was looking for a meal that tasted fresh and had a bit of complexity, but the food ended up tasting uninspired. It's a cool little place, but I go to a restaurant to eat, not hang out, so it's not somewhere I see myself going back to any time soon.

text: Everyone in Tucson raves about Sabino Canyon, and I've certainly enjoyed my hikes here. During my first year in Tucson, I walked to seven falls once every other week just to see how the process of the seasons changed the land. It was very convenient to get to from my apartment at the time. The landscape is typical Southern Arizona-- beautiful. If you choose not to ride the tram... Okay, Sabino Canyon has a tram. Makes some of the higher hikes easier to access, but this is just wrong on so many levels, and really distracts from the enjoyment of the place. If you choose not to ride the tram, you are left walking on paved roads for at least the first mile of your hike. Awful. Additionally, there are too many artificial structures like bathrooms. Anyone out on a walk should realize, the whole world is a toilet. No need to go enshrining them. I've also seen artificial dams on streams. There's a photo posted on Yelp of the warning signs of Mountain Lions. While mountain lions are most likely to attack where suburbia encroaches on their habitat, this isn't much of a worry unless you do real hiking. And if you're doing real hiking, this isn't the place to go. Additionally, they murder any lions reported and jail the activists who try and disrupt the hunts. Please, if you're fortunate enough to see a mountain lion on your visit here, do not report the sighting. A good place to bring your elderly relatives on a visit to Tucson if you can't talk them into someplace better. So I've been informed by a site member that the last mountain lion attack was on cyclists at dusk. Meals on wheels! A person on a bicycle can resemble a deer to an animal that doesn't know why bicycles are, and are usually targeted for attacks. Dusk is Lion feeding time. We see the same thing in Suburban L.A... Not a good place for bikes at dusk.
label: NEG

text: According to Science, 70-75% of what we perceive as taste is really smell, which is why food is never as good when you have a head cold. The relationship inverted means that, if there's an overpowering, distracting smell while, the quality of your gastronomic experience will suffer for it. India Grill punched me right in the nose when I walked in there for lunch. Cloying incense, vaguely chemical, swept out onto the sidewalk like walking by the candle store at the mall. Normally, I would've yielded to the crashing wave of scent, letting it carry me back out onto the street and on my way, but I was determined to try this place. The former 1st Ave N location had served some pretty good (though monopolized) buffet and, though Green Chili Bistro was great, I wanted to explore options. Both Green Chili and India Grill suffer from the need to cater to bland palates - I guess the average Floridian can't handle the heat - but India Grill was missing out on the flavor, too. Butter chicken, Tandoori, vegetable curry, and everything else we tried elicited the idea of Indian food, but not the deep expeditionary feel of exotic spices trooping across your tongue. Gulab Jamun, a dessert cake ball soaked in sweet syrup, tasted vaguely plastic. There are two reasons that I will go back: one is that I heard the dinner menu is significantly better than the buffet offerings - this makes sense and I will give them the benefit of the doubt. The second is that my visit was within a week of them opening. A guy wheeled in their beverage mini fridge while we were eating. I'll hope that they can get into a little better groove and dish up some exciting flavor. Surfing the smell back out onto the street after the meal, I looked across the way at Green Chili Bistro, and its savory welcoming smells of food, and knew what I'd choose for lunch next time.

text: I'm from New York. But I love NOLA. LOVE LOVE LOVE. It's so charming and there's really no other city in the US that has such unique regional cuisine. It's located in a charming Southern house-- albeit, a far trek (30 minutes on the the St. Charles Streetcar) out to Dante St. in the Tulane area but so worth it. You'd only know of it if you're a foodie (it's not well advertised to tourists in other words). This place really puts some of the high profile places in New York to shame. Onto dinner! I started off with a Kir cocktail- very sweet and delish. I started with the creamy crawfish (mmm) and corn chowder. Deliciously creamy, deliciousy good. With fresh, non messy to eat crawfish. My sis had the gumbo- which did not compare to the chowder. (On a seperate note, I was in general dissappointed by the gumbo down there. It was watery and just didn't have enough flavor in the way that my Mom's gumbo had growing up. Maybe it was the lack of spice- it didn't feel like there any andouiille and the chicken was dry. Onto the mains. I had the seafood platter- SPOT ON. I realize that I hadn't had any land animals since I was down there, but the seafood platter seemed to good to pass up on considering we were all panicking about the oil spill! It came with: paneed scallop- good (with light breadding so didn't make you feel sick and fat afterward), swordfish (mmm my fave) with crawfish etoufe- sorry if spelling is wrong), then 2 baked oysters (this was....the worst part of the dish because the cheese was all mushy and I didn't taste much of the oyster- or anything really), and in the center.... the most delicious shrimp shortbread. It looked like a little souffle and had the most wonderful buttery texture.. I mean DAMN, it was good. It really made the dish for me. Others had: the breaded rabbit- also well known as Brigsten's. Very juicy, very tender. The halibut with mashed p's; this was really boring. I mean, it was meaty, and big- a nice big chunk of fish but I really you could have had this anywhere. Another diner had the duck- which is always well known at Brigstens. I almost went for this vs. the platter- and glad I didn't. It was good but after a while you kind of got sick of it. It wasn't dry or anything- trust me, it was delish. But it wasn't as tasty as duck meat could be strangely. We passed up dessert- because I'm really trying to diet. Wah wah. BUT I would have had either the pecan pie or the bread pudding in a heartbeat considering those were the famous picks. Best meal in NOLA. NOLA is amazing amazing amazing but really, go to Brigsten's. So worth making a ressie and taking the StreetCar uptown! It's good for all types of occasions; I went for myself but it's also great for a romantic occasion or even business - saw a bunch of Japanese business folk at the table next to us. GO!

text: This is a really great restaurant. The staff is very friendly and willing to offer suggestions or even talk with you about anything. Even when the place is busy, the servers never seem rushed. It is very nice inside. They just recently remodeled and it is pretty modern now. I feel so comfortable there. It is roomy and I love that they always let us take our time. We order a lot of food and stay for at least an hour. We typically start off with the vegetarian appetizer. It is fried food with about 4 different selections. I don't particularly like their samosas. They are too greasy. Then, we get one of the dosas. I've never had a bad dosa. These are delicious. hot and crispy with great filling and wonderful coconut chutney that I could eat with a spoon all by itself. We order several naans. I prefer the garlic, but onion is great too and you can't go wrong with the plain. their bread is less greasy than a lot of other restaurants. Most of the meals here are good. I wasn't fond of their mushrooms, which tasted canned, but I enjoy every vegetarian dish I order. Especially the Saag Paneer. I just can't stay away from that. They always politely ask which type of spice I would prefer, giving me the "Indian Spicy" option as well! Even if I haven't been there for a couple of months, they still remember what I order and how I like my food prepared.
label: POS

text: I love Target as much as the next white person, but this is definitely a sub par Target. Their grocery selection is OK, but TBH, I'll go to Whole Foods or Winn-Dixie for groceries, not Target. But when I want things like a pillow for my bed, they had absolutely NONE in stock. This doesn't seem like a very exotic item to me... One of the worst things about this store is figuring out the traffic clusterfuck that is the intersection of Veterans Boulevard and Clearview Parkway. Actually, getting here off I-10 is no challenge at all, but getting back on? Forget it.

text: I have eaten at Sovana numerous times over the past few years and each time the experience brings me back. Pros: 1. The Food. Consistently good (even Craig LaBan gave it a rave review last year) and the menu changes from time to time. There is a 100 mile section of their menu as well, meaning they try to incorporate at least 90% of the ingredients from local sources. 2. Service. They don't let the high school kids ruin your meal by being your server. Some of the servers appear to stay for many months and they are knowledgeable about most things on the menu. (to include their artisianal cheese plates) 3. BYOB. It used to be BYOB only. Now, they have a full bar, but for a $5 corkage fee, you can still bring your own. 4. More space. They have recently expanded, which means more seating, which means less waiting, which means better overall experience. 5. Pizza. While I don't order it there as a main course, I know those who have and they are always happy. Also, if you have kids, its nice to be able to have an adult meal and let them have some pizza. 6. Near Longwood Gardens (for those out of town tourist looking for a good meal, it is only 2 miles away). Cons: None really. Quality food, consistent service after many years. The true sign of a good restaurant. Check it out.
label: POS

text: We'll never go back to this Carino's after a string of disastrous visits. Just a few highlights of our Sunday night dinner escapades include: Ordering family style entrees and being given bread plates to eat our entire meal. Being given LITERALLY six noodles in an order of kids macaroni and cheese (We did send it back and they gave us more, but STILL!) Getting "trainee" servers without any training or anyone to assist them, on more than one occasion. Waiting 20+ minutes to be seated when there were MANY empty tables Being told by a hostess that we'd have to wait, watching her walk away and then not seeing her again for 10-15 minutes My overall assessment is that this restaurant is struggling. They can't keep a decent staff on hand because servers rely on tips and they can't make tips in a slow restaurant. So the restaurant is left with lots of teenaged employees who aren't being properly trained and are kind of left feeling bewildered and lost. I don't blame the employees for any of the issues we've experienced here, I blame their lack of training and support.

text: THANK YOU CARRIE E.!!! This is a fantastic hole-in-the-wall that we've driven by dozens of times and never even noticed. Tonight we were in the mood for take out and decided to stop by. With the platter you get 2 sides and cornbread (supposedly since we didn't get any and didn't notice until we were home :( ). We had BBQ chicken. One platter was more than enough to satisfy two, so plan to have leftovers if you order one for yourself. The meat fell off the bone it was so tender and juicy and I was practically lapping up the BBQ sauce when we were done. The green beans were okay, but the mac n cheese was deliciously cheesy and peppery. You can get takeout fairly quickly, but I actually found the inside of the restaurant quite nice - brightly covered walls and tables enough to seat around 25 or so comfortably.

text: Honestly, I've been here once, but it was sooooooo good.... I was in Santa Barbara for a wedding, and Jake's is "Just Around the Corner!" from their apartment. A handful of us went there on Saturday morning, around 10:30, and the place wasn't crazy crowded. There were 6 of us, and we got seated right away. We just had to wait 2 minutes for them to shove two tables together. They've got a couple TVs, and the one closest to us had the Wiggles on, but since the other one had News, we caught a story we wanted to watch, and requested a channel change. Rather than sticking us with whatever channel they chose, we simply got handed the remote, which was nice. The place only serves Breakfast & Lunch, but I can see why they stick to their specialties. Before we had ordered, we got a plate of muffins that we honestly some of the best I've ever had. They were a cranberry muffin, but the inside was soft and moist, and the outside was crispy, just we way a muffin should be. I knew then that breakfast would be yummy. I ordered something called "The Charleston". It comes with 2 or 3 eggs (your choice based on your appetite), canadian bacon, grits (which I substituted for Hash Browns, because I hate grits), and tomato slices. I have a thing with eggs. I always order them over-easy because I hate runny egg whites. The problem with this is that 95% of the time, the yolks are harder too. I like my yolks runny. This is the first time in I don't know how long that my eggs, when ordered Over-Easy, actually came out over-easy. The hash browns were perfect, nice and crispy, but still soft in the interior parts. The tomato was on the slightly not quite ripe side, but nothing to complain about. other people at my table were raving about their breakfasts as well, and I think we all ate more than we really should have. I know I would have been loosening my belt, had I been wearing a belt to loosen.
label: POS

text: Some mornings, I just need to have something substantial for breakfast. I don't normally drive past too many places with enticing options (McDonald's anyone?), but sometimes I take a slight detour and hit Einstein Brothers. Their bagels are good, but what keeps me coming back is the Lox Bagel - it's always a welcome improvement to my morning, even if I am dead tired or hung over (yes, smoked salmon is a weird hangover food, but I love it). It's not easy to find lox at many places that are convenient to me in the morning, so I appreciate Einstein offering it. And the staff never has any problem customizing it to meet my various wishes (low fat cream cheese, no capers or onions, add cucumbers). I stopped by last Friday for lunch. It was a really dreary day, so I was craving a nice hot sandwich on filling bread or a cup of soup. Apparently everyone else in Fishers had the same idea -- the line for Panera was nearly out the door! I didn't have the patience, so I went down a few doors to Einstein to try lunch for the first time. I might have ordered the wrong thing -- the Italian Chicken Panini, but it just wasn't good at all. The chicken had an odd flavor and texture, and I ended up not eating most of it. For the price, it was not worth it. From now on, I will stick to the lox!

text: Zee frites, zey are fantastique! Thick-cut, crispy on the outside and tender on the inside... I was in carb-lover's heaven. A sneaky spice percolated through the cheddar-jalapeno cup, but the cheese was undetectable -- it was much more like a zingy mayo. Lemon-dill played a cool counterpoint to the hot fries; a fountain Diet Coke cut through the salt attack. One "regular" sized fry cone, an extra dip and a medium fountain drink set me back $5.40, and I'd definitely return when I'm craving some spuds bathed in bubbling oil.

text: AMAZING AMAZING AMAZING! Earlier this spring, my boyfriend and I went to New Orleans on business, and he made dinner reservations at Bombay Club. I was expecting some boring little British joint, but instead I had one of the best meals I've ever had in New Orleans (and this is including Court of Two Sisters and Brennigans)! To start with, the British Colonial decor is lovely and an interesting break from the faux-French decor found in so many NOLA establishments. Halfway through dinner a charming gentleman in a darling seersucker suit played old rat-pack classics on the piano, interspersed with witty commentary of the guests. The wait staff was charming without being annoying, and served a perfect dirty martini (very high praise from my boyfriend). I had a delicious Bloody Mary followed by an equally delicious glass of white wine (I wish I remembered what it was - our waiter recommended it). However, all of this is easily overshadowed by the food! MY GOD! I ordered the BBQ Shrimp, and it was NOT what I expected! The shrimp was seasoned in a spicy concoction that might be called BBQ, but such a delicious and marvelous combination of flavors really should be called "ambrosia"! The sauce was plentiful (which was good, as I asked for more bread, to wipe up every last drop!), and the shrimp was cooked to perfection - moist and tender. Just writing this review is making me salivated for Bombay Club again. I don't even recall what my boyfriend had - I believe that I growled at him when he tried to have a taste of my dish though!
label: POS

The other stops along the way were all good and the establishments made us feel very welcome. We were offered water at more than one stop and a place to sit as well. I have done culinary tours in Seattle and San Francisco, but this one was by far the best one. It was fun to hear tidbits of information that felt like you were getting the inside scoop on the city. text: As a New Orleans resident, the Hotel Provincial left much to be desired. I decided that for my birthday, I wanted to stay in an older, supposedly haunted hotel in the French Quarter. Hotel Provincial was one of the few that had any availability for the weekend we wanted to go, so we booked it. Granted, we were just using the hotel as a place to clean up and get ready before dinner and as a place to crash, but the room was nothing to write home about. Pretty small and sparsely decorated and had issues getting the AC to pump out cold air. The shower was a nightmare. I am only 5'5 and the shower head was barely at chin height. The water either scalded you or gave you hypothermia- no in between and I usually have a good finesse on New Orleans plumbing. Also, the drainage was terrible and by the end of my shower (less than 10 min.) I was standing in water half way up my shins. There were lights burnt out so I have to figure out which lights weren't "necessary" at that time and switch out the bulbs. Normally, I am not a nit picky hotel guest, however, knowing that New Orleans and the Quarter has so much better to offer, I do think the Hotel Provincial should be able to get away with charging almost $200 for a Saturday night PLUS and additional $22/night for parking. Then there was the housekeeping staff....The "do not disturb" sign was up on our door and liking to sleep in, we put off checking out til the last minute. The maids opened our door twice while we were in bed and after we had replied "No thank you!" to their repetitive knocking. The best part about the hotel was the location and the bell man/valet guy who was super-friendly and extremely helpful. I've stayed in much better historic, quaint boutique hotels and next time, will book more in advance so we don't get stuck here again.

Let me preface this by saying that I've had many a Monte Cristo in my day and Bennigan's will always be the king. Many restaurants out there sell slightly fried (but mostly soggy) ham and turkey sandwiches and pawn them off as good ol' Monte... Don't be fooled. Cheddar's, on the other hand, is the real deal. One bite into that crispy, golden brown mess of powdered sugar and I felt a little piece of me die; the piece that always held Bennigan's as king. Now that the corporate restaurants have gone out of business leaving only select franchises open, I think Bennigan's will be happy to have such a worthy predecessor.

text: I rented a car from Dollar at the Nashville airport and departed at night with a snow storm bearing down. About 30 minutes from the airport, I noticed that the window washer didn't function, which was a major safety problem - the windshield was obscured by road salt and dirt and it was nighttime and snowing hard at this point . I had to pull over a few times to manually clean the window with melted snow. I finally found a store and bought a gallon of anti-freeze washer fluid. And I found that the washer reservoir was completely empty - it took the entire gallon to fill it. Which means that Dollar didn't properly inspect the car before releasing it. The washer still didn't function so I called for Dollar roadside assistance. They told me that they'd come out to my location with a towed replacement car, but if they found that the washer was working I'd be liable to pay for the large expense of towing the replacement car. I told them that wasn't fair - but was told "that's the way it is". I went back to the car and tried the washer again and found that it worked. I figure that frozen lines may have thawed from the engine heat . All told, I spent an hour on the side of the road, searching for a store that sold washer fluid in rural Tennessee on a Sunday night and on the phone with Dollar Roadside. When I returned the car, I told the agent of my experiences and asked for some restitution for the fact that Dollar had rented me a car that was not properly inspected and ready for use - I figured a free rental for a day or two would be fair. The agent offered me a $10 rebate! That's right, $10 to pay for all my troubles. I told her to keep the $10 and that Dollar had lost a customer. When you have a choice, I recommend renting with anyone but Dollar.

text: On February 29th of 2008 I organized a small group of friends of mine to to be charged an enormous amount of money for possibly the worst dining experience of Chinatowns history! Woo Hoo! Someone sent me a link to what sounded like the dinner of a lifetime: Join Chef Poon for a traditional 10-course Chinese New Year Banquet featuring dishes from 8 nations. It sure wasn't difficult to convince some friends to join me since the menu sounded absolutely wonderful. When we arrived at 1010 Arch street in Chinatown we found ourselves ascending a flight of dirty carpeted stairs that rewarded us with what looked like a wood-panelled storage room turned into emergency shelter/Chinese banquet room. You see, there was an abundance of personal items and restaurant supplies such as old chairs, lamps and boxes of Christmas decorations piled up along the front part of the 2nd floor space. There was no pretentious covering this stuff up. No, it was there it was flavor! The tables set up for our party and the other groups of victims were actually stainless steel work bench tables you might see in an industrial kitchen. But of course these were covered with white table covers that were bleached, and yet still stained, so often they were holy. Folding chairs were covered with images of Chef Poon, which would be creepy if not for the striking resemblance and level of class that one would see at Buddakan. Steven Starr, eat your hear out. Also, my group being fortunate, we were placed at the much sought after tables with the best views. We were actually in the space deemed "the kitchen" The equipment and sinks were only a mere 5 feet from our table! Nonetheless the mood was one of anticipation. If the place was THIS humble, imagine how great the food must be! So we began with ordering a round of drinks. We had a choice of generic Chinese beer or a glass of cheep box wine for a bargain $6. We had no idea what was in store for us. The meal was over in less than 40 minutes and perhaps that's a good thing. I wish you were there.... Oh.. let me walk you through it! No, no, it will be my pleasure to share this! The first 2 "courses" were some mouthful-sized appetizer tastes that were actually pretty decent though tiny. (Try and read the following as if you're training for the speed reading championships.) These first courses were brought out at a leisurely pace of one per every... oh let's say 2.5 minutes. It's a good thing though, since each of us had such supermarket-sample-sized portions we often were able to consume each before the next part of the feast arrived creating a sense of pride and accomplishment. Honestly, there's no finer dining atmosphere better than that of a pie eating contest and this was damn close to it. So, as each dish was delivered to our work-bench table we found ourselves slowing down. It was similar to when a child discovers something that causes pain and is reluctant try it again. Larger dishes to be shared were brought out and and presentation occurred all at once so it really started feeling like a feast. The presentation of some seemed aesthetically pleasing, while others were a bit scary. Mostly though the seafood was fishy. The Bass was greasy and the salmon tasted old, like "honey we should've thrown this out a week ago" old. The Fried rice dish was sweet and unpleasant while perhaps the lowest point of the meal was the Lobster dish. A large dish of linguine was covered by pieces of lobster broken to hard chunks still in their shell. They were delivered with no tools to crack the shells or retrieve the lobster meat. Digging with a fork seemed useless but in a way I was glad the lobster was till in it's impenetrable shell; it protected it from being contaminated by the tangy-sour and glowingly artificial red BBQ sauce which stung the eye as much as the tongue. And being Chinatown, we certainly were treated to our well deserved happy ending. The sumptuous dessert consisted of a half-inch square of still mostly frozen cheescake/cookie pierced with a toothpick which held the single white grape on. MMMmmmmhmmm. And then, the generosity flowed when Chef Poons staff rushed out to clank onto our table a half glass of Cook's sparkling wine. So in the end we each paid $54 per person (in Chinatown!) for what we all agreed was our worst culinary experience to date. *Please note, the delay of this review is partially because this event predated my Yelp awareness and I had tried to suppress these memories. Forgetting is hard though since lately when my friends and I experience unpleasant meals or find ourselves greatly ripped off, we say we've been "Pooned". It's become a handy verb.

text: UPDATE: This has become my regular lunch spot. Everything on the menu is fan-freakin'-tastic. Last weekend, I enjoyed the Sashimi. It was incredibly fresh, flavorful and delicious. I just got back from CJ Palace today and, for the first time ever, I ordered the Crispy Beef lunch for $7.50. I swear to the Internet, this was the most divine Crispy Beef I have ever had the pleasure of consuming. I've had a lot of crispy beef in my day. It's always pretty good. But CJ Palace's version is above reproach. The beef was actually crispy without being crunchy. Somehow, they managed to cook the meat in such a way as to simulate a "pocky-like" exterior while maintaining a rich, juicy interior. The spices they chose for the beef were in perfect balance and filled me with a sense of serenity and purpose with each and every bite. I urge you all to seek out CJ Palace between the hours of 11:00am and 3:00pm and order the Crispy Beef Lunch with Fried Rice and Hot & Sour soup. Do it as soon as you can. You owe it to yourself. If you die without tasting this Crispy Beef, you will regret it. Your spirit will wander the earth, haunting the living and showing up on footage appearing courtesy of the SyFy Channel as moans of tormented hunger emanate from your spectral maw and invade the minds of your next of kin, filling them with the uncontrollable urge to drive or fly to Northern Nevada just so that they can retrieve the Crispy Beef that you neglected to enjoy in life and bring it to your grave so as to end your otherwise everlasting curse. So try it today! Old Review: This is the best lunch spot on the planet. First, let me emphasize that this place is a Chinese/Japanese restaurant. You can get delicious food from either cuisine here. While the sushi is great and all, this review is more about coming to the restaurant between the hours of 11am and 3pm to enjoy lunch. The Lunch portions are every bit as big as the dinner portions, just considerably cheaper. So when you choose to order off the Chinese Lunch Menu or a Lunch Priced Japanese Bento Box, you know that you're going to get full. Everything on the menu is wonderful! The Chinese dishes all come with your main entree, fried or steamed rice, an egg roll and a choice of either egg flower, hot & sour or miso soup. Allow me to take this opportunity to say that this place has the best Hot & Sour Soup in the US. You'd have to fly to China to top it. The Japanese Bento Boxes come with either Teriyaki Chicken, Teriyaki Steak, Teriyaki Salmon, Sesame Chicken or Tonkatsu (a delicious, succulent breaded pork cutlet with tangy sauce) as your main entree, a big, fresh, crunchy Japanese salad with a peanut sesame dressing and a California roll, some delicious sashimi or in the case of one Chicken Teriyaki Box, a serving of Charlie's Tuna. No matter what you choose here, you'll get full, the quality will please you, and you'll end up paying less than $10 per person. The staff is friendly and they remember your face. They're attentive, keeping your glasses full and your needs met. Just remember, if you want to enjoy the best part of CJ Palace by ordering one of their amazing Kung Pao dishes, you'll probably want to specify "extra spicy" as their standard fare dish is mild enough for small children to enjoy in comfort.

text: The quest for the great Philly Xiolóngbao, also known as soup dumpling, or my night out with my buddy Jim: First off, let me say that my friend Jim and I were poised for a huge let-down from this quest's first conception. In fact, he christened it the GXLBD2010 - or, the Great XiaoLongBao Disappointment of 2010. Our quest was to seek the soup dumpling in Philadelphia's China Town and to find a specimen worthy of our affection and loyalty. We had low expectations as he had previously dabbled in the dark arts of Philly soup dumpling quests and we both felt like we had already had the best soup dumpling on offer in the region in Flushing, Queens at a magic spot known as Nan Xiang where the soup dumplings are made by the hands of angels (http://newyork.seriouseats.com/2009/02/best-soup-dumplings-nan-xiang-xiao-long-bao-flushing-nyc.html). There had been some recent buzz around town, though, that Philly was now home to some spots offering some perfectly fine soup dumplings, so with doubt in our hearts and the memory of Nan Xiang driving us to find soup dumplings closer to home - we set out. It is important to explain what, in our opinion, a soup dumpling should be. It should be a delicate little bag of soup compromised of savory pork (or pork and crab - depending on which kind you order), which is all swimming in delicious broth encased in a delicate dumpling wrapper. The skin of the dumpling should not be too thick, but should be tough enough to contain the soup and meat. The meat to soup ratio is important as you don't want a dumpling that is dry, nor do you want just broth and no meat. The key is balance and you know when it is right. We decided that we would sample every pork soup dumpling we knew to be on offer in China town. We girded ourselves with a cocktail and set off to our first destination: Dim Sum Garden. We ordered the pork soup dumplings and a cucumber salad. The place itself is more cheery inside than one might expect given its location under the Market East "overpass" next to a bus depot. The décor was bright; all was clean and inviting. The tea was good, which we took as a positive omen of things to come. However, when the dumplings arrived, the wrappers were gummy and the insides had a bland pork meatball, not much broth, and some liquefied pork fat that we dubbed "meat goo." We decided that these soup dumplings were not horrible, but nothing in comparison to those on offer in Flushing. In addition, the cucumber salad had seeds in it and the salad was over-dressed in sesame oil and soy sauce. The pieces were unevenly chopped too, which is something that does not affect flavor but does belie the care that the kitchen takes with its ingredients. On a 1-10 scale - these dumplings got a score of 4. See my review of Sang Kee (http://www.yelp.com/biz/sang-kee-peking-duck-house-philadelphia-2#hrid:6clxlgVLTR-HljLTZUeeag) - our second stop. See my review for Sakura (http://www.yelp.com/bi...), which won by the way, for our last stop.

The hot dog is topped with mustard, onion, sweet pickle relish (usually a dyed neon green variety called "Nuclear Relish"), a dill pickle spear, tomato slices or wedges, pickled sport peppers, and a dash of celery salt; sometimes, but not always, cucumber slices." The cornucopia of flavors and textures will win you over. Cool, crisp, hot...all having a get down. The fine ladies at Hot Diggity Dogs do Chicago justice. She was completely unapologetic about our long wait. She handed us some menus and went to get some water for us. She didn't leave any silverware, so I had to steal some from another table. For an appetizer, we ordered the baked zucchini rolls, which came with a side of marinara sauce. These were actually very tasty. Definitely expensive, but unique and yummy nonetheless. For our pizza, we decided to go with the one with fingerling potatoes, parsnips, pancetta, parmaggiano, onion, and rosemary. The pizza came out pretty quickly, but as the waitress came over to bring it to us, she dropped half of it on the floor. Awesome. She apologized, and gave us the half that didn't drop while she went back to have another pizza made for us. The pizza itself wasn't too bad. I'm not a huge fan of thinner crusts, but this was decent. While the pizza was definitely unique, it was missing something. I don't know what. A hint of sweetness (maybe using a sweeter cheese or something? I'm no chef. I don't know!) would have been nice. It just sort of fell flat. All in all, this place gets a huge 'meh' from me. I've had better pizza elsewhere. I think I'll come back one day (I really want to try the pizza with the fontina and apples), but I don't know when that day will be. Everything was overly expensive, and it really wasn't a good value. If the food was excellent, I can easily overlook the high price, but it just wasn't.

text: How do I begin to sing praises in order to convey the fantasticness/fabulousness/ all the other Rachel Zoe jargon conveying amazingness that is Swap? I will take a gander. Ultimately, Swap has singlehandedly eliminated my need to ever go to Lakeside Mall or Canal place, and has given me the wonderful ability of clicking delete when I get a sale notice from Banana or J. Crew because I know I can get the item at Swap in the same condition for less money. First, the owner, Michelle, is fabulous. It is like she has read every how to make your employees and people around you respect and love you book on the market. Or maybe it's innate for her. I don't know. Michelle is a genuinely kind person, who signs every single one of her business' emails with every single store associates name. In a world of faceless corporations, that means a considerable amount. Swap discounts items on a schedule. I know they do at 30 and 60 days, so you can take a gamble and watch an item if you are in love. Swap has only been open for a little over two years, and nearly half of my wardrobe went to be consigned there and the other half has been rejuvenated by it. My finds include Theory shirt dresses for 15 dollars, silk Club Monaco skirts for under 30, Coach wallets and wristlets, Tory Burch clutches for under 100, a Guess red peacoat that was Blair Waldorf worthy for under 70, banana republic silk tops, etc. How did this happen you say? Michelle opened her store in a section of town that has wealthier liberal arts schools literally 2,500 feet away (tulane and loyola) and is wedged in a wealthier part of new orleans. So, an influx of a revolving market with a disposable income. Brilliant! She works her butt off to get the word out about her store to New Orleans' ladies who lunch who then bring their garmets here. (Thankfully) There is no hipster ridiculous pretentiousness here (Im lookin' at you Buffalo Exchange) and they are always kind when you consign your items. I have never been treated anything but wonderfully by Michelle and her crew. If you are in the area, make a point to stop here. Honestly, I would work here for free if it were legal, but well, we both know there are labor laws. note: sign up for store emails because Swap loves coupons as much as you budget fashionistas do, and they also have an ebay edition of their store.

text: If you're from the East Coast, like me, you probably only learned about bubble tea within, say, the past few years. Bubble tea is a tea drink, obviously -- although it's sometimes more of a fruit juice -- with little balls of tapioca floating around in the bottom, giving the beverage a fun and, according to one acquaintance, erotic texture. My favorite beverage in the Bubble House arsenal has always been the chai, with extra bubbles -- extra, err, eroticism? And my number one and number two items from the menu are: a) the Vietnamese hoagies, which once brought me to tears with their surprise peppers and b) the dumplings, which, admittedly, are hard for a restaurant to get terribly wrong, but they're also hard to get just right.

text: Fantastic! My husband and I had a wonderful anniversary meal here. We ordered the winter tasting menu, so we were able to sample most of the dishes that were on the menu that night. The highlights: Amuse-bouche: panko-crusted rabbit--I've never eaten rabbit before and now I'm sold. I could have eaten an entree portion. Soup: Creamy butternut squash with a beatifully seared scallop in the center was delicious enough, but hidden underneath the scallop was some sort of minced porcini mushroom sauce. YUM! Main entree: Venison tenderloin with a chestnut puree and baby brussel sprouts. I never knew that venison could taste like this. I could have licked my plate clean, but instead used their warm sweet-potato rolls to soak up every delicious drop. Our server was friendly and unpretencious, and her wine recommendation was great. Our dessert came with 'Happy Anniversary' written in chocolate across the plate. We sat in a half-circle booth, which is perfect for a romantic dinner. text: Ate here for lunch with some colleagues one day. It has a fun vibe, but what's the deal with Mexican places being "zany." It's like: you want pizza: you can go to a real pizza place or you can go to a "zany" pizza place (Chuck E. Cheese). This place (and so many other Mexican places) seem more like Chuck E. Cheese interpretations of the Mexican dining experience. I guess if I was here for a happy hour or a fun night out on the town, rather than a sober, margaritaless meal with work associates, I might have appreciated the decor more. Ah well, just one man's opinion. On to the food: I lived in Phoenix for a while so I'm probably a bit prejudiced in terms of what I want/expect from Mexican/Tex-Mex food. I want fresh tortillas, succulent juicy meat, and some kick - some caliente sabor! I had the chicken enchiladas and some sort of polenta fries. The enchiladas were a little too mild for my tastes (again, this is just my opinion -- you may find them just to your liking). The fries were crumbly dry and somewhat flavorless. I'd call them a total dud and I'd be surprised if they were still on the menu. Service was nice. The drinks were certainly tempting. And for lunch, we walked right in and got a table. So they get stars for all of those things, and I'll give them a pass on the general silliness of the place since it's really just a matter of personal preference/style, but they lose a few stars for ho hum cuisine. With so many other great places to dine in the city (including the many other S. Starr places that are way better), I don't think I'll go back.
label: NEG

text: Naked Chocolate Cafe is the Citys hallmark for all things chocolate. Center City location was excellent (theres now one in University City behind UPenns VanPelt Library). As you approach the cashier, you walk along the counter with all kinds of chocolate bonbons and confectioneries behind the glass case. It is a veritable chocolate wonderland. Whenever I go, I order a petite Aztec hot chocolate, European style. European style means the chocolate is served THICK, not watery. All their desserts look good, but Im not aware of any other place that sells nudos (think: firm cupcake, but pyramid shape). As such, thats what I order. If only they sold churros to compliment any of their European style chocolate, anyone who spent time in Spain would, without a doubt, BOLT towards Naked Chocolate like they do in Pamplonas running of the bulls. Whenever I visit friends who moved from Philly, I would bring them a box of chocolates from Naked Chocolate. The place can get crowded on Friday and Saturday nights and finding a table (especially for a group of four or more) can be a challenge. text: Imagine, if you will, a stay in a luxe hotel with wonderful linens, huge towels and high end toiletries in a room that exudes old world charm. Two nights in a row I awoke to water that, somehow, bubbled out of the toilet bowl onto the travertine floor of the bathroom. In addition to the toilet, on the second night, there was a black ring around the bathtub drain where gray water had backed up through the drain. On top of all of this, upon returning to my room in the evening after reporting the first unfortunate toilet incident (12 hours earlier), the room had not been touched by housekeeping. How could a hotel that prides itself on service allow this to happen in the first place? Yes, there is turn down service. Yes, the public rooms are the grandest in Philadelphia. Yes, I was offered to change rooms. Although the staff comped my breakfast, that was all that was offered. Alas, I shall NEVER return to the Bellevue.

text: There are several locations of this store, but the one I'm most familiar with is the Wesley Chapel location. Half of this mart resembles a Whole Foods organic shopping center, and the other half is just plain...strange. The side that has the organic and free trade food is pretty impressive in its selection. It definitely serves a previously unserved need in this area, as the regular grocery stores typically have a poor selection of organics. In my opinion, this is Nutrition S'Mart's best feature. Now, as for the OTHER half of the store...the shelves are chock full of questionable nutritional supplements, new age/alternative health books, some sort of stage where presentations take place, homeopathic remedies, new age CD's, and a mish-mash of many other new age snake oil products. I'm definitely not saying that NONE of it works; perhaps some people find benefit in these sorts of products, and in this market people can purchase whatever they wish. It just seems very questionable to me to see this strange assortment of tacky, flea market magical potions and solvents that doesn't seem to blend well with the other half of the store at all. If Nutrition S'Mart got rid of the new age clutter and just expanded the grocery section, I'd like it even more. But it seems this store has an identity crisis. They need to figure out if they want to market upscale organic groceries, or be a new-age bookstore and trinket shop. It's just a little too strange when they try to be both.

text: The whole place is one big mellow vibe. As one sales person in a surf shop once said, "I can't complain. I live where people come to vacation." We've been coming to Carpinteria State Beach for years. It's our regular for getting away since it's close enough to the SF Bay Area and south enough for the water to start getting warm. We bodyboard and there's usually something that you can ride, whether it's stand-and-drop or paddle to catch a wave. In the summer, I've been able to wear a shortie and even just a vest. Most of the time, though, we're so cold-blooded that we need full suits since we're in the water for a while. Definitely more comfortable though than Santa Cruz area, closer to home. It seems to be warmest in the summer and early fall. So, Labor Day get aways are warmer than Memorial Day. One thing that can be a funky is that sometimes there are small oil slicks and you'll get tar stuck on stuff out in the water. It's minor, but some people kind of freak out over it. Local hotels have little tar removal packets. After spending the morning playing around in the water, call in a to-go order at The Spot. Pick it up and chow down on the beach. See the envy in the kids eyes who have their nutritious, but less fun whatevers. Here's a video of dolphins, present a lot of the time, feeding pretty close to the shore: http://www.flickr.com/photos/47079906@N00/3621106700/

text: If I could give Gentle Ben's less than one star I would. The food is bland and the service is horrible. I went on a game day with some friends and had to wait about 30 minutes just to get a glass of water. When I finally got it, it tasted faintly like beer, making me wonder a bit about the cleanliness of the restaurant. For my meal I ordered a Western BBQ burger with chicken instead of beef and got my food about 40 minutes after ordering (drinks other than water didn't come until about 5 mins after this). The chicken was flavorless, the bacon was pure fat and was hardly cooked, and the BBQ sauce that was supposed to come with the sandwich was absent. Additionally, I had upgraded my fries from the original seasoned to the beer battered, but this part of my order was screwed up as well. I informed my waiter of the problems and he brought me my BBQ sauce and the correct fries, but took his time in doing so. By the time he brought it my food was barely warm. A friend of mine ordered chicken tenders with ranch, but was never given the ranch. She barely touched her food because the chicken was so dry that the ranch was absolutely necessary. She asked the waiter for it three different times, but was ignored each time. She finally went up to talk to someone at the bar and got her ranch about 5 minutes later and by this time everyone else in our party had finished their meals. My party talked to the manager about the issues we were having so he was aware of what was going on and talked down to us and treated us like children. We were not compensated in any way for what had happened and we didn't even get an apology. Epic fail. To top off this splendid evening at Gentle Ben's, the bathrooms were absolutely repulsive. Only one toilet in the women's restroom was working so there was a line of about 6 people. The floor was wet and sticky, the toilet was dirty, and the only water coming out of the faucet was scalding hot. I've been in port-o-potties nicer than this. All in all, this was not a good dining experience for me or any of my six friends. I had been to Gentle Ben's a few times before and wasn't in love with it and after this I can assure you that I will never go back. Get your act together, Gentle Ben's.

text: Maybe if I had under developed taste buds like a child, I would have liked this place. Too much stuff going on everywhere. If I was stoned it would have freaked me out big time. I have been to many other Italian restaurants, that had the essence of Italy, without literally bringing Italy into the restaurant. Enough on that part. The place was a ghost town so seats were plentiful. This place can accomodate a large number of people, which is good, because it seems to be a family style restaurant. The menu has a variety of dishes, which I really didn't focus too much on since most of the dishes on the menu are for families. A small will feed like 2-3 people and large dishes feeds 4+. There is a small section for individual sized dishes, which I ordered from. Nothing was too exciting, so I ordered the spaghetti and meatball. The drink menu had wines and a few cocktails. The beer list had the usual players, Heineken, Corona etc. Blah Blah. When we got our dishes, mine was exactly as it said. Spaghetti with "Meatball." One giant meatball on top of pasta. Thrilling. The meatball was so fresh. No taste at all. Not enough salt or pepper could put spice into the sauce or the meatball. I was so "under"-whelmed. Service was good. Although we were one of the only people in the restaurant at a late hour, our waiter was very pleasant and attentive. Forgettable food from an unforgettably, visually stimulating restaurant.

text: Usually at 11 AM I'm in the middle of my REM cycle, but when in Philadelphia and awake for brunch, I dine at XIX. This prix fixe lunch is all you could ask for, and features a fabulous buffet of "things" for people who eat. Since I don't, I just like to stare at the food and imagine what it would taste like in my mouth. The first time I saw the sign for XIX outside the Bellevue on Walnut and South, I thought it was a help group for cross-eyed drunks with huge noses. And since I was looking for a Jewish husband, the first word out of my mouth was "oh my God!" When I got up to the 19th floor, sat down at a random table, and started to pour out my life story of drugs, booze, and my celebrity boxing tragedy against Judge Judy, I'd caused a whole table of 90-year old socialites to go into cardiac arrest. And that is how I became the single-most mass murderer in American history. My fave thing about XIX is that not only is the name in Roman, but the food is also Roman. How do I know it's Roman? Because one time in Milan I had a really bad trip, and found myself surrounded by towel-wearing men, manchego cheese, and cold cuts that looked surprisingly like the ones in the XIX buffet. Or maybe that was just my last trip to the bath house. I forget. I can't keep track of my sex life any more than I can keep track of my social security number. Hence why I'm always making up a new one every time AmEx cancels one of my cards. If you're scared of heights, XIX is enclosed by walls and windows, and has the most fabulous views of the downtown. The architects basically designed the view so you can't see any poor people, which is perfect for me. Poor people make me lose my appetite. I have a whole slideshow of street bums that I'll look at to control weight gain. hEllO, it's like the new thing in dieting. Competition for the brunch/lunch scene is fierce on Walnut Street, and if anyone knows anything about the word fiErcE, it's me. XIX is high-end, sexy, and aside from being a wonderful lunch spot it's also a cute place for drinks and date nights. Also, if your date is going less-than-perfect (i.e. he suggests you "split the bill"), you should know that there are no bathrooms on the same floor as XIX, which means you need to take the elevator; hint hint, hitting that Lobby button is far too easy after "excusing yourself" to the ladies room. For a trendy lunch spot and some delish Roman food, try XIX. And ladies/gay men: don't forget about the elevator. This restaurant is totally designed for bailing on a bad date. If I were you, I'd schedule a bad date just to experience the architectural bail-out masterpiece. Speaking of which, I'm on EHarmony right now... This has been a Review by Fulgencio

text: Dined here 6 June 2009. Total for 2 with tax was $186.90 (tip extra) but that included an overcharge. The two us arrived without reservations on a Saturday night around 6:00 and left at 8:30. They were able to seat us immediately, unfortunately adjacent to the piano in the middle of the room, the location of the piano not only obscures vision within the room but we had trouble hearing each other and it was a distraction. The room itself is very comfortable, and has has great ambiance - with the brick, and wood available in this old "Boardwalk" location. Perfect for those special dinners or romantic evenings. Dress up or dress business casual. Not a spot for small children - and I would not want that given this is positioned as upscale dinning with a price point to match. That said we were there simply to eat and waited months after its grand opening to allow them time to polish the rough edges of the operations. The restaurant was busy and I would say that by 7:30 and as we left every table was taken. Our server for the night was a youthful young man, and was accommodating through the night. Asked if we wished to order a drink - we advised we would look through the wine list while deciding what we would order simultaneously. Although we are very familiar French, Italian and Spanish wines, we confessed to the waiter that we are limited knowledge or Portuguese wines. Sabor does not have a Sommelier on staff (or even for core weekend night hours). We knew we wanted a full bodied red - and he suggested a 2006 Cortes de Cima Chamine (Alentejano) ($43). This is of course a Tempranillo with a dark intense red colour with red berry fruit aroma and some smoky notes. Over all easily drinkable and a good choice for this evening and familiar to us as we often enjoy great Spanish Tempranillo. We started with the Algarve fish soup ($12 each). The soup was highly flavourful with a rich fish broth with a moderate amount of fish. It arrived hot and in a nice sized & shaped bowl of 8-10 oz. Following soup we enjoyed a rather large plate of Charcutaria for 2 persons ($24) which contained a selection of cured meats, cheeses, pate, marinated vegetables. This was very enjoyable, and with the fresh bread served would be an adequate meal with the soup. We might have stopped right there - and should have in hindsight, but we wanted to try the main dishes to see what the kitchen could so. My partner ordered a medium rare Steak and Frites ($39) which is a grilled 12oz. rib eye steak, home cut fries, green peppercorn cream sauce. He thought it flavourful and I thought it was medium not medium rare and so covered in sauce it was impossible to tell how it was prepared. I did not have a great experience with my first choice. I ordered the Broiled Octopus ($28) flame broiled octopus, roasted red peppers, onions, garlic, olive oil, black olives. It arrived a colourful-sight to the eyes, but the octopus was extremely tuff. These were 3 pieces and the thickness of a big mans thumb and 4 in. in length. They had been grilled, sear marks were evident. I eat octopus often and in fact had octopus the week before at a Chinese restaurant that was similar thickness size and it was extremely tender. Of course the Chinese restaurant serves many many pounds of this a day and all fresh. I concluded it was previously frozen and hence tough as leather. I sent it back as unacceptable and ordered a salt cod fish dish ($28). This dish was very good, flavourful and pleasing to the eye. The server advised it was the most popular dish ordered. We did not try dessert as we simply could not eat more. We were charged for the entree we returned (or part of it?), and only discovered this later that evening (we trusted the server had removed it as he said he would). My partner looked at the bill but did not pick up on the overcharge. To tell us there would be no problem and then charge us is a little nervy to say the least. We will speak to the Manager when we have a moment to seek a credit. To be fair though this is how we rate this place: Dining Room: 7/10, Service: 5/10, Wine List: 4/10, Food: 6/10,(Soup 8/10) Prices: $$$+ steep for the calibre of this restaurant. Soup for Two: $24, Charcutaria: $24, Entrees: $39 $28, Wine: $43. Total: 158. CC Slip: 178.00 before Tax and Tip - so overcharge is $20.00 Tax was: 8.90 tip was extra.

text: Emeril's didn't just serve Nova and I the best meal we had in New Orleans. It served us the best meal we've had all year. I started out with a Cajun-style gumbo, which was rich and hearty. Nova was equally pleased with her starter, the barbeque shrimp. The shrimp were plump and plentiful. In fact, this app offered more shrimp than the more expensive shrimp and grits entree Nova had at Lüke a few nights before. When it came to our mains, we continued to be impressed. I ordered what I've affectionately dubbed 'beef with a side of beef,' a large plate that paired a perfectly cooked filet with a delicious shepherd's pie filled with tangy BBQ shortribs. It was total overkill and I loved every bite. Nova, on the other hand, ordered a butterflied pork chop with a green mole glaze, which was accompanied by a heaping of sweet potatoes. She enjoyed this dish as much as enjoyed mine, which was evidenced from both of us cleaning our plates. After this indulgent meal, we hardly had room for dessert. Wanting a little something sweet, we choose to split the chocolate peanut butter pie with an Oreo crust. It was just as decadent as the rest of our meal. And to think, we almost didn't come here at all. We originally had reservations at Domenica, but considering our disappointment with Lüke, we didn't want to give our money over to another John Besh restaurant. When searching online for replacement options, I stumbled upon a recent NYT article praising Emeril's as the "best meal that had in New Orleans." It was certainly was ours. In fact, the only thing I'd knock was the service. Emeril's employs a team of servers for every table and it came pretty apparent early on that our group wasn't coordinating with each other. Still, the food was so good, the hiccupping service really didn't bother me that much. Just plan to be there a while.

text: I came here in May of 2007, however, since I listed it as my "last meal on earth", I only thought it fair to write a review. A friend I was visiting in Philly suggested that we dine here one evening. I had no idea what to expect, but as a Francophile, I was excited to indulge in a classical French degustation menu. So the four of us enter the exquisite Parisian salon which consists of 2 floors, completely candle-lit tables, chandeliers, and a fireplace. I'm a sucker for an intimate, romantic ambiance so I already like this place upon first sight. I don't remember exact details, however I am reminded of the impeccable service which included a team of waiters who tended to the four of us in synchronized gestures. For each dish that was presented, they would lay the covered silver platters in front of us, and simultaneously lift the covers to expose an art display of French cuisine. The team of waiters would also walk together in a uniform line to/from the kitchen. At one point, I excused myself to use the restroom, and "my waiter" lifted my napkin off my lap, set it on the table, and walked me to the restroom... and if that wasn't enough, he patiently waited right outside the door! I still remember coming out of the restroom, a shock of surprise filling my every emotion, and then thinking, "what if I was in there for a really long time doing you know what?" He then walked me back to our table, pulled out my seat, and set the napkin back on my lap. Okay, so the FOOD... OMG!!! French orgasmic... to say the least! The dining experience here involves a prix fixe dinner of either a 6 course menu or 10 course menu written in French. I am now just recalling the foie gras with black truffle sauce and it's buttery consistency just melting in my mouth! Yummm! After dinner, the waiters rolled out a cart with an array of cheeses. One of the wonderful things about this place was that one of the members of our party is vegan and my fiance doesn't eat red meat... yet the chef catered to them with specially prepared dishes. Oh, and the DESSERT!!! When that famous all-you-can-eat dessert cart rolled out... I had to grip onto the arms of my chair to prevent myself from doing the "happy-dessert dance". It really is "all you can eat"... meaning you can sample as many beautifully-created tarts and fluffy cakes as you want! Then you are romanced with a platter of petit fours!!! I felt like Marie Antoinette surrounded by Alice in Wonderland pastries! I was in heaven! Complètement magnifique! A couple of things to note: Some might say the dress code is business casual... but I would lean towards the dressy/formal side. There are so many cougars in this place you feel like you are at a zoo. The dining experience can extend to some hours so prepare for a late night there. If you are comfortable spending money on fine dining, then you will have no problem when the bill comes. Some say it's overpriced, too expensive... but let's admit - it's all relative. (For the four of us, our bill was just over $800, excluding tip. However, we ordered cocktails to begin the night as oppose to a bottle of wine or two, so prepare for a more expensive check if you're ordering wine.)

So I was very excited to see a dermatologist for some medication for my mild acne and just to ask few questions. The receptionist was polite as was the young lady that brought me to the exam room. And what's a zep? It's pure heaven, that's what it is. Or hell, if you care about cholesterol and longevity. A zep is simply a sandwich on a Conshohocken round roll that's jam packed with cold cuts, cheese, condiments, etc. I had the cheesesteak zep which, if my doctor was there, would have ordered an angioplasty on the spot. A cheesesteak WITH cold cuts between the bun. Man was it good. Lou's also serves breakfast, but I've never had it. The zeps are just too tasty. Inexpensive, a lot of local Norristown flavor, and honest food that will lead you to an early grave, this is a must! What, you want to live forever??

The koobedeh came on a very generous pile of rice, and came with two large grilled jalapenos and one whole grilled roma tomato. The koobedeh was spongey, oily, and bland. The rice was flavorful though. It also came with 3 large slices of "naan". This was not the wonderfully blistery chewy naan I've come to expect, but basic flatbread that I suspect was not housemade. The rice pudding was a gelatinous sweet mass sprinkled with cinnamon and slivered almonds.
