text: I wish Center City would get a decent movie theater, so I don't have to go to the forbidden suburbs to see a big budget movie. We all know that the Columbus Blvd theater isn't an option and The Bridge on Penn's campus is usually crowded and filled with rowdy college students. So Cherry Hill Loews it is. The denizens are of typical suburban fare, teenagers and couples out on date night. The ticket kiosks are a plus, as they make the area when you first walk in less crowded. But there always seems to be a line at the concession stand where a pimply-faced teenager is haphazardly scooping your popcorn. And the popcorn is horrible! Most times it is stale and too salty to begin with. Please, Center City Philadelphia, I beg of you, get a decent theater! Stat!
label: NEG

text: We decided to visit Chinatown on a Sunday to find some breakfast. There were not many choices for breakfast in the Reading Terminal Market. We walked into KC's Pastries and picked the peanut butter with mochi bread, coconut pineapple bread and a slice of mocha roll. The bread was soft and not overly sweet, better than some of the bakeries in Taipei and better than any of the Asian pastry shops I tried in the DC area. For 80 cents each, the bread was a bargain. In the DC area, it would cost anywhere from $1.10 to $1.65 each. There was a lot of mochi/coconut inside of the bread. The pineapple crust on top of the bread was really delicious, too. The mocha roll was very disappointing. It did not have any coffee taste, not sweet at all and there was too much cream. Since the cream had no taste, it tasted a bit like soften butter (in a bad way). We went back and bought six more bread (3 sweet and 3 savory). We loved the sweet buns but did not care for any of the savory ones (we got staty beef, roasted pork, curry chicken). The bubble tea seemed very popular here, but I didn't get a chance to try.
label: POS

text: This place should be ashamed of themselves. If they were in ANY other location other than the absolutely dying Chestnut Hill Area they would be out of business. But since Chestnut Hill is dying, and they are one of the few remainig restaurants, they will still be packed, just bc it's Chestnut Hill. Both were enormous (we had to get to-go boxes for our sandwiches) and included a delicious cookie and salad. I was impressed with the friendliness of the staff and the size of their portions. Great place for lunch to sit outside on a nice day. Highly recommended.

text: Who knew St. Louis could be so hip? The Grove area has it going on these days - first a giant sign that now lets you know exactly the name of their 'hood, now a bicycle-friendly bar! Seems like our fair city is starting to keep up with the rest of the world... Stopped in Handle Bar for a quick drink with a gal pal the other night. It was empty inside, but I got here right at 5 pm. In addition to cheap drafts during happy hour, they also have a "Bartender's Special" - that night it was Guinness. I wasn't having it, but I know we have some yelpers out there who are fans. I tried the Six Row Whale - MAN! That's some good beer! Had I not had other plans that night, I would have been content sitting at that bar and drinking myself silly with Whale beer. My companion and I tried to order an appetizer, but the kitchen wasn't opening until 6. And about the time we were packing up, our cute little bartender brought us a plate of hummus. I felt terrible 'case we didn't have time to eat it, but I'm thinking she was able to put it to good use (i.e., her tummy). Come check out this cool bar! It's in a great STL area, the drinks are cheap, the staff is nice and they care about the planet. What more do you want, people?

text: This place is okay, but I think that I was expecting a whole lot more since it's mentioned so extensively as a must go to place for anyone visiting Santa Barbara. I think that it's worth a look, but I wouldn't say that you need to allocate a lot of time for this visit. Other than the wharf itself, there are some seafood restaurants and small shops. I wouldn't say that Stearns Wharf is disappointing, but I do think that it's overhyped.

text: Holy moly wow!!! What an amazing cupcake find!! The outside looks like a clothing store, and the inside is very unique.The store is set up really cool with the cupcakes in cabinets, so it gives this real boutiquey feel . The sweet potato cupcake with pecans and cream cheese frosting was to die for!!! The plain buttercream was divine as well. I really wanted to try the red velvet, but they were sold out. It's very cramped in here spacewise, and they don't accept credit/debit cards either. They're pricey, too, so I would definitely only go here for a special, special occasion. A dozen cupcakes would run over $30.
label: POS

text: Today, I ventured out to see what all the gossip was about in Chef Garces new establishment. Upon arrival, we were greeted by a very attentitive staff who seated us immediately. Bread and water arrived within seconds of being seated. We started with the margehrita pizza. The crust was tissue thin but the copious amount of salt added to the crust destroyed the taste and ruined the pizza. Next was the potato and leek soup with seared sea scallops. This was absolutely perfect! The soup was delicate with a superb consistency and the scallops were seared to perfection. Our next dish was a pasta course which was made fresh on location. We enjoyed the lamb ragu and fusilli with poached egg. Both pastas were 16 to 18 dollars but left us feeling very short changed. At this price, the portions could definitely be a bit heartier. Each pasta was delicious but not an absolute for the budget conscious consumer. Dessert featured an assortment of cookies and French pressed coffee. Both were reasonablly priced and complimented one another wonderfully. We were able to get a 4 top table but those who came in later during the lunch rush were seated at 6 and 8 top tables that already had other customers seated there. So you maybe bumping elbows with other customers while eating during high volume times.
label: POS

text: The Gallery is a funny place. It's bizarro mall that doesn't have the store you know, it has a store that is the other-world equivalent of it. So, instead of Gap, it has Net. All of these stores are technically boutique stores in that they are the only location of this store but are in mall-store clothing. Weird... It also has a EB Games and a Gamestop, which are the same company and, yet, not viewed as redundant. What I dislike about this place is that it closes at 7 on Saturday. I know that this is to keep the roaming gangs of kids from gaining too much momentum and causing all kinds of trouble but, still, 7? Really? I guess it says what kind of place when it's cornerstone stores are Kmart, Burlington Coat Factory, and Old Navy.

text: The heat finally lifted last night and the weather was way too gorgeous to drink inside... But rather than hitting up Sasha's (an old standby), I said to the boy: "What about that beer garden on Leona? You know, that little hole in the wall bar?" He had no idea what I was talking about. (Typical.) I'd never been there before, but had driven by a few times -- and always knew it would be my type of place. Boy, is it ever. The "beer garden" is basically a backyard with a nice white picket fence around it, filled with picnic tables. Why do people dine here? *****UPDATE: Since this last review, I have eaten here once and added one star to the review. text: I work up in Zionsville, and this place has become one of my favorite local barbecue joints over the past few years. That lovely aroma mixes with the sounds of classic Chicago blues music as you walk inside. It's a cozy, friendly place (though service is often slow) and an excellent place to go with friends, family or more laid-back clients for a meal. The meat has just the right amount of smoke to it, and I often have a tough time deciding between the pulled pork or beef brisket, which are both good. And, if I've got a real appetite, you know I will be going for the rib tips lunch special, which is available all week. As an appetizer, the Brunswick Stew is a nice choice--kind of a spicy, dark broth with chunks of pulled pork and tomatoes in it. And, as the young lady above said, it's mighty hard to forgo the fried biscuits and apple butter--a longstanding Hoosier delicacy. I really have not found many foods I don't like there. Everything I've had has been good. However, if any of you subsequent reviewers end up trying the deep-fried ribs, please post something about it. text: So every so often I return to Indianapolis to visit family, and every time I experience severe culture shock. Yes, I truly belong in LA. First, I'll forgive this place for sporting a truly uninspired name. That said, there wasn't much to praise about this place. We arrive, a party of 5. Not an unusual number for a restaurant, no? Well the hostess wants to simply put a 5th chair on the end of a table for 4...and there would have been no room for us to all fit, legs under the table where they belong. An empty table set for 6 is next to the too-small table, and we inquire about using that one. No, the table that is set for six is used for parties of 7 to 8. Yeah I don't get that either, but 15 minutes later the hostess got 3 other people to put 2 other tables together to accommodate us. The place was almost empty, mind you. The table ordered a cornbread skillet to share. While it tasted good, this is way too much food. Seriously, it was like a cornbread birthday cake sliced for 6 slices. Huge. Our party had some serious eaters in it, yet quite a bit went to waste. Simply too much food. My father ordered a salad. It was not what I would call a salad, as it had one long piece of romaine lettuce on it and then some meat. Gross, and definitely a ripoff. Entrees were a mixed bag. While I cannot recall the exact names, the following dishes were ordered: 1) Hot pot fish (x2) 2) Brisket 3) Ribeye** 4) Spicy Penne in a Light Creamy Vodka sauce with chicken Hot pot fish was well-liked. Really good according to the two ladies who had it. My father ordered the ribeye, and he thought it was good, but "adequate." Nothing groundbreaking here, but nothing glaring, either. The brisket was universally panned. Brisket is supposed to be slow-cooked, imparting a very tender, melt-in-your-mouth texture. This "brisket" was deemed to really be sliced pot roast, as it was dry and chewy. The diner and his wife (she had a bite) were not happy. The penne ala vodka with chicken was also not what actually came out. There was no cream added to the sauce at all. This was straight-up red marinara sauce, not the classic pink sauce one would expect from a penne ala vodka dish. It was edible, but not what was ordered. Penne was really small in diameter, a little over-cooked, and the chicken was super dry. The sauce was NOT a "light creamy vodka sauce" as advertised, and instead was a marinara sauce. It wasn't awful, but had I known what I would be served, I would have ordered something else. Note on entrees: if you want to split an entree, they charge you $5+ to split. This is outrageous, even in Los Angeles (it happens, but it's not really common). This place is not of a caliber where this would be expected, and it reeked of pretension. For dessert, several bread puddings were ordered and split. No one was wowed; this is very average bread pudding. It had caramel drizzle on top, and it is honestly too sweet. The whipped cream on the side was loaded with confectioner's sugar and was deemed inedible by everyone. Each order of bread pudding was split by 2 people, though not one plate was finished more than 50%. This portion size was more out-of-control than the cornbread skillet. I don't like places that charge super high prices for mediocre-at-best food, while serving so much of it that much goes to waste. NO ONE could eat the portions at this restaurant as part of a healthy diet. This is also not health food. text: Bar Tonique is easily my favorite bar in the French Quarter. Even though elements of the décor are modern, it seems well-suited to the neighborhood; maybe it is the dark, exposed brick and chalkboard menus that make Bar Tonique seem more rustic than fancy? It definitely has a laid back, casual vibe. Bar Tonique specializes in making well-crafted cocktails using quality ingredients such as fresh squeezed juices and house-made tonic water and ginger beer. On my last visit, the bartender discussed the several different types of house-made simple syrups and when/why you would use each one. Some people may find Bar Tonique's menu easier to negotiate as it is inclusive of many classic cocktails (with a few updated versions). This summer I enjoyed a Blanche Dubois on several occasions, a delightful combination of strawberries, mint, Death's Door Gin, Senor Curacao, house-made orgeat, and lemon juice (this is a seasonal drink but it's also listed under punches on the menu). If you are not a diehard cocktail fan, never fear-- Bar Tonique carries an eclectic selection of wine and beer. One of my favorite things about Bar Tonique is the daily special, for example Thursday features half-price cairpirinhas. Earlier this summer on a Friday, I enjoyed several servings of a $5 punch, a version of a pisco punch made with pineapple. Not only was it delicious, but it was also a great way to try something I normally wouldn't. The only drawback (for me) is that Bar Tonique is not convenient to my house. While I like it *almost* as much as Cure, Cure's location wins every time. If you love cocktails and are in (or near) the French Quarter, you should check out Bar Tonique.

When we arrived the line was long, as we had expected but surprisingly moved pretty quick (almost half the time the staff had anticipated). The menu features many unique burgers including the LA (avocado, watercrest), the Napa Valley (goat cheese, lemon honey mustard), & of course... the Philadelphia (cheese whiz, onions, hot peppers). I ordered the Classic but forgot to get it crunchified! But the un-crunchified burger did not disappoint, along with the fries and onion rings that were equally delicious. They offer an array of sauce options as well: the standard ketchup & mustard, plus chipotle ketchup, jalapeno relish, & burger sauce. You're also suppose to get a side of "fry sauce" but for some reason they forgot to give us some. Service was pretty quick & the staff was consistently friendly (sometimes too friendly). The decor of this place is awesome. It's not trying to hard to be fancy nor is it overly cheesy. Although it is a bit overwhelming with it's tall ceilings and excessive floor space. It almost looks more like a cool bar rather then a restaurant. All in all I highly recommend BBP. Bring a friend & an appetite and you're good to go.

text: When friends from other cities come to visit, they often make note of how many people on bikes they see. It's quite simple, really. Faced with one of the worst public transportation systems in the world, why would you not want a bicycle? I know it's made me more of a bike enthusiast. Most subway stations are disgusting. Buses are often late, or don't come at all. Prices keep rising, but quality does not. Now, I know they're poorly funded - surprising with Rendell as governor - but come on, guys. I will say one thing - since moving to West Philly, all routes in and out of here are surprisingly reliable - the 21 and 42 buses I've never had a problem with, and the trolleys are all right. Service in and out of South Philly, however, can be a different story. Sometimes, the 23 bus would never show up. And the 47 bus was always way overcrowded - not sure why they don't add an additional part to that bus like other routes to North Philly (the 33, the 57, etc). Riding SEPTA is always a gamble.

text: I'm surprised by the Yelpers who think this place is overpriced. A dinner for two, stuffing ourselves on sushi, usually comes out to about $40. For good sushi in the Midwest I don't think that's unreasonable. The rolls here are mostly delicious. My friend and I don't go for tuna, which makes us unusual in the sushi world, but there is such a variety of rolls here it doesn't matter. The Wasabi Special, Washington Avenue, Alaska Roll, and the new Yummy Roll are all favorites. Hurricane is tasty but has a bit of a fishy taste from the crawfish. If you like crawfish you should be fine but if you're not a fan, beware! you can definitely taste it. Service is fast, the rolls are the right size (not the supersized ridiculous rolls some places serve, but big enough to please), and the quality is consistently good. Service is fine - they keep our glasses full, but don't hover. Atmosphere is nice in a town rife with dives, chains, and noisy family restaurants. The best recommendation I can give is that I dine here at least twice a month, or else I start craving it!

text: Pat's IS the quintessential cheesesteak joint in Philly. Whenever one of my friends even utters the word "Pat's" I usually just put my shoes on because we're going. We've gotten to the point where we'll just look at each other and say, "You know where we SHOULD go..." Winter, summer, spring, or fall - it is my understanding this place is open 24/7. No questions asked. There's usually a line at 3:00 a.m. and my brother bought one at 8:30 a.m. once on his way to a business meeting. Yummy any time of day. Geno's is across the street, and they apparently make a very similar steak, but I refuse to eat one. The line at Pat's is always longer, so that must mean it's better, right? We've dubbed Geno's "The Circus" due to their over zealous neon lights. It's ridiculous, actually. There's a homeless guy who wonders around Pat's cleaning up and giving people napkins if they need them. He's awesome. We usually give him a couple bucks. Don't be nervous. He's polite and friendly. The steaks: Order a heart attack. It's Whiz, provolone and American cheeses. It's delicious. The rolls are on the softer side, and the cheese and grease will drip so exercise caution. My friend always orders a "pizza pepper with" that has hot peppers and pizza sauce. He loves it. They have a few specialty steaks like that one on the menu, but you should really go with something standard like a "whiz with" for your first time. Steaks are like $6 or $7 these days. My brother decided he was going to eat five heart attacks in one sitting. It was December. I left after he put three down because I was freezing my ass off. (The seating is all outside.) He ate five, didn't swallow the last bite til he was going over the Ben Franklin Bridge. I don't think he returned for over one year. The cheese fries are bangin'. Order EXTRA cheese fries and get the "swimmers" at the bottom using a fork. So much cheese. So much delicious. After years of Coke products, they recently switched to Pepsi. I was sorta upset but I'm over it now. They still have a good variety of sodas to choose from. You can bring your own bottle of water or something. No big deal. Be discreet if you are drinking alcohol. I'm pretty sure it's illegal. Bottom line, Pat's is the place you should go if you are from out of town and want to get the "Philly cheesesteak" experience.

text: A friend recommended this place to me, so on my last business trip to the area, I went out with some coworkers and other random folks. It's a pretty standard brewpub as far as decor goes (lots of wood, dark enough to be a steakhouse, visible brew kettles, etc.) with a huge lean towards the sports theme. Service was good, especially considering we were a large party later in the week. The waiter was quick, and on the ball with recommendations and such. The food was. . . well, ignore the haters. The food was pretty good for what it is. I don't expect a brewpub to have the variety and imagination of a tapas place or "fusion". I expect bar foods and other traditional American grub, and I expect them done well. And yes, kids, they did that just fine. The jerk wings were good but not great, however, the volcano sauce (or whatever they called it) you could get on the side made up for that. Hot enough for my nearly dead taste buds, and yet still tasty. I had a pasta dish with chicken that fit the bill of comfort food to have with a beer, and it was spot on. As a note, when they tell you the portions here are big -- especially with the pasta dishes -- the are NOT kidding. I am not a small man, and I still had enough for two meals, and that was without the breadstick. And to save the best for last. . . the beer. It IS a brewpub, and this is why my friend sent me. Holy hell, the beer was good. I had a decent IPA, and a sip of a friend's raspberry wheat that were damn good. The real kicker, however, was the oatmeal stout they'd literally just tapped earlier that day. It was a special deal that they made in a small batch and served at room temperature. That one was good enough to put in my personal Pantheon with beers from Dogfish Head and Stone. It's been months, and I'm still sad I didn't have an empty growler in the car. So yeah, I'm totally going back when I have to go up again for work. I totally dug this place. ~EEE~

text: I've lived five blocks from this amazing Music school for over a year and never once attended any of their free concerts. Well, now that I'm over that first step, you can expect to find me back here again and again. Every week there are a variety of concerts held in their very own Field Concert Hall located inside their beautiful old building on the eastern side of Rittenhouse Square. The term I should use is actually "recital" and not "concert" because for the most part, the free performances you are seeing are either student or faculty recitals. There is definitely a more casual aire when you enter the theater as you can tell from the attire of the audience from suits to skater garb replete with long-board sitting under their seat. Also, the performers often have a more informal relationship with the audience, addressing them sometimes between sets or to add a few remarks about the pieces they play. And it's hard as a performer to hide from anyone in this intimate concert hall. At my count I would say there are about 265 seats. The stage is raised high enough so that the person in front of you isn't completely blocking your view. As a room, it is (to my ear) perfectly silent when all is still. There is very little echo and the sounds that emanate from the instruments ring true and clear. Take the time to stand at intermission as the seats are cushion, but not that comfortable. For evening concerts, I would advise showing up at least 20 minutes ahead of time to get a decent seat. If you want to view -- for example -- the piano players hands, you'll need to get there earlier to get a seat in direct line with the performer. If you have a moment, step inside the building as it is a well preserved model of the architecture of its time (late 19th Century). Full concert schedules are available and up-to-date on their website.

But the good news is - the sushi doesn't make you gain weight.... because my two mediocre rolls cost me $38, and I threw up when I got that bill. text: Right off the bat, this review is more so about the way this theater is mismanaged than it is a review of the theater itself. First, let's talk about the theater. It is a truly beautiful facility inside. I absolutely love the decor and style. It is a unique fixture on a street that I wish could find a way to jump start. Even though it seems to have cost a ton to restore, I think it was worth it (one could however, provide a reasonable argument otherwise). In the decade or so that I have lived in Tucson, it showed me that at least some things could find a way to reach completion (Rio Nuevo anyone??). Another plus is that they sell Nimbus Beer. Nice to see them vending local brew. Also, the staff really does seem to try to be helpful, courteous, and professional. At least that was the feeling I got from the handful of shows I have seen here. That all said, there really are no good shows that come to this theater. It is simply not used for live performances as much as it should be. Instead, it is a glorified movie theater for re-airing old classics. Yeah, this has it's place, but really, why spend that much money restoring a theater to only really use it more or less as a clubhouse for you and your aging friends to "relive the glory days" of theater. And that, sadly, seems to be what the committee that operates the Fox is intent on doing. I believe they have fallen into the fear that if they allow live acts to dominate the stage, then the place will be torn apart. So instead, they have a beautiful theater that is really under-used. Sad in my opinion. But to leave on a positive note: if you do decide to maybe take a date down to the Fox for, say, an airing of Casablanca, make sure to head to the balcony to settle in to one of the love seat-style chairs. What a great touch for a balcony!

text: After a night spent bopping heads at a swank jazz club downtown (Sweet Lorraine's), and a handwritten list of places to try for brunch provided by the hostess, we settled on LPK as the place to try, mostly because of the name. We arrived at 10:45 to find that it didn't open til 11:00. Attempting to pass the time by hitting up one of the drive through daiquiri stands, we were relieved to discover that they were not open til noon. Way to have some class, New Orleans. 11:00 clicked in, the front door was unlocked, and we were the first into the empty restaurant. Payment was simple, prix-fixe settled before you approached the buffet. The initial buffet browse was promising, everything looked good except for the paltry chopped salad. I wasn't worried, because who goes to a creole brunch buffet looking for a nice fresh salad? I dished myself a sampler platter and tucked in. My smile grew with every bite. Crab and Corn chowder was a perfect balance of cream and salt, while creole shrimp had just enough kick to compliment the rice they were spooned over. The fried chicken was amazing - my friend bequeathed it the honor of 'best ever,' and lit a slow burn on the back of your tongue after the first few bites. White beans and sausage were perfectly cooked and richly flavored. My personal favorite was the carrot souffle, which I quickly realized was maybe an eighth carrot. The other 87% was flour, sugar, and eggs. It tasted like a fluffy sweet potato pie with a vegetal finish. Desserty, but not as desserty as the bread pudding with a vanilla brandy sauce. I ate til I couldn't move, and then had a last plateful. Go there.

text: Those of us indian women who have gotten our eyebrows threaded for years know that $10 for eyebrows and ANOTHER $10 for upper lip threading is actually rather pricey. I have gotten just as good a job for eyebrows and upper lip for about $10 total in West Philly and in the suburbs. I'm used to going to someone's basement or garage, where you pay next to nothing, the person threading remembers your name, and your eyebrows come out looking extraordinary. But since I live in Center City, I had been going to Shanthi Medispa to have my eyebrows done by Shilpa every so often. I suppose I pay largely for convenience. But no more. Even though Shilpa does a fine job, I will NEVER go to this place again. To explain - I went to Shanthi for my usual eyebrow and upper lip. I always pay by credit card. I was told by Shilpa that they no longer accept cards as of February 1st 2010. Fine. I get my eyebrows done, go to an ATM to get cash, and come back to leave my payment. I come back and give Shilpa payment in the office. As she is counting my cash, I see on her desk a signed credit card receipt from the previous customer, dated the same day, for $12 - ie, eyebrow threading plus tip. I couldn't believe it. Why would they accept someone else's credit card for the same service, but not mine? Then I come onto Yelp, and see a review dated 2/23/10 that stated there was a "credit card minimum" but that day the company had "let it slide" for that particular customer. So the whole "we don't accept credit cards after Feb 1st" was obviously not true. So clearly, they don't have their story straight. Do they accept credit cards? Sometimes. Do they have a minimum? Sometimes. All I know is that I wanted to pay by card, something I had always done, and they allowed someone else to, but not me, and lied to me in the process. Even if there was a minimum, I would have exceeded it given I would have paid at least $20 for eyebrow and upper lip, and they had accepted a card transaction that day for $12. I suppose no matter how good my eyebrows come out, I see this as a sign of disrespect for the customer. If I am going to pay for convenience there are other places to go where they do just as good a job and don't lie to you (anjuthreads comes to mind, or one of many places in the suburbs). So I gave Shilpa my money today, but I didn't appreciate being lied to. And I will never, ever go back.

text: So Newstead Tower Gastropub is closing and the Steph says to me, "Andy, we need to go before they close. They were nominated the Riverfront Times 2008 best burger." So I says, "I'm down with burgers." We show up at about 7pm and were told the wait was about half an hour. WAY longer than I'd stay normally, but they're going out of business, so fine, we'll stay. Around 7:30pm we're seated and place some orders. No honey mustard? No Barbecue sauce? You're out of bacon? Ok, I understand you're going out of business and you don't restock as much as you used too... fair enough, let's get some fries, rarebit and burgers. Around 8:00pm we get a ridiculously small amount of run-o-the-mill steak fries (pomme frites). The rarebit we got came in a container similar in size to an ENORMOUS thimble. All for the low, low price of $8 dollars. Yikes. Now all we had left to eat was the burgers. 8:20pm - we tried a few different draft beers while we waited. 8:45pm - ordered second round of drinks 9:05pm- After noticing that two tables whom had been seated AFTER us were finishing their meals, we inquired about our GD food. The waiter, while polite, only smiled and said that with their operations shutting down in the near future they had been gearing down production and had not expected such a turn out. He apologized and said he'd do what he could. In the meanwhile, another server, whom I can only assume was a manager of some sort, came out and did her best to compensate for the horrendous service. She offered to comp some of our drinks and she explained that their primary chef and a significant portion of the wait staff had left- moved on to greener pastures- and they had called in every favor they could to make it through this last week of operation. I appreciated her condolences and frankness- but I didn't feel it made up for anything. Around 9:15pm, after another couple of heated conversations with our original waiter, our burgers finally came out. They were dry, tasteless and lukewarm- obviously rushed out in an attempt to appease us. The total on the check came out to about $50 (that's after a round of drinks had been discounted). I understand that you're going out of business. I can understand that things are hectic because you're not restocking products and your primary chef left and you've been slammed by surprise onslaught of customers wanting to get in their last taste of Newstead before you close. But if this is the last taste you manage to leave us with, maybe you should have closed a week earlier? Just sayin' ...

I am guessing that the bulk of the dishes that were ordered were hard-core Malaysian dishes, i.e. they do not taste like what you'd expect from a typical Asian dish, because I haven't yet met an Asian food style that I didn't like (Korean, Chinese, Japanese, Vietnamese, etc.), but I enjoyed very few of the dishes that we ordered. Most had a very strange or off taste and/or smell. An example, one of the appetizers that was ordered is called Rojak. On the description for this dish it states "Please ask server for advice before you order!" and there's good reason. This is a fruit salad from hell that has chunks of fruit, vegetables and octopus in it served with a shrimp paste sauce. The smell and taste of this dish is roughly the equivalent of rotting fish stored in an outhouse in August. I kid you not. We could smell the plate long before the waitress even got near our table and my wife and I were like oh no, please tell us that the sewer just backed up in the bathroom and that's not our dish we're smelling! It was. I ate some of it just to see if I could. It was nauseating. I realize that it is obviously an aquired taste as the Malaysian people at our table devoured it. Now I am a VERY adventurous eater and don't turn my nose up at things very often but even my wife was shocked at how few of the dishes I enjoyed and didn't have to force down. There were about 7 or 8 dishes between appetizers, entrees and sides that we ordered and only 2 that my wife actually enjoyed eating and like 1 additional dish for me. The rest were just....UGH! I think I would like to try Banana Leaf again some time but next time I will definitely be doing the ordering for myself.

text: Let me start by saying that I am a big fan of provel cheese. I wouldn't say that I'm a die hard fan nor would I make the claim that it's "DA BEST CHEEZ EVAR!" but I do enjoy it on occasion. Enter Imo's pizza, another iconic restaurant with a long standing tradition in Saint Louis- famed for being one of the first pizzeria's here to not only use Provel instead of Mozzarella, but also claim to be the pioneers of thin crust pizza. I can't say I'm a huge fan of their pizza. Please! Be reasonable! Before you throw the first stone, hear me out! Do as I did when I went this last time, order your favorite pizza and get half of it mozzarella and half provel. I got a deluxe. I really liked the provel side. I like that the cheese is creamy and sweet. How it somehow homogenizes the tastes of all ingredients into something rich and unique. I also have to admit that it's easier to eat since I don't have to play cat's cradle whenever I pull a slice from the pan. All in all, I can see why this unique flavor has kept Imo's in business over the years. A taste of the mozzarella side provided some further insight. Without the unique flavoring of the provel as a crutch, the pizza was, well, terrible. The veggies on my deluxe were sopping wet (not to mention the whole damn pizza!)- most likely an indicator that they used frozen vegetables. Which is a violation of Pizza 101- NEVER USE FROZEN INGREDIENTS! Running the frozen stuff through the ovens only thaw the ingredients...which means you end up with a lot of excess water on the pizza AND uncooked ingredients. Additionally, all ingredients were somewhat flavorless compared to the provel side, and, as the last straw, the mozzarella was very tacky and chewy- a noxious entity in it's own right. If I woke up in the middle of the night craving pizza, would I hold vigil until Imo's opened? No. If I were passing by an Imo's and felt a craving for pizza, would I return? Probably not. But for those who have never experienced provel on pizza, I think it's worth a shot. Just once. Why not?

text: This is the first time I've desperately wished Yelp had the option of giving zero stars. The Nathan Bedford Forrest Memorial, which is beside I-65 South in Brentwood, is probably Nashville's most appalling landmark. And I'm not only saying that because of the historical and racial implications--it's also aesthetically atrocious. The address I've listed for this abomination is actually approximate. The statue and its collection of surrounding Confederate flags (approximately a dozen in all) aren't actually on Oakley and Regent, but the site is between that point and the interstate. You can check out Google Maps' satellite image or street view of the area from I-65 just west of the address I have listed. Forrest, who is best known for his work as a general with the Confederate Army and his role as "Imperial Wizard" of the KKK in the years following the Civil War, is depicted in this statue as a ghastly, screaming dwarf. The horse on which Forrest rides makes the general look like a nine-year-old with a radically contorted face wearing a false beard and a skirt. The statue is on private property owned by a Nashville attorney. This means the eyesore is there for better or worse, and none of us can do a thing about the fact that it is clearly visible from the interstate. The statue has allegedly been shot at numerous times, but some of us simply take solace in the fact that it makes Forrest look like a stunted, maniacal idiot.

text: I've taken Apex bus 5 times now, going from Philadelphia to New York. It could learn a few crucial lessons from FungWah in terms of service. Getting on Apex is easy. I usually buy my ticket online and then you have to bring your ID (drivers license) with you to sign it at the front desk in the Apex office on 11th st. The bus leaves promptly, it's very quiet and smooth and the ride takes from 2 to 2.5 hours usually. The bus ride to get BACK is another story completely. The Ticket Ladies/Hawkers are NUTS. You walk to the corner where the buses go off from and as you walk by they'll slap you on the back and yell in your ear "Philadelphia?! DC?!" You will then say where you're going, they will point to a portion of the street where a crowd is waiting and say "Wait here, 5 minute!" You will then wait for between 1 and 45 minutes for the next bus to wherever you are going. It is also crucial that you make sure that you have the right ticket hawker. I have accidentally gotten on the wrong bus because a Chinese woman slapped me on the back and said "PHILADELPHIA LEAVING RIGHT NOW RIGHT NOW LAST ONE" and I thought she was Apex. The main problem I have with Apex from NY to Phila is that they will sometimes delay the bus in order to get more passengers. So, even if the ride up the bus was half empty, going back to NY it's usually packed. Bring your own toilet paper and hand sanitizer as well. If you buy a ticket online, try to buy it for slightly later than you want to get on, because they'll usually accept a ticket from a later bus. I personally like to buy the ticket online so that I have an assurance that I have a seat at SOME point if the bus is full when I want to leave. Sometimes they will make the whole crowd move to another street and board the bus. I think this is because of the questionable legality of their bus parking. There will be pushing and shoving, and it's up to you whether you will nobly hold back from the fray or push your way onto the bus, but keep this in mind: even if you have a ticket, if there's no room on the bus you will have to wait. I give it four stars because it is fast, usually convenient, usually relable and cheap. I recommend it, and I would also recommend that the NY ticket hawkers get like, ponchos or something to identify themselves with one particular bus service.

text: Ok, true confessions. I used to work at Grand Cru... so.. no bias. Ha. But seriously. I've worked at other wine and spirits stores as well and I've moved away from Nashville and no longer work there so I feel at least a little comfortable giving an honest opinion. Grand Cru is awesome. Really. The staff is well-educated and truly excited about the products on the shelves. The management generally tries to hire people with a background in wine, beer or liquor and it shows in staff recommendations and ability to answer questions. That said, don't come to Grand Cru if you know you only ever drink Yellowtail Chardonnay and that's all you're interested in buying. Do they have Yellowtail Chardonnay? Sure. In two sizes, even. So.. I guess go ahead and come, if that's your reason. But the reason Grand Cru deserves five stars is that the staff is knowledgeable enough to be able to get you a bottle of Chardonnay that you'll love even more that's still in your price range. This is the store to come to if you're ready to shake of the chains of the advertising world and try something new. Whether you want a $10 bottle of something that goes great with pizza or a $150 bottle for someone who considers themselves the snobbiest of the wine snobs, this is the store for you. Make yourself a regular and the staff will even start setting things aside that they think you'll like based on what you've bought in the past. Come in on Saturday afternoons for wine tastings at Portland Brew next door (bonus: they're free!). Buy a case and get 10% off the total price. Buy a half case and get 5% off. Ask for Jason or Jim.. they won't steer you wrong. Grand Cru -- as the name implies -- is more geared toward the wine drinker, but the people seeking liquor or high-alcohol beer also have a place here. When I left they were still expanding the selection of imported and other high-alcohol beer but even then it ranged from the Arrogant bastards to the Chimays to the Jefferson stout aged in bourbon barrels (can't remember the name of it.. but get it. It's spectacular). They have a great selection of scotch, including scotch gift sets that any whiskey drinker would be pleased to receive. Ask for Jason and he'll talk your ear off about which scotches come from where and why that makes them unique and amazing. Take aways: Go to Grand Cru for wine recommendations Go to Grand Cru for scotch recommendations Go to Grand Cru on Saturdays for free tastings Go to Grand Cru and ask for Jason -- he's the all-around expert Go to Grand Cru and ask for Jim -- he's a wine-maker extraordinaire Go to Grand Cru.

We went late at night, so the lighting was pretty dim. For a Friday night, (although it had been the coldest night in the last few days) it wasn't that busy. We shared an order of Pad Thai and an order of Snowbird dumplings. The pad thai was definitely different from those found at LA thai places. The texture was much more softer, lacking the crunch of raw beansprouts, carrots, or cabbage. The flavor was also much milder as well. The Snowbird dumplings were mostly for show. They were undeniably cute, but for $8.95 for five dumplings... definitely something I wouldn't order again (unless I was with someone else who wanted to see them in person). We also ordered some Thai Iced Tea, which was rather good. I would probably rank it up in the top 3 or 4 Thai Iced Teas that I have had in my time in LA and in St. Louis. We then finished off the meal with some lychee sorbet. The sorbet was of good quality, not too icy, and you could definitely taste the lychee. Overall, it was a pretty good experience and I would definitely come back to try other dishes.

text: I really don't want to give this place any stars. My husband wanted to take me somewhere new and nice for my birthday so he made reservations here. The bar side, with tables outside, looked fun and we saw a good crowd enjoying the evening with some pretty drinks and tempting bar food. We entered the restaurant side expecting it to be even better and were seated immediately by a woman we assumed was the hostess. She didn't seem very welcoming but we didn't care. We were excited to have a good meal and a nice time and figured our waitress would be nicer. We sat down and noticed the restaurant was completely empty except for one other table . . . maybe that should have been our first clue. I opened my menu to find it that it was stained with food. GROSS. Is it really so difficult to replace the paper inserts with clean ones? it's not like we were eating at a run of the mill chain restaurant. I pretended not to notice the stains and looked at the choices, which all sounded pretty good. Then the hostess lady came back. My heart sank a little when I realized she was going to be our waitress. She asked for our drink order--even though she hadn't provided us with a wine or beer list (and I saw that the only other people in the dining room had one). I told her we were still deciding and then asked if they had any specialties. Maybe that's an annoying question, but since it was my birthday I thought I'd try something more exciting than a glass of wine. Her reply was simply, "No," and she walked away. That was literally all she said. This woman did not smile once at us. She didn't offer us a wine list. She didn't give us any suggestions--I understand if the bar doesn't have signature drinks, but usually a (friendly) server will ask you what you like and suggest a few things. My husband wanted a beer but she didn't even stick around long enough to tell us what was on tap. We just stared at each other wondering why she was so unpleasant but we were still determined to have a nice time. We decided on what we wanted to eat and closed up our menus, waiting for her to return to take our order. And we waited. And we waited some more. Finally, feeling uncomfortable as the other waitress went back and forth, seemingly pretty attentive to the other table we whispered back and forth, "Ok, should we just go?" "Give it a few minutes." "How long?" We never leave a restaurant after being seated. We are insanely non-confrontational. We never want to be *those* people, never satisfied, huffy and demanding. But I just kept thinking that this was my birthday dinner, and if we stayed it was obviously going to suck. She was going to treat us like crap, and my husband was going to feel like he ruined the night by choosing this place. We realized that she had completely disappeared, so we left. We didn't rush or anything, and no one else who worked there seemed to care or notice. No one asked if they could help us or if there was a problem. We ended up going to Honey, which was delicious and fun, and the servers there were very sweet and friendly. I will NEVER go back to Bobby Simone's, not even to the bar there, and I advise you to avoid this place, too, at least until they get their act together and hire some decent help.

text: Shangri La! Much like its semi-mythical namesake, the restaurant is shrouded in lore. A full-on, vegetarian cafe/restaurant in the heart of meat-mad St. Louis? It sounds like a mirage, an explorer's story that's more wishful thinking or fatigue-inspired false recollection. But venturing down to nearly the terminus of the criminally underrated Cherokee Street strip, you soon find out that the cafe is very, very real. It's not a perfect place. I've had better veggie fare, although this is the type of joint that wins massive points for knowing their audience. It's mostly uncompromising towards non-vegetarians but not militant (notice the only meat on offer, salmon, which pops up in three dishes), and always friendly, plus the menu's massive range (excellently mimicking what a proper diner ought to offer with great stuff like a veggie meatloaf platter) goes a long way towards balancing out the sometimes average quality. More than anything else, Shangri La is a refuge for the meat weary. Its '60s thrift store decor and space-age plastic tableware, bright colors, and enthusiastic, tattooed/pierced alterna-hippie staff wrap you in a comforting, accepting embrace. It's also a prime location to dig in to healthy, vegetarian fare or to snag hearty comfort food that both soothes the soul and satisfies that occasional animal flesh craving, but won't quite give you a coronary in the process. Of special note is Shangri La's vegetarian brunch, which knocks the one over at Mokabe's into a cocked hat. You won't wait for a table, you won't be overwhelmed by the din, and while the spread wasn't as ginormous, upon walking away I felt more satisfied. As a word of warning, the buffet selection varies and can be somewhat meager: on my last visit, there were hash browns, a tofu scramble (of sorts), blueberry pancakes (that were delicious but basically and weirdly cold), a green salad, some type of veggie sausage patty, and the meal's crown jewel, insanely tasty brioche french toast. Wash it all down with multiple cups of dark, freshly roasted coffee and you've got enough fuel to power you all over south city till dinner time rolls around. I can't stress enough the quality of the coffee, by the way. It's easily one of the top 5 cups of joe in the STL, and possibly the best that isn't made one cup at a time. In fact, a bottomless mug and one of the handful of sidewalk tables is a reason alone to frequent the place. That said, actually doing so is one of the strikes against Shangri La. Their small-scale, DIY ethic unfortunately means they're only open Thursday through Sunday, and that they don't open till 11am, 9am on weekends. But while the schedule is odd enough to prevent it from becoming a daily haunt, Shangri La's variety, dedication, and radiant, living room vibe are more than enough to make it a destination when its doors *are* open.

text: Yes, it's in a Mall, and that's just not the best way to start things off...but, let's say...it's Tuesday night...your partner is working late or at a townhall meeting...so you show up to the Keystone Art Cinema a little early, and there's J Crew...an oasis amongst a barren mall -- a mall that's empty ain't so bad is it? J Crew is not your older brother's J Crew. 10 years ago...it seemed like Ralph Lauren's Outlet in Cape Cod...then, somewhere along the way...they became a place that says, "hmmmm...if we could do it all over again, let's take 1960 and give it a good name in fashion." J Crew has wised up. And, they've grown. It's a bit like a mini-department store. The biggest shift is they've brought in brands that they love...Levi's, Jack Purcells, Ray-Bans, Timex. They're looking to brand themselves, "Timeless," via other brands...yeah that'd be a stretch if they're styles weren't timeless. As a guy...I want to buy clothes that last a lifetime, and that don't look like clothes I'd wear when I was 16. The service is attentive, and interested. The prices...still steep. But say..you buy one thing here once...let the purchase be your carrying card to go in here whenever you want and wander...they have so many options it's a bit cavernous..and there's therapy to standing in front of a giant wall of denim. How else will we ever find out about wing-tips and bow ties with denim unless we really consider them in person? This place allows that browsing. Note at the Register: They will ask for your email. It's all over from there...if you give it. You'll get catalogues and emails every week. Most of the people just seemlessly gave it to them, which I was really surprised and impressed by. text: I have to say that my first experience with Han Dynasty was with the owner/manager who picked up the phone on a Tuesday night. To say that the owner/manager was extremely rude, is the nicest way of putting it. My sister and I were walking there and thought of calling head to see how busy they were to see if they could accommodate us - if not, we planned just to go somewhere else. I called and asked if there was a need to make reservations for dining that night. He replied by asking what time, and when I mentioned that I was asking because we were walking that way (arrival within 20 mins) and was wondering if there would be possiblity of seating. He responded (again, rudely), "Well, I guess it doesn't matter about reservations. Luck for you we are dead and you can have a seat." We walked into the restaurant (better decorated that most Chinese restaurants) and waited for our server, the owner/manager who had answered the phone came by with our server and started speaking to us as though we were complete morons and stared at my nephew as though he was a piece of trash when he (age 2) was playing with the chopsticks. Speaking over our server, he made suggestions rather rudely and short with a level of curtness that I was not ready for. Being a 2nd generation Asian American, I tried to trust that maybe he had not fully acclimated to the American culture. We ended up ordering Fried Taiwanese Sausage (for the nephew - he loved it) semi-sweet and well, tastes like a sausage. Fish Dry Pot It was pretty good with a nice spice, but not a total Szechuan Gastronomic experience that othershave described it as. It was pretty good compared to the bad and mediocre Szechuan restaurants that are out there, but nothing to write home about. This dish was the start the slew of entrees that were unbalanced. The Chinese 5 Spice overpowered almost everything. That is all I could taste - but then again, I am not a huge fan of it - too much anise/cloves? Chicken Hot Sauce Style The flavor, I could tell, was good, but the sauce was so over-starched, it might pretty much was a gelatinous goop of good flavor mixed with the tinge of too much corn starch - mistake only poorer cooks would make. I was pretty disappointed. There was a pile of minced garlic sitting on the top that seemed a bit much of a punch of flavor to this already flavorful dish. I understand the need to garnish a dish to make it look fancier than your local Chinatown dish, but it just was not balance with this edible garnish/whatever it was. Salt and Pepper Style Shrimp How can you really go wrong with fried food?!?! This salt and pepper shrimp was pretty good, but all I could taste here was the five spice powder, too. The server that came was pretty good at his job - friendly, warm and understood English, but I felt bad that the owner/manager kept on showing up and ruining our experience by staring at us (wanting us to relinquish the table faster no doubt) and making his own suggestions. Overall: Atmosphere: bare, but better than most Chinese restaurants (at least more westernized?) Service: Fine as long as the Owner/Manager doesn't get involved Food: Better than most Szechuan cuisine I've had, but slightly above average.

text: Bangkok is one of those restaurants that, if you didnt know about it, you would never discover it. And that would be a terrible shame, because it's got some of the best hot-pot in town. While it's name indicates Thai cuisine, I would say it's an all-around general Asian restaurant. Bangkok's specialty is hot-pot, which is not exclusively a Thai tradition, I don't think. I used to live near this restaurant; it was practically in my backyard. Bangkok is located in a residential area, not on a main street, so it's hard to spot. It's exterior looks pretty no-frills too, which makes it even harder to find. I wouldn't be surprised if passers-by thought it was an abandoned garage. But don't let it's outward appearance deter you from trying it. For those of you who aren't familiar with hot-pot, it's basically where you get this big pot of water on your own portable stove at your table, and dunk whatever you want to eat into the pot so it cooks. It's kind of like a buffet and DIY cooking. Well, when I put it that way it doesn't sound great, but it is, and it's fun. They have a buffet table of raw food that you can choose from. You just heap your plates full of stuff you want, take it back to your table and cook it in your pot. You can leave your food in the pot for as long as you want, depending on whether you like things kind of rare or fully cooked. The buffet includes a variety of rice noodles, Asian vegetables, meats, and seafood. The rate you pay is similar to that of a buffet, a flat fare for as much food as you can eat. So the more you eat, the better the deal. They're open late nights on weekends, something to keep in mind if you find yourself looking for something new one weekend. It's fun to come here with a group of friends, and dunk as you chat. It's an experience that should be tried at least once!

text: I have lived in the Reno area for six years now, and have eaten at PF Changs in Reno (on Kietzke) many, many times over the years - mainly lunch. I was extremely disappointed in our lunch just the other day. My husband ordered grilled salmon with asparagus; I ordered the orange peel prawns. Well, first we had an unbelievably surly waiter come to our table and fling down the 3 sauces. With no explanation at all (not that we needed it, but still) he mixed up the sauces in a bowl while asking us for our order. Then he stomped off to the kitchen to deliver it. Sheesh. Our plates arrived and I had to absolutely frown in disappointment at what I saw! The grilled salmon was utterly, completely devoid of any marination, seasoning or sauce. Yes it was grilled. Period. The asparagus, similarly, not even oiled first! It was grilled. Period. The salmon was way overcooked, resulting in a dry, tasteless and even fishy flavor. YUCK. The asparagus was absolutely tough and rubbery from lack of proper cooking. My orange peel prawns were better on the flavor scale, but one look at them (before even tasting) proved they'd been done up in a big pot hours before. The sauce had completely coagulated into a thick paste. Gross. My taste confirmed this: the dish was barely lukewarm and gloppy with sticky sauce. The waiter came over to ask how our lunch was just as my husband and I were muttering expletive deleteds, over our pathetic fare. i had an absolute snarl on my face and did not even trust my tongue to respond to the question. My husband at least shared his gripe, saying, "Um, this salmon is kind of simple. There appears to be no seasoning." To which the waiter glared at us, turned on his heel and stalked away. Feh! I don't know who's on the lunch-time shift at Reno's PF Chang, but here's how you do salmon: marinate it for one hour in honey, soy sauce, fresh ground black pepper and grated ginger - a splash of sherry would be good, too. Then, grill it at a LOW (yes, low) temperature to almost mimic a poached salmon - it will come out delectably soft and flavorful. As for my prawns: geez guys, can you make them right before serving them? Cuz the sauce simply has to be more liquid and fresh, NOT gummy and coagulated. There is a huge billboard off Hwy 395 that says "Give in to the craving. PF Changs"!!! I have to guffaw at that now, cuz it was the billboard that made me want to GO there. Then we had the disappointing lunch and I will never return. So much for my craving - for freshly cooked, superbly cooked meals.

text: Ok here's what I love about Aveda salons: natural products, well thought out products, sustainable from a long time ago before it was hip. As well when you go to the concept stores, they always draw you in with the scents and a cup of hot tea. And even though it's a bit more expensive, sometimes you splurge and get something. You feel good coming away with a shopping bag of products. You know you're on to something good that goes w/ your beliefs. You know that you can have it everyday, until the last drop in the bottle etc. But here's my thing: A few years ago when the St. Pete institute first opened up I went there, because "Oh my god, there's an AVEDA here now!!!" Having come from another state and gone to them a lot for products etc, over about a 10 year period of time. But usually I never went for services. So one day like I said some years ago when they first opened in St. Pete, I thought that since it was a school I might be able to get "exclusive-like" services for cheaper than going to an upscale salon. As an intro tester to see how they'd be, I made an appointment for a back facial which included some massage. I couldn't wait for the day. When the day came I was so excited!! Nevertheless, I was not disappointed. It was my first time being in a spa like atmosphere. It was awesome. The student who worked on me was awesome. She quietly explained everything she was going to do and prepped me for how I would feel. Example is like if they tell you they're going to put something on your back and say this may feel a little cold/cool. I made another appointment. What happened to my girl? I found out she graduated and who knows where she went. This next experience was not great at all. I had decided to have the same type of treatment, plus add a regular facial. This girl just went ahead doing everything, her timing was not good, she didn't prepare you for anything and would just glob some cold, startling amount of goop on your back!! That's one lesson. Don't get attached to any of them, they are students and they will eventually graduate and possibly move to Vegas. So again don't get attached... But here is my biggest problem with the Aveda Institute in St. Pete. For all the times I had gone there for services or to drop in to pick up products, there was a time I finally decided to graduate myself to making a hair appointment. When I decided to make a hair appointment, I was told to hold on a minute while they went to get someone who specialized in my kind of hair. The person came and sat down with me out front. She most politely as she could told me that they really aren't able to do my "kind of hair"... African American hair... You can't imagine how that made me feel. You just don't know. Oh, I thought I was on to something. I just knew they would be my one stop shop for everything for my "spa" experience for however often I could afford it. I was willing to pay. Hey wait a minute, I had paid!! I had paid all those times I had other services. I had paid everytime I dropped in for more product (understanding the reputation of how great the it is )from over 10 years ago of using it. I had paid everytime I had gotten a service and was escorted back out to the front by the student to peruse and be persuaded to buy the products used on me that day. I think that I had well deserved to have services for my "kind of hair"!! Why, with Aveda's universal appeal is that one area that seems unable to be cared for? The person who sat me down informed me that they really didn't have anyone there at that point (I guess in the slew of students) who understood nor was able to do "Afro hair" as she called it. I slunk out of the salon feeling pretty dejected. I really don't think she meant anything personal by it. I could tell she was just being honestly sincere which is why I did not pursue it on a legal level. But I really agree with her and observed that she must be right, due to the fact that in walking through the salon, you generally do not see diversity of people nor hair textures, (despite advertisement.) Again why is that? It shouldn't matter what ethnicity the students are who are attending, the institute is losing out, because they will have trouble drawing a certain clientele. As well and more importantly they are giving their students a disservice to not be well versed or trained in the diverse world that they live in. Many of their students may be kicking and screaming later after graduation when the salon they dream of getting into is already inundated with those who handle a set number of hair types. They should live up to their progressive credo and teach their students to dream bigger and maybe even have their own salon because there is another clientele out there who are just as progressive. There is more to a strand of hair than meets the eye. As from the musical Hair "Hair, hair, hair...Long, straight, curly, fuzzy,Snaggy, shaggy, ratty, matty!!

text: I'll admit it. I've been called a yarn snob a few times in my day. You won't find me with a stash of Red Heart acrylic in my closet. Loop is my happy place. All of the yarn is neatly contained in little white cubbies or hung in color-coordinating hanks from the white walls. If you dare to spend a few minutes sitting on the green couches in the store's center, you may never get up again once your needles start clicking. I have really come to love the staff and Craig, the owner. The two Kathy's (different employees both named Kathy) are my favorites by far. They know my name and greet me enthusiastically whenever I'm in, even if it hasn't been for months. Not only does Loop offer beginning knitting, but also a range of interesting classes and special workshops to keep your skills sharp and your interest piqued. Craig makes sure to keep things interesting by inviting special guests to the shop for book signings, parties, and demonstrations. Loop's trunk shows are always inspiring me to whip up something new. Yes, the yarn can be off budget for a lot of folks, but the quality of the products they sell is well worth the extra dollars and cents. There are also plenty of offerings that won't bankrupt you. The sale section is usually packed with low-cost goodies. I love that Loop always has Noro and Koigu on hand, and a healthy dose of Blue Sky Alpaca - fibers that many stores do not carry. I acutually find the selection (more types of fibers and more weights of yarn) here to be better than Rosie's Yarn Cellar. I think Craig does a wonderful job of changing up his inventory, adding new things for his customers to try every season. I love that they are never low on stock in the summer, a typically slow season for yarn. Whether you make this your regular Local Yarn Shop or not, Loop merits a visit or two if you're a serious knitter and in the city.

I also believe that I'm a fairly good judge of a quality establishment as I used to review restaurants professionally. Sadly, August was what I would like to call a restaurant that simply tries too hard, but woefully fails to deliver. The setting is lovely, but that is all that I convey that is positive. In summary, the service was abysmal and the food, although decent, was nothing special. I think that the hype received over this restaurant is definitely not merited. text: Meh about sums it up. I'd give it one and half if I could. Tired is the word for McCormick & Schmick's. I wanted to take my wife out to dinner for her birthday and she decided on seafood. We were planning on going to The Oyster House but it was closed for Labor Day and we ended up at McCormick & Schick's. The restaurant definitely has the name recognition and prestige so I didn't even bother pulling up Yelp or reading any reviews. I wish I had. It looks great on the outside but once inside you can see how it hasn't aged well. It probably was something else 20 or 30 years ago but now it's dated, old and tired. I agree with a previous reviewer that the booths are uncomfortably small. We ordered drinks which were just OK but priced high ($14 for a well martini and $12 for a well margarita) and started with sampling of Oysters. This was the the highlight of the meal, 4 different types of oysters and all were pretty good or great. We split a wedge salad which was, again, just OK but garnished table side, again showing how stuck in the 70's M & S's is. I got the 6oz fillet and the stuffed shrimp and the wife got the Lobster Oscar. I ordered my fillet mid-rare and it came out full well. Out waiter was very nice and visibly frustrated at the kitchen's mistake, I guess because he even came back over to verify the temperature I had ordered, and the manager came over to personally apologize which was also nice. The second one came out very rare, full purple in the center. By that time I didn't fell like waiting so I ate it. It was a so-so cut of meat so it really suffered from not being cooked properly. The shrimp themselves were not bad but the crab-meat filling was really bad. The wife enjoyed her meal enough but wasn't excited about it. Needless to say we didn't stay for desert. The only saving grace was the service, which was good albeit a little slow, and the bread. Thank god for the bread. Won't be returning.

Additionally, the internet connection was great the first night, but terrible the second (mainly because we moved rooms). I started walking around and it seems they only have 4 (total) WiFi Access Points in each one of the stairwells placed on the 4th Floor. If you end up coming to this Holiday Inn, try to request a place by the stairwell on the 4th floor or you'll definitely feel the degraded speed. I wanted to mention a few other things about the hotel as well. We ordered a movie from the room and the quality was just poor. Words can't describe how poor it was... it was like we went back in time to Analog and the bunny ears just couldn't get the tv station. Also, some of the Ice machines weren't working which required me to go onto a DIFFERENT floor on the OTHER side of the hotel just to get Ice. I will definitely not be staying at this hotel again if I'm ever in the Saint Louis area for more than one night.

text: After sampling half of Little Saigon in Southern California and basically eating Vietnamese food for my entire life, I can safely say that Viet Huong is pretty good. While it does not boast the best Vietnamese fare I have ever eaten, it certainly has a good selection of Vietnamese favorites at a very great price. As far as taste and value are concerned, this is the place to go. Let's start with things I did not like. The Pho here is pretty standard, nothing special here. If you really want good Pho, you should probably go to a place that specializes in it. That being said, it is not horrible either...it's just standard. On the other hand, the Bo Luc Lac was off the mark, being slightly overdone and under-seasoned. Next time I go, I will definitely shoot for the fried squid instead. Now on to the positive things and why this place is so great. What I really liked is their Banh Mi Bo Kho. I get Bo Kho at pretty much every Vietnamese restaurant and use that as a benchmark. The stew was quite exquisite. It was seasoned with a strange mix of herbs I have never tasted before in Bo Kho. It is an extraordinarily unique flavor that I urge everyone who goes here to try out. Now, I am not much of a quail eater, but I quickly found myself eating through half the plate in no time. It comes with the salt/pepper/lime mixture, but the quail was so good on its own that the mixture went almost completely untouched. Also, we had some of the lobster and it was delicious. Can't really say much more about that since it is lobster... The establishment was quite large and well maintained. It was reminiscent of some of the small mom and pop shops back in California, except it was about 4-5 times the size. The service was neither exceptionally great nor terribly bad. We got our tea refills in a timely manner. Our entrees came out at random intervals, instead of all together. The staff was friendly and answered all of our questions. For the price range, the atmosphere is exactly what I expected. In the future, I will definitely check out their Banh Mi (since Philly has terrible sandwich shops) and their Nem Chua from the bakery. In summary, everything that this place does well, they do it extremely well. Not everything on the menu is going to be the best you've ever eaten, but the good items will definitely have you wanting to come back--and ignoring all the stuff you didn't like =]. With the prices so low (the Banh Mi Bo Kho was about $5) and with certain items that are so good, this place deserves top marks. -C

Some of my favourites are eclaires, "hockey puck" (soft pastry with crunchy chocolate topping, filled with cream) and amaretto balls. text: This is quite possibly the worst cajun creole food on the planet. I can only say possibly because it's the worst I've ever had and I haven't been to every cajun restaurant in the world. I had some questions before ordering and the young lady (YL) behind the counter wouldn't let me finish a question before blurting out an answer to what she thought my question might be. YL: Are you ready to order? Me:I have some questions. Can you... YL: I can give you samples of stuff. Me: Thanks, but what I really would like to know is... YL: It's all on the board if you want to try it. Me: What is the... YL: blah blah blah blah blah I finally gave up. The chicken and mushroom etoufee tasted like someone had rushed to make milk gravy and accidentally spilled some rice in it. Imagine gravy made with too much flour and then undercooked. This is so far from a roux, that I thought we were at Bob Evans. The seafood gumbo looked and tasted like beef barley soup, complete with shredded beef and rice instead of barley. Still can't quite figure that one out. We sifted through it, looking for something that resembled seafood in the peppery beef broth and finally gave up. The jambalaya was watery, bland and had no cajun flavor characteristics. It was literally like someone made uncle Ben's rice and at the last minute said, "darn, we forgot the sausage and all that other jambalaya type stuff. Quick, throw some in it before you serve it." The crawfish casserole was...um...well, just read about the jambalaya above and replace "jambalaya" with "crawfish casserole". Shrimp Po'boy. It's supposed to be on a hard bun, not a soft one. The shrimp and the side of hush puppies had the same flavor. I'm assuming there is deepfry'omatic 3000 in the kitchen where everything goes in one end and comes out the other. It was about the only edible thing in our meal. Certainly the only thing we finished. Tea is out of the fountain, not brewed and tasted like a mud puddle. Long story short, it get's one star only because you can't give a place negative stars. For $7 less, we could have gone to Yats and had larger portions of the best cajun creole food outside of New Orleans. No offense to Mia, but this is not what cajun creole food is supposed to taste like. We really hoped this would be good, because it's so close to our home compared to Yats. We'll happily make the extra drive. I need to add this after the fact. i went to their website and looked at the menu. The pictures of the dishes are nothing like what was served to us. Extremely misleading to say the least. Edited on 6/27/08 to add the following: I'm not affiliated with any restaurant, let alone a competitor of mudbugs. My taste buds are just fine and able to differentiate between all kinds of flavors, textures and consistencies.. When I was there almost a year ago, both the food and service were horrible. Perhaps in the last 11 months they've gotten their act together. If so, kudos to them. They had a long way to go and it wouldn't have been easy. Judging by the other reviews, you'll either love the place or never go back a second time.

They have a wide range of dishes organized on their menu based on vegetables, meats, and seafood categories. They have some pictures usually on the same page, although it would be more beneficial to people unfamiliar with their dishes if they could display everything. The service here is really good too, and matches the quality of food you get here. This restaurant does not look like anything flashy on the outside, butit is well worth your time to come here and treat your tastebuds! text: Rating c 2 stars out of 5 Everyone has to eat sooner or later, so we might as well talk about it. Agree or disagree, your replies are valued. Please allow me to preface this review with 2 comments: 1) The ambiance and feel of Bella Luna, was for me, awkward and more than a little bit dated. 2) It pains me to give any restaurant with heart a negative review. Their hearts are in the right place, the food and service? Not so much on the night we visited. It was a Friday, and we met the in-laws for a birthday celebration. We had reservations for 7pm and it was a "dark and stormy evening" in Tucson (not something we get to say very often). We arrived on time and had taken a moment in the car to read some of the evenings' specials on-line. My better half commented on the special menu seeming a bit heavy. Little did she know how prophetic that observation would turn out to be. I don't know if any of you recall Pee Wee Herman's Saturday morning kids show with the secret word? Every time someone said the secret word of the day, everyone screamed and the secret word would drop from the ceiling dangling on a piece of string. The secret word for this restaurant: HEAVY. We walked into what I can only describe now as one of those awful Vegas-styled Holiday Inn lounge act duos performing in the bar area. You know the kind, he plays an electronic keyboard that doubles as a karaoke machine and she sings along. I asked to be seated as far away as possible. I want to be clear here. Put him at a real piano and her singing some jazz standards with an occasional cool cover song and drop the quasi Karaoke and I would have loved them. They did not suck; their show did. One other issue I had on arrival. When I place a reservation at your fine dining establishment, I like for you to not be apparently stunned when I actually show up. I wasn't sure if it was that they were stunned I personally showed up, or if it was they are generally stunned when anyone shows up for a reservation. We stood for fifteen minutes while the hostess scrambled to turn a table for four into a table for four and then sat the five of us at it. The Service? A clearly overwhelmed, under-trained and under-supported staff did their very best to accommodate us. I'd like to also say that our waitress deserved the 20% she received. Some hints for Bella Luna Owners and managers: Asking about getting a table drinks at a fine dining establishment without having provided the table with your wine list in advance is an amateur mistake and is indicative of a lack of training and support. It's really stupid to not give me a list of things for me to spend money on. In most restaurants those are called the main, wine, and dessert menus. Not having enough staff to help out or even wait on your reserved tables means you aren't in the game to win. You failed your staff miserably and if I were them, I would ditch you. One of the ways to placate customers that are waiting too long for a table is to ask them to please have a seat at the bar while you "make arrangements". It takes the heat off of you and us, plus I am a lot more fun, generous, and hungry after a couple of drinks. Since you had no bartender behind the bar I think it might also be the reason you have no patrons at your bar. Zip, nadda, not a soul at the bar. Again, my experience in the hospitality industry tells me that bars are only effective at generating income when you have a bartender standing there ready to take an order and then the cash. While we are on the subject of alcohol. When you bring wine to the table, there is no excuse for not having "red wine" glasses available. Of course, on a camping trip I will drink wine straight from the bottle, but we weren't on a camping trip, were we? Now lets discuss two more things that should never occur in a dining establishment that wants to get more than $20 per plate. 1) It is not OK to seat one table so close to another that your wait staff has to yell at us to be heard and has to do a complicated contortionist act in order to be able to place items on the table. 2) When it comes time to serve dessert it is not OK to plunk down a handful of silverware in the middle of the table for us to scrap over and then scurry off. On this night, management was entirely missing. No one in charge was marshaling or supporting anyone. I had the rest of this posted at my website and Yelp made me take down the link, sorry.
