text: Probably the best coffee in Tampa, and in my mind, one of the best coffees I've had anywhere. Of course I happen to love tradition, and their coffee satisfies my desire for great tasting Cuban coffee. Naviera coffee is located in the historical Ybor City district, which is the old Latin quarter of Tampa, where Spanish, Cuban, and Italian immigrants worked in the cigar factories, and congregated in restaurants and social clubs. To give you some perspective, Ybor city itself architecturally resembles somewhat the French quarter in New Orleans. While a little sleepy during midweek, it's a neat place to spend a couple of hours in the afternoon for lunch and coffee, followed by a stroll down 7th Ave. Naviera Coffee doesn't look like much from the outside, but their coffee packs a punch. They roast coffee in the back, and serve traditional delights in the front. My favorite is the Ybor special: Cuban Espresso, with a touch of condensed milk. Soooooo good !!! While the seating area and sit down atmosphere is lacking, the coffee is so worth the visit to Ybor. Even our former President Teddy Roosevelt paid Ybor a visit before embarking on his journey with U.S. troops to fight and free Cuba during the Spanish American War (early 1900s). His troops even invented the "Cuba Libre" drink during that time, when they combined coca cola and rum for the first time in Ybor. http://www.elmolinocoffee.com/

text: The Produce Place manages to pack an incredible amount of quality stuff into its tiny interior. It has saved me several times from having to buy yucky grocery store preservative laden bread and it's handy to pick up some fresh locally grown vegetables, of which (space allowing) they have a decent selection. If you want to cook dinner, this is not the place to go in searching for recipe ingredients, rather, go with an open mind and create something from what they have. They have a nice selection of quality organic cheese, local milk in a glass bottle (you can take it back for a refund) and a limited selection of rather pricey organic deli meats and bacon. The back wall is lined with bulk bins of various legumes and grains, which are probably the Produce Place's best value items. They are not open on Sunday, and they close at 6:30 on weekdays, which makes it difficult sometimes to catch them when they're open, but I'm always happy when I do and I can indulge my cravings for San Pellegrino Aranciata or a nice Virgil's root beer, and pick up some Provence or Great Harvest Bread, and a block of yummy cheese.

El Vez is definitely one of the most unique and trendy restaurants in Center City. Price: 4.0 Stars Meals are moderate to high end in pricing but definitely worth the asking price as the quality of ingredient is high, as well. Drinks are also moderate to high end in pricing but strong, delicious, and properly prepared. The margarita pitchers are definitely a good option for groups and the bar selection is strong. Location: 4.5 Stars El Vez has a great location in Center City found just east of Broad Street on Sansom. The restaurant is easily accessible as a center piece of its area. El Vez is located near other popular bars/restaurants/lounges as well. Overall Impression/ Miscellaneous: 4.0 Stars El Vez is a great restaurant and ideal place to socialize and drink. The social atmosphere, location, food and drink selections make the venue a top Mexican restaurant in Philadelphia. The only drawback is the popularity of the restaurant, which is a good drawback to have. Even though getting a table for dinner can be a long wait on weekend nights, the bar makes waiting an almost pleasurable experience. I would definitely recommend going to El Vez for dinner and drinks.

We ordered the octopus and it was awful. We actually sent it back. It tasted like frozen octopus with no flavor and basically dissolved in our mouths. The snail bruschetta was way too salty. The stuffed clams lacked flavor and were too salty as well. We began talking to the table next to us when they saw us send back a plate. They too said their food wasn't good. For dessert, the server was raving about the tiramisu. It tasted like whipped cream with cinnamon on top. He also said his favorite dessert was the pear tart. It was awful. It had no flavor. text: Wasn't terrible, but I would probably try a different hotel next time. First, the positives: As others have mentioned, the staff is very nice and accommodating. I didn't have a *ton* of interaction with staff, but enough to know that they take pride in customer service. The concierge helped me out with my parking issue (see below), which I greatly appreciated. We stayed in a corner king room, which was pretty spacious and well-decorated. The bed was comfortable & I slept OK. I did use the room's iron and was pleased that it was a newer hotel iron and worked just the way it should---not a given in other hotels that I've stayed in! Negatives: Paper-thin walls and doors. I felt like I could hear every movement of the people in the room next door and had to keep the TV on to drown out the noise. They weren't being loud or anything, just getting dressed, I guess? I kept waking up because it sounded like someone was in *our* hotel room rifling through our stuff. I feel like most of the sound came through the door that allowed us to turn the hotel room into an adjoining room. Parking --- I drive a 4Runner with a Yakima roof rack installed. So, okay, it *is* a big vehicle but I would absolutely not call it over-sized. I don't normally have issues parking in parking garages, but my vehicle could not fit into the Sheraton's garage. Luckily it was a weekend and street (meter) parking was free and allowed overnight. Otherwise I would have been pretty screwed. This is minor. I probably should have called the front desk and I'm sure they would have taken care of this. But I guess I'll mention that our TV seemed to not be programmed properly. The remote control did not work at all, and the channel numbers did not match what was printed on the guide. So we had a tough time flipping channels to find the one we wanted. But, we found this out when we got in around 11 PM and I wasn't about to call anyone to fix it. Also, the TV set was a "standard definition" 27 inch-ish tube TV and not anything big or fancy. Wasn't a deal breaker for me, but others might care about this. Again, this is probably something I could've & should've called the front desk about, but I'll also mention that our room's air conditioner seemed unable to reach the set temperature on the thermostat. Our room stayed at a solid 75 degrees-ish during our stay and never dropped to the more-comfortable set temperature of 71. Wasn't a huge deal, but I wasn't quite as comfortable as I otherwise would've been. Finally, the bathroom: didn't affect me because I am short, but the shower head was only about 5 feet 9 inches off the ground. I'd imagine that this would be a problem for a tall individual. Also, the bathroom had no exhaust fan. This meant showers made the room even more hot & humid. Also, if anyone decided to make any stinkys, the other occupant(s) in the room got to enjoy it.
label: NEG

text: Not really all that impressed with the theater for feature-length films. (I'm roughly 5'8" for reference, kids should fit just fine). - Dimmer than perfect projection - Domed screen (while this is nice for a planetarium setting or nature films, it's a bit distracting for feature films to potentially miss out on something in your peripheral vision) I'm going based on a $14 showing of Inception (~140min), and while I'm not dissapointed that I gave it a try, I likely won't be back to see any more blockbusters here. text: Southwark's high yelp rating is well deserved. I went for dinner on Saturday and left feeling quite satisfied. I thoroughly enjoyed the martinez and will not hesitate to stop in for another vintage cocktail in the bar area the next time that I am in the neighborhood. For my meal, I ordered the pan seared scallops, which were delightful! The dish was accompanied by a refreshing salad that included avacado and pistachios. I was able to taste my boyfriend's order of the sirloin steak, which was amazing! The grass-fed beef was tender, buttery, and a bit chewy. Should I return for dinner, that will be my selection. The dining area is dimly lit, has a nice view of their courtyard, and is modestly decorated. Service was top notch! Our server was thorough, knowledgeable, and personable. Dinner at Southwark is an excellent choice for a date night or a good place to stop in on a night to get a quality cocktail. text: I was at the Shops at Brinton Lake with my family and we decided pay a visit to The Fresh Market. Wow, what a great looking store! Fresh looking produce, the joint is clean, wonderful aromas and a plethora of fancy items to select from. With a start like this, I was expecting great things. It was just before dinner time so we figured we would meander over to the deli area to see what we could find. They had quite a selection of rotisserie chickens available. One of the gentlemen behind the counter asked if I needed help and being the gentleman that I am, allowed him to assist the nice lady who was there next to me. So I got the #2 guy. This guy had the personality of a dry sponge. His appearance was questionable as well. If I were to suggest a different career for him, I would suggest that he be a tool booth coin collector. We could not wait to get home and eat dinner since the car smelled of freshly made roasted chicken. So I go to cut the chicken only to find out that it is not cooked all the way through. Yup, still pink inside. Are you freaking kidding me? I didn't want to make dinner, now I have to finish what they started. I know that $7.99 is not a lot, but if you are advertising a cooked chicken, then make sure the damn thing is done! Chef's thermometer, invest in a couple of them. I have to imagine that they have hired makeup artists to make their salad because it looked great on the exterior, but once you got past that, they put the rest of the shit produce that nobody wants. text: Two words: Food Coma! That's exactly what will happen to you after eating at Lottawatta Creek. Located in Fairview Heights, this restaurant was tres populaire with my college friends due not only to its close proximity to Edwardsville (Go Cougars) but the fact that $12-15 would get you stuffed! With leftovers. If you didn't catch my drift, the portions here are huge. Massive. Back in the day, I used to order the kid's chicken tenders and would still have leftovers. Unfortunately they caught on to my scam and limited that option to people under the age of 12. Not sure what 12 year old could finish that much chicken, but that's a whole different story. All of their entrees come with a choice of two sides. I recommend the mashed potatoes (with a little bit of skin mixed in there) or the green beans. The only drawback of eating at Lottawatta is the whole "eating healthy" debate. Everything there is fried or doused in butter. It's great if you are looking to build up your reserves for winter hibernation. But if you're just a regular person, your waistline will suffer. That and watching people gorge on huge plates of greasy food is not terribly appetizing. But the sheer amount of food you are served is a great deal and as long as you don't dine there two-three times per week (and work out immediately after when you do eat there) you should be fine. Especially if you can ignore everyone else at the restaurant licking their plump fingers after a buttery, lip smacking meal. Paints a pretty picture, doesn't it?

The menu doesn't contain much "flair" but for perfect, delicious California cuisine, please look no further. The best part? We could actually hear ourselves talk. There are plenty of places in Santa Barbara to get good food, but few that get the atmosphere right too. text: I used to be a regular at The Delachaise in 2003-2004. I do not go there nearly as often, but it is still in my rotation. Since its opening, The Delachaise has had several chefs and countless bartenders. There is one thing that has stayed constant; The Delachaise is a great place to eat and drink. The Delachaise has always been known for its wine selection. It was the first bar where I could consistently find gruner veltliner by the glass (I still can). If anything, I think the wine selection has improved over the years. The wine specials (a red and a white) are always good, yet very affordable. The Delachaise also has a great selection of liquor and beer. The Delachaise was the first bar to bring the "gastropub" concept to New Orleans (without ever calling it that). The menu has changed a great deal over the years, but it has always featured high quality food. My favorites on the current menu are the Flank Steak Bruschetta (watch out, the pesto is loaded with garlic, but the steak is delicious), the Grilled Cheese Annabella, and those famous fries (fried in goose fat!). If you are looking to hang out, drink a nice glass of wine (or two or three), and have a bite to eat, then The Delachaise is where you want to be.

text: SCREW this place. Every time I go it's somewhat 'eh' anyway. Yes, they were busy, but I WAS standing AT the bar (not inthe crowd around it or anything) and watching them help other people around me even though I'd been there first. The only reason I did finally get help was because some stranger hanging out there took pity on me and yelled and waved his arms to get the bartender's attention. Angry at being disappointed from the all-consuming task of pouring Long Islands, though, he rolled his eyes and made fun of the nice man trying to get his attention. I'm aware shouting at the bartender is a faux pas, but jesus! Then they didn't even have Jim Beam and I was charged $14 for 2 shots of Jack Daniels, even though I think their well drinks were 5 or 6. UGH I hate getting ignored at bars for so many reasons. 1. I have better things to do at bars then wait, sober, with no drink, while my drunker friends wander off and get lost. 2. Bartenders make so much damn money in tips, and I'm standing there WANTING TO GIVE THEM MORE MONEY and trying my best, and they aren't letting me. 3. I start getting paranoid. Am I being purposefully ignored because I seem really drunk and they shouldn't serve me? Do I look like shit cuz I just got off work and they only want people who dressed up here? The cold seafood platter was fine, but it's hard to mess that up. Aside from the food, the restaurant was as cold as a meat locker. We had a hard time enjoying the meal while shivering and covering ourselves in napkins just to stay slightly above frigid. We asked for the air to be turned down, but the response was that it would take a long time because the space was so large. I hate giving low ratings, but for as much as we spent ($100/person), it should have been much better. I hope this is only a result of being new. Final thoughts... So things get left out and go bad, fast, especially since there is an oven right next to the "cold" food trays. In my case, the spinach artichoke dip was not just room temperature but also tasted old. We asked the waitress to heat it up and for some fresh bread (since the bread was hard as a rock) because the dip is supposed to be served hot with bread for dipping. I don't think us getting sick was her putting something in our food. I have had many great sandwiches from the COSI restaurants and I was always satisfied, but the experience I went though has made me never want to set one foot in that place ever again. text: In search of an engagement ring I googled "unique engagement rings." And just by chance (it seems), I found Krikawa (accent on the 1st syllable, I learned later). This was over a year ago, and while I ended up using a family heirloom for her engagement ring, we ended up getting our wedding bands there. Where to start? Let me list some thoughts: designs, customer service, and something about the company. Designs The designs are really superb. A nice mix of modern and classic designs with their own twist, many of which have won awards. We liked some of the more naturalistic ("delicate leaf") and the mokume designs. Customer Service From the beginning, Krikawa was super friendly without being pushy or over-eager. At first it seemed like a long shot because they're in AZ, they don't do trunk shows (they're too busy filling orders to do that). So how can you possibly make to order something as important as your wedding or engagement rings? Well, if you're as moved by the designs as we were, we decided to give it a shot. Their website is very attractive and has very detailed photos of all their work. They sent us samples of the rings that we were ordering, the mokume-gane designs. Now, the photos, all most shot in macro and very professionally done, did turn out to look a little better than the rings. Let's face it, a ring isn't a huge thing, and so while the designs were very clear and stark on the photos, blown up at 5x practically, they were more subtle in real life. We were educated about the various finishes and etchings one uses to enhance the look of the multiple metals in the mokume, some as subtle as fine, highly sanded wood grain that you can barely see, and others very heavy, like tortured metal that you can feel by touch. We got a lot of consultation from them: what's a good gem for gardeners? (not emerald) What kind of metals and etching should one get for swimmers? (Sterling will tarnish in the pool, which will enhance the etching while darkening the luster of the ring) How will various metals wear with time? (Pt and Pd are only displaced; Au can scratch/rub off). Because we were able to get several samples, we knew exactly what we were getting. We were and continue to be very pleased with the final results. They were very very patient and very comprehensive with us in their email communications. I don't know how they do it- I'd be tempted to keep emails so I could reuse them; but we always felt they were directly addressing our concerns and questions. They were very good on timelines and deadlines too. Company Other reasons we like this place are that it's a family run business, the owner is passionate about making and selling lovely jewelry, and they used to be part of 1% for the Planet; and now seem to be part of the Responsible Jewelry Council. They sell Polar (Canadian) diamonds, cultured diamonds, and otherwise only Kimberly Process diamonds (which, BTW, some believe rely on too narrow of a definition to avoid being blood diamonds: http://tinyurl.com/yf3pgey). I don't know if similar responsible practices are possible with other gemstones. They also introduced us to different types of gold (rose, yellow, green), and to alternatives to platinum, which we also appreciated. As I've learned more about jewelry, I realize that there really is a lot out there. It boils down to taste: if you like what you see on their website, you shouldn't hesitate to learn more and give them a try. Make sure you get samples from them too.

text: My first time in New Orleans, and I spent more time in Angeli than anywhere else. Thank God for them, too. Open late, and serving delicious food in a lazy, comfortably open atmosphere. If I lived here, this would be the place where I would sit to read books. Kudos for the black and whites projected in back of the bar. My roasted eggplant panini sandwich was cooked in some kind of wonderful, with an absurdly rich and tasty pasta salad with a vinegary kick (those kalamata olives will get you...) and a fresh greens salad. The eggplant was warm and buttery, with an amazingly smooth tomato aioli, and the deep-dish pizza style bread was crisp and perfectly seasoned. Such a satisfying, more than generously portioned, and somewhat healthy meal. Everything down to the ruby tomato slices was fresh-made and worth the pleasantly long wait. I spent almost five hours here one night. Tip extra for the casual, almost East-Village waiters. Do not use the bathroom while here, unless you like bar stalls which haven't been cleaned in a while. Sorry. I had to warn you.

text: LOVE this place! We've taken two sets of out-of-town guests here because we were looking for a vegetarian place in NOLA. A bit hard to come by. I found it on Yelp and had a great experience both times as did all of our guests. The servers/chefs/owners are personable and extremely knowledgeable, with great recommendations on things to try. The food (in traditional New Orleans style) is truly unique and delicious but doesn't leave you with that heavy feeling many places around here do. It's pretty fusion-tastic with ingredients like corn fungus, but I have yet to try anything bad off the menu and I sampled off of almost everyone's plates! The meat dishes are as good as the veggie ones. Things to be aware of: It's quite small. We did easily fit a group of 8, but it was pure luck that the only two large tables (which are next to one another) were both open (tho I think there is a back room and during nice weather, there is outdoor seating); the portions are not huge; it's a little pricey (about $15/plate); the menu is small but changes regularly (or so I hear). I love it's location, a true hole-in-the-wall. I hope it stays a local secret for a while longer! Check it out, you'll love it!

text: Oh, Cafe Brasil, I'm disappointed in you. It's always a little unnerving to be the first patrons of the night, but usually things pick up and you're put at ease... Not this time. We were first in the door and only two other tables were filled by the time we left. Not a particularly good sign for this churrascaria. There are, sadly, plenty of reasons to avoid Cafe Brasil. The fruit flies are pretty high on my list. If I'm not enjoying a picnic outside, I generally don't enjoy swatting bugs away from my food and drink throughout an entire meal. If I was dealing with four fruit flies at my table alone (and I was actively engaged in battle with them), I'd hate to see the unattended buffet. Yikes. I also wasn't really impressed by the service, which was surprisingly inattentive and slow (we were practically the only people there!). Our waiter was far more interested in strumming a little ukulele guitar thing to the piped-in music than he was in checking up on us or refilling our glasses. The atmosphere of the restaurant didn't really do anything for me and it seemed especially dreary without any other customers around. I was sort of saddened by the whole thing. The food, luckily, was not as sad and dreary as most everything else. Justin really, really enjoyed his feijoada (black beans cooked with sirloin, bacon and sausage), although he did surmise that the sausages were like, packaged breakfast links or something. Still, he liked it. I had the peixada, cod with coconut milk, palm oil and fresh herbs. The serving was large and the fish was good--not as flavorful or complex as I thought it might be, but it was good. I don't think either dish was worth the price, which averaged about $20 each, but luckily we had a buy one/get one entree coupon. Was it an off night at Cafe Brasil? I'm not sure. I'd heard some good things about the place and it IS pretty huge, so I hope for their sake they fill up somewhat regularly, but it really fell flat for me. If you do decide to give them a shot, at least heed this piece of advice: do not, under any circumstances, order the special Brazilian red wine drink mixed with condensed milk. Just don't. I don't know what I was thinking; I must've been tricked by the menu's assertion that "you will be surprised!" I was surprised, alright. Won't fall for that one again...

Those ran about $50. So I bought my ridiculous candy and left as someone else was being plied with bubbly on the way in. Luckily, my wife was in a sharing mood and we both enjoyed the truffles. They were really, really delicious and well-made. When eaten slowly (this is what chewing money feels like), the nuances of the layers were distinct, and the tastes quite superb. I won't fault Teuscher for that. But thanks for nothing for not offering me wine when you're clearly lavishing it on the other suckers throwing down way too much for candy. I won't be going back. I can think of better ways to spend the money. Oh yeah, if you do stroll in and start to put an assortment together, brace yourself for the hit, cause shit's going to be astronomical and you'll look like a homeless cheapskate if you need to walk away from the sale. On the upside, that candy money will go waaaay farther across the street at the rite-aid.

text: Wow no one's reviewed this place yet? Really? This was our default Fathers Day outing. Due to the inclement weather, we opted to try a museum we'd never been to, The Toy and Miniature Museum in Wilmington De. When was someone going to tell me that it no longer existed?! Apparently, it waas run out of a guys house and he couldnt keep it up anymore. My GPS Chewie, was making up for past misdeeds and suggested a number of alternatives in the area. Since it wasnt actually raining, we decided to try the Brandywine Zoo. It was only a 10 minute drive from where we were. The Brandywine Zoo, is located in Brandywine Park, a beautiful stretch just outside of downtown Wilmington along the Brandywine river (anyone sense a theme?). The Park itself is reason enough to come. What made it even more majestic is that the recent weather has made the river look like the Colorado Rapids. The sight, sounds and smell were uplifting. I could have stayed here but the kids were promised caged wildlife. The Zoo is a short jaunt away from the river. Rain seemed imminent, but we were determined. It was $16 to get in, but since Mama Nature threatened to piss on us, we opted for the membership at $45. This way, it didnt matter if we had to retreat, we can come back as much as possible( as well as over 100 Zoos in the States). This is a small zoo. Even smaller than our favorite, Elmwood park in Norristown (which was included in our membership). I dont mind small zoos. One of my problems with the Philly Zoo is theres almost too much to see in one visit. They had many stations open to learn from teenage volunteers ( note to self: get kids involved in something like that) and to do crafts (they made me a tie!) Highlights were the monkeys (no great apes, just tamarins and marmosets, whom I love) toucans, Tigers, and Otters. I also have to point out that the gift shop had reasonable prices. Many gift shops have been known to gouge. There was a little snack bar which we didnt partake of today, but seemed good for the future. Even Mother Nature behaved and blew the clouds away giving us some sun. It worked out well because on what could have been a busy Fathers Day weekend, turned out to be not so crowded due to the weather. It was amazing how many people came out of the woodwork, when the sun poked his manliness through the clouds. Didnt bother us because we had already seen everything unmolested. We will be back. And not just because we got the membership. Its a fun daytrip and a great diversion. Plus ive seen at least 3 animals poop there and ould like to add more to my poop journal.

It was just pretty much inedible. I actually have had better, more flavorful burgers at McDonalds. However, the fries here were good. This is the only reason it gets 2 stars and not a 1. But they weren't good enough to save this little food court upstart. A few things I have found out since my visit: First, you can call any beef whatever you want to call it. From the website 'the straight dope' : "...Just because something is labeled "Angus" or "Black Angus" doesn't mean it's the same quality as "Certified Angus Beef." Angus beef is further differentiated by USDA grades such as "prime," "choice," and "select," giving us such labels as "Certified Angus Prime," indicating the best Certified Angus Beef. " http://www.straightdope.com/columns/read/2219/whats-the-big-deal-about-aged-beef-and-angus-beef So, although they advertise 'black angus' - that doesn't mean its any better than the grade of beef that McDonald's or anyone else uses. However, its been an industry buzz word for a while and many have bought into the idea that it is a better grade of beef. And since they have no grade of beef on this 'Black Angus' burger - I have to assume its either the cutter, canner or utility grade - if its black angus at all. Also, if a store is outside handing out a coupon for dollars off their food just to come and ORDER (not necessarily to come back) this should be a sign that they are desperate for customers. All the other restaurants are handing out samples of their food to have you eat there - they are handing out coupons to get you to buy.

text: I have never been inspired to write an online restaurant review...until now. I have finally found my elusive Holy Grail: the worst meal I have eaten in 40 years of life. I didn't even know I was searching for it, but when it was served to me yesterday, I immediately recognized it. A masterpiece of awful. I was just sad it was in this particular restaurant, which, from the outside, had always intrigued me since its days as the Dew Drop Inn (get it? get it?). But this minor disappointment was just one of many I experienced during my first--and last--meal at Bruno's. First, the praise: The coffee was drinkable, though after the meal we had I would not have been surprised had it been utter swill. And the server was friendly, though not particularly attentive, and disappeared for long stretches, though the place was fairly empty. Now, the blame: How on earth can you screw up a turkey club? a TOSSED SALAD, for God's sake? How dare you serve such an awful cheesesteak, in Philadelphia of all places? And we're not even picky eaters. We'll eat at Applebee's and Houlihan's. We have eaten at nearby Sorrento's, which (at least on the night I went 10 years ago) served pretty terrible spaghetti. I will eat synthetic whipped cream on saltines, if there's nothing else at home, and find it reasonably palatable. But I can't imagine returning to choke down the dry-beyond-belief turkey in my sandwich or the gristly and congealed-looking meat in my companion's cheesesteak. (Did I mention the burned, almost charcoal-y bread on the club?) If you wish to end up digging out lettuce and tomato in your sandwich with a fork in an attempt to forage for sustenance, by all means go to Bruno's. And if you get lost in Fairmount Park and finally emerge, delirious and starving, at the far end of the Wissahickon Trail a week later, with your taste buds killed off by burning thirst, we'll understand if you stumble into Bruno's. As for me, whose companion picked up the tab, the meal was not worth what I paid for it.

text: The Natural Cafe!!! No wonder you have such great reviews! I was second guessing my choice when I arrived at the Natural Cafe when I was reading the menu. It seemed a little more naturally adventurous than I originally thought. LOL! Is naturally adventurous even a proper phrase? By that I mean it seemed to be overloaded with vegetables, some I've never had in my sandwiches, and the soups were quite interesting. Lima bean Vegetable soup? Corn bisque? Veggie chili? Lemon herb dressing? I'm not a lemony person I guess you can say. I'm DEFINITELY happy that we decided to stay and eat!!!! Everything was SO good. I'm surprised my body didn't reject all the natural, healthy goodness and instead accepted it quite willingly. We had a half sandwich/salad and a half sandwich/soup which we shared. I'm not a fan of tuna sandwiches generally and it was SO good here! Not over saturated with mayo. There were sprouts and many other veggies in my sandwich. The bread was grainy yet delicious. The lemon herb dressing was FABULOUS too!! Let me tell you about their 500 veggie chili. Okay there aren't 500 veggies but there's a lot in there! Lots of veggies and beans that aren't in "normal" chili and it was SOOOOO yummy especially with their blue corn tortilla chips. The turkey sandwich was good but definitely get the tuna instead! Great meal + water + sparkling apple juice and that's a GREAT LUNCH. If you're ever in SB, definitely check out this place! Also, if Natural Cafe heads down to OC or LA will someone please keep me informed? LOL :)

text: I have been taking our cat Basha to the Cat & Bird Clinic for over 10 years now. About 6 years and some change ago, she had withered away to less than half her weight. We thought the end was near but after a few tests, it was discovered that she had diabetes. We ended up giving her insulin shots and her weight came back and she was fine. Subsequently, Basha came down over the years with glaucoma, high blood pressure, arthritis and lost one of her eyes to a stroke. But she was a tough little beastie and forged on for another year and a half. She finally gave up the ghost last week. I want to thank the amazing staff in general there for always being compassionate both with Basha and with our bank accounts, as sometimes we didn't have the money to pay in full up front. They were clearly more interested in keeping Basha alive and healthy than the money, and I suspect they were equally enamored with our little Ichabod Crane-like feline. I just received a very kind condolence card in the mail this morning from Dr. Sellers and it very much touched my heart that she would take the time out of her day to compose it. Very professional and very compassionate! I would recommend this pet clinic to anybody in the world, and have never left their office feeling anything less than totally satisfied with their work.

Second, when I opened the case looking for my old pickups, they weren't there!! Had I not asked, THEY WOULD NOT HAVE GIVEN THEM TO ME!! Third, and most insulting, was that I got the guitar home and it DID NOT WORK. I took it back immediately and watched as the incompetent technician opened the guitar up again and realized that he "forgot" to install the ground wire. From what I understand, installing pickups is a straightforward process--like changing one's own oil, maybe, except with a soldering gun instead of a big bucket to catch runoff black sludge. I entrusted my guitar to someone who I thought would have the know-how to get the job done and was completely let down. AND, please let me say again, it took two weeks!!

text: I went to grad school at Penn, plus I've taken a night school class a few years after graduation. I am truly grateful for the excellent education I received. Nearly all of my professors were engaging, respectful, and beyond knowledgeable. Even the night-school prof for Japanese wasn't content to just practice rote vocabulary drills; instead she used creative exercises to get us speaking and thinking in Japanese. The fact that Penn is a behemoth among local universities is a source of strength. Every department of any size can offer a rich, diverse course list, plus you can usually take courses from other departments. Penn's financial aid system alone could earn it 5 stars. I came from a working-class family, yet several other top-10 schools offered little or no financial aid. Despite accepting me off the waiting list, Penn provided a generous need-based grant. It wasn't full tuition by any means, but it was by far the best deal I found. Penn has also been savvy about managing its real estate holdings and investing in University City. Penn's urban renewal efforts have turned U. City into a lively, safe, pleasant place. By buying land in West Philly, Penn has left itself plenty of room to grow in the future. If you don't appreciate how significant that is, visit Georgetown, with its tiny (but beautiful) main campus and scores of rented buildings -- yes, they have to rent buildings for classrooms and facilities in the highest-priced neighborhood in DC -- that are bleeding the university dry. To the posters complaining about the undergraduate rich kids' elitism, cliques, and lack of intelligence: Do you really think Penn's rich kids are special? Spoiled rich kids are over-represented in every college across the country. I went to a second-tier college for undergrad and it was swarming with them. Penn is big enough that you can surely find "your kind" of people somewhere in the throngs. Yes, it's hard to deal with people you don't like. Welcome to real life.

text: This was my second time at the steakhouse in the past two years, and I was surprised at how much the food had deteriorated. The first time, the place was not so busy and the meat was delicious. This time, the place was jammed and everything except the mashed potatoes and popovers was bad. Even the service. It revealed itself as what it really is: a big indifferent wildly overpriced cafeteria. I had three cuts of steak, and they were the fattiest pieces of meat I've ever encountered in a restaurant. Ghastly pieces of glistening gristle. I shrugged off the first piece -- shit happens -- but it was nasty. The second piece, however, was equally yellow and what little meat in it was stringy with fat and muscle. By the third piece,a 2-inch square of "garlic-flavored sirloin" -- gristle rolled in burnt garlic (blech!) --my stomach was beginning to roil as I gazed at the mounting plate of picked-apart blubber. My dinner companion thought I had to be exaggerating. He forked a piece of the "meat" from my plate and popped it into his mouth, at which point he got a funny sick look on his face for there he sat, his mouth full of nasty rubbery fat. He had a decision to make: eat his words or eat a big chunk of cellulite. Even though he hates to be wrong, and will eat nearly anything, he spit the fat out: it was that disgusting. My last attempt was a bit of parmesan-crusted pork tenderloin, which was dry but tasty and, praise be, trimmed of fat. However, by then my appetite and my patience were shot. All I could think of was that this festival of fat was going to cost me $50 plus $10 for a glass of cheap wine. And tip. All that for a tricked-out cafeteria. When the waiter brought the check I pointed to all the fat on my plate. He responded like a cafeteria clerk, noting in a flat voice that "some cuts of meat are fatty." Of course! That's why we trim them, pal, before charging people $50 for pieces of low-grade sirloin. Pony up for a ginsu knife and some quality control, Fatty de Chao! And for you carnivores: save your money and go to a cheap steakhouse, where the meat and the check won't make you sick to your stomach.

text: I can't believe no one has reviewed this awesome sandwich place. It's been open almost a year. City Market is a side project of the woman who owns Cafe Galleria on S Main. Their tag line is "Where the dedicated vegan and unapologetic carnivore can eat together in harmony" or something like that. In other words, they are very vegan friendly but I still love them. Aside from fresh deli sandwiches, hot breakfast items, panninis, quiches, salads and soups they sell a few specialty grocery items like dry pasta, sauces, a few stir fry supplies, basic milk, eggs, cheese, fruit AND Pirate's Booty, my favorite snack ever. They're also very reasonably priced, deliver on weekdays, make a decent cappuccino and have fabulous pastries in the am- I mean the best croissants I've had since I was in Paris, baked on premises an hour ago. Go EARLY- they sell out quick. Best Part: The Super Italian: Prosciutto, sopressatta, cappy ham, provolone and whatever else you like. Or for the vegans, The 'Lil Debbie: a bunch of green stuff I don't like and hummus on a pita. My vegan friend says it's good. Also, lots of nice semi-locally bottled drinks- MASH and Boylan's Pure Cane Sodas, in addition to the usual Coke and OJ. Other Best Part: I LOVE that they slice the meat/cheese to order for each sandwich, not ahead of time. I hate going to Subway and imagining how long that slice of swiss has been sitting around. Worst Part: Lunchtime on weekends is pretty crazy. I recommend sitting at the counter with a friend or a book in case your order takes a few minutes. The seats are rarely full, most people take out. Service is very friendly, but occasionally a bit slow. There are only a few people there who have any experience. The place is still pretty new, so they're working out the kinks. The sandwiches are worth the wait.

text: Finally! Some REAL Mexican in the Philly area! After years of a lack of Mexican, and then five years in LA where the real Mexican flows, I was happy to finally read reviews and find this place. I quickly grabbed my mom, and off we went for some Mexican. And it definitely didn't disappoint. A quick word, though - it's not exactly in the most welcoming of neighborhoods. Then again, many of the best ethnic food places aren't. The interior is pleasantly Mexican kitsch, with stylized murals adorning one wall and the ceiling. A relatively sparse table layout leaves the place feeling a little cold and empty, but provides plenty of room to navigate. A telenovela was playing while we ate, which provided for some fun conversation starters. The menu is deliciously authentic, with dishes that your average American would not recognize. Tacos, enchiladas, fajitas grace one small page, while more traditional "platos fuertes" take up two pages. While more expensive, these "strong plates" will provide a great journey into the far more varied cuisine of Mexico than generic Mexican places would like you to believe. I enjoyed a giant platter of enfrijoladas, tortillas stuffed with meat, topped with refried beans, lettuce, tomatoes, sour cream, guacamole...the works. The beans were excellent, which is a pretty good indicator of the restaurant. However, I was a little disappointed in the carnitas that I chose to be my meat - it was a little on the dry side. I no longer live in the Philly area, but I know Taqueria La Michoacana will be on my list of "to go" places whenever I return. And most importantly, my mom has decided that she will return on her own whenever she wants Mexican.

text: Phonoluxe is the black sheep of the Nashville record store family. You've got the Ernest Tubb Record Shop downtown (and the tourist hole annex at Opry Mills) which is recognized, because of its tourist appeal, as the patriarch of the whole family. Then there's the Great Escape, the matriarch of the family, with its flourishing and oft-times overbearing store down on Broadway and all its children spread out across the Southeast living their own lives but never straying too far from home. She means well, but sometimes she can really get up your ass. Grimey's is the cool aunt. Ya know, the one who comes to family functions wearing a leather jacket and proceeds to drink too much wine, then steals you and a few of your cooler cousins away to tell you stories about how she used to hang out with the Ramones and Patti Smith in NYC. But Phonoluxe, well, the family tries not to mention him. He's the uncle that time forgot, the weird one, that one that you weren't really allowed to hang out with when you were a kid. But then you got a little older, out from under the protection of mom's skirts, and you found out that Uncle Phonoluxe was, well, he was kind of awesome. So you'd sneak over there with a little money and a few beers that you managed to steal from your dad's fridge, you know, back in the early days of your Kerouac stage, and you'd just sit and listen to Uncle Phonoluxe for hours. He'd tell you stories of big legged women who were loose with their charms and who would whisper the secrets of the universe to you as you drifted off to sleep in their arms. Or stories of keen eyed road warriors whose world was built of leather and chrome and rock and roll. Or maybe he'd let you in on the world of the juke joints, with their ribald men and women, howling like a pack of wild, hungry dogs into the great gaping night of the world, wanting like nothing else to be heard above the roar of evil and despair and ignorance. Uncle Phonoluxe was shabby and wild-eyed, and it wasn't always easy to be around him when things got rough, but the things he taught you were the things that would save your life on all those dark, wicked nights that you would encounter throughout your nomadic twenties. Dad may have provided for the family, mom may have shepherded you through the days of your childhood, and cool aunt Grimey may be the family member you speak to the most, but there's not a day goes by that you don't think about Uncle Phonoluxe, and everything he showed you.

Every restaurant, except for the occasional few, carry the same mass produced dreck and forget the grocery stores unless we're talking AJ's killer selection. I found Catavinos and I have been thrilled, if not a little shocked, to find that they carry so many wines of quality, all under $15. The owner, Yvonne, is a very nice woman with a dynamite smile and a great attitude towards wine. Her palate is superb, too. I have been in the shoppe (as she calls it) on several occasions now and I have never left disappointed by her recommendations. I tell her what I like and she says try this, or try that and let me know what you think. I go home and open a Chilean Carmenere or a Washington blend and I am always so surprised. Wine has always been a "you get what you pay for" proposition. Not any more. I joined her wine club and I get two bottles worth at least $30 each for a total of $35 month and, thus far (3 months), I have been very pleased with what she is giving out. One month we had a California Cab that would have competed with a $70 bottle I would have been drinking otherwise. She also does tastings which are fun. I have met some wild and outgoing people there. She has a loyal following and they seem like a good group. Do yourself a favor, go in and ask her for some recommendations and see if you are not just a little shocked at the value for the money.

The Signature is more of a traditional pizza with a layer of cheese, topped with spinach and crushed seasoned tomatoes. If you're in the mood for something with a little heat, try the marinara pie. Just crust, spicy marinara sauce, topped with grated asiago. Simple and truly satisfying. Service is great, but expect them to be busy on the weekends! The line is usually out the door. Be advised, they have strange hours and are cash only.

text: I had been meaning to check this place out for a while so today I did. Being called a tap house I had a pretty high expectation for the selection & I would say that was just about met. They had a lot of great things on tap, mostly things that were fairly common micro brews and a few unique ones. There was a shortage of IPAs but I really can't complain considering what my local options usually are... although if you bump stuff like bud and such off tap you'd probably free up some valuable room for a few more beers indicative of a tap house. The menu had some intriguing choices but I was surprised at the limited options. No soups & the few entrees they had were all in the same "a little too high for a bar" price. While I'm talking about price, just in general I felt most everything except for the beer was over priced. Keeping with the theme of being overpriced, at the end of the night I had a tiresome drive ahead of me so I asked how much it was for JUST Red Bull, no vodka... just a can with stuff in it, and was told $10.50 regardless of vodka or not. REALLY?? I'm hoping this is just a case of lazy data entry in that maybe the computers only have a button for the mixed Red Bull drink which even so is lame, it doesn't take much effort to make some simple options available. A lot of places actually make it a point to offer the nonalcoholic drinks at a lesser cost or sometimes free as a way to encourage designated drivers so this totally threw me off in every way. The food I had was well made and tasted great but some "should have been simple" questions I had when ordering were met with a deep lack of knowledge despite proclaiming the complete opposite. I asked how the fries were served and described exactly how I thought they might be based on what dish they were served with considering what I've seen elsewhere locally (which is very common) and the server had no idea what I was talking about. She went on to seemingly make something up on the fly about how they're served. When they came out they were EXACTLY what I had described and not at all what she had said they were. On the surface this isn't a big deal and they were delicious none the less but how do you work in a place and serve probably TONS of what is a very common item and have no clue about them? I later asked a different server about another menu item, "Fingerling potato hash" and if that was just a cute name for mashed potatoes. She said "yes, they are mashed potatoes" and when I asked the typical "Have you had them, are they good?", she responded with an overly enthusiastic "Oh we're required to try everything on the menu here and everything is freshly prepared... etc" in the classic "tow the company line style". Again when these came out they were the polar opposite of mashed, they were cut seasoned fingerling potatoes. Again they tasted great but how do you get something so simple so wrong and play it off like you absolutely know. I think I speak for most people when I say it's safe to assume and completely reasonable for a server to have NOT tried everything on a menu, especially considering the increasing number of food allergies and vegetarians. So if you haven't had it don't lie or talk around the question with a training book answer. I'm really hoping that the servers aren't trained to say that but it sounded like the typical response someone would be instructed to say. Knowledgeable service... that's what kinda sealed it for me. I really honestly do not have a very high bar set for what I consider to even be great service and again I don't expect a server to have tasted the whole kitchen but everyone should at least be able to describe the menu and make some small popularity based suggestions if they haven't tried the food. Both of them were very nice and did come back a fair amount of times to check on me but I just really dislike it when it's obvious someone is just winging it and expects me to believe it. I'm just glad I didn't have any beer questions. I'll remember to bring a bank roll next time in case I want a limited edition Red Bull to keep me awake on 95.
label: NEG

text: I live right around the corner from Feder's Fresh so it's really convenient for me. The best part is being greeted at the entrance with a huge spread of delicious samples. They usually have the fruits that are in season. (Is the plural of fruit fruit or fruits?) I tried the purple potato which I honestly would never buy except that I had that sample. They also have a bowl of pita slices (which they make themselves) and lots of great dips and salads to go along with it. I really like the babaganush, red pepper hummus and roasted garlic. Most - maybe all - of these come from a place in Brooklyn and are kosher. The next best thing after the samples is the smoothie bar. They use fruit and only fruit, which is great. I'd recommend adding yogurt. It is so fresh and simple - its those times that I think, "I could totally do that myself." But why would I when they do it for me and very affordably? As for the produce, the prices are pretty good. The vegetables are fairly fresh but the fruit tends to be riper than at 'normal' stores so plan to eat them right away. The selection is pretty good - I haven't looked for something that I didn't find there. Overall, I enjoy shopping here because it's small, clean and less hustle-and-bustle than the nearby Whole Foods. I should also note that the address says Spring Garden, but the entrance is actually on 19th Street.

text: It's a big, spacious place, and they make a lot of beer. The Sampler is most certainly the way to go - only $6 for 4oz tastes of every beer they have - for us, this meant 11 4oz samples for $6. That's nearly 3 beers for $6. Awesome! Unfortunately, the beer quality was not quite as good. The light beers are average at best (though I don't enjoy light beer, so take that opinion with a grain of salt). The Oktoberfest beer was fairly average, the dunkel weizen was not anything I'd remotely consider 'dunkel.' The Anvil ale, especially the cask conditioned version, was excellent, and the porter was good as well - dark, chocolatey, and with a nice bitter finish balanced by the maltyness. The food was filling and tasty - sweet potato fries were fantastic, pork tenderloin was perfectly tender, and the catfish was delicious (though they don't entirely get the concept of red beans & rice). There was also a suprising number of beautiful girls hanging out on their own or in small groups - looks like quite the place to go out drinking if you're a local. Prices were perhaps a shade high, but the menu is enormous, and the service was stellar - fun, friendly, and very perky (but not annoyingly so).

text: 1 star for service and 3 stars for food = 2 stars i had such high hopes for rooster. not only and i a lover of breakfast foods, but i am also quite fond of david bailey's other two establishments in st louis, bridge and bailey's chocolate bar. rooster seemed like a sure thing. i was sorely mistaken. the main problem with rooster is the service. we went on a weekday morning around 9am. we walked into the fairly busy restaurant, and stood awkwardly in the front of the dining room waiting to be seated. eventually we figured it must be a seat yourself kind of place, and found a table. it took at least 10 minutes for a sever to bring us menus and take our drink orders. another 10 minutes passed before we received our drinks. we then placed our order for 2 crepes. 30 minutes passed before we finally received our food. knowing we wanted to split a sweet crepe as well, i put in the order for our nutella crepe at this time. the food at rooster is just ok. my wife and i each had a savory crepe of some sort, and also shared a nutela crepe. everything we ate was decent, but nothing was memorable or exciting at all. i also felt the prices were a bit high. this is something i am ok with if the food is excellent, but this is not the case at rooster overall, rooster was a huge disappointment. our meal, which consisted of juice and 3 crepes, took an hour and a half, and cost around $40. i would have been more satisfied at bread co. for half the cost and an eighth of the time. david bailey, i love bridge and the chocolate bar, but rooster really needs to step up its game.

text: You know, I hate to disagree with the majority of reviewers here, but I didn't think Wasabi was anything special. Granted, I did visit during a very busy time (Friday evening around 6pm), but I don't really think that was any excuse for the poor service and insubstantial rolls I received. I ordered a Rainbow roll and a Rasta roll (I believe), and while they were tasty, I felt like they had skimped on the amount of fish and other ingredients in the roll. Also, the rolls weren't very tight, and I felt like they were hastily put together, as they were falling apart as I tried to eat them. I may be out of line here, but when I eat dinner at 6:30, I don't want to have to go somewhere to eat 4 hours later because I'm hungry again. I also thought the prices were a little high for the amount of food I received. This is why I usually try to avoid the more "trendy" sushi restaurants...too much "atmosphere," not enough substance. In addition to this, I felt like the service was definitely lacking. Granted, it was a peak time to eat, and I was at a two-top at the back of the restaurant, but I don't think that's any excuse. Our server barely spoke two words the entire time we were there, and I felt like she just didn't pay a lot of attention to us. Finally, there is one more thing I have to get off of my chest. For a restaurant CALLED Wasabi, I thought it was almost ironic that they had some of the weakest wasabi I have ever tasted. I am not the biggest fan of the stuff, but I do like it, and when I can put an amount that would usually bring me to tears in my soy and not be gasping for breath with tears running down my face, something is wrong. I am sorry to disagree with everyone here, and maybe I'm just spoiled by my favorite sushi place, but I was simply not impressed. I doubt I'll be going back, especially when my favorite sushi place is so consistently awesome. Why take a chance?

text: I have a love-hate relationship with Great Scot. It is a block and a half from my office, and I used to live just three blocks south of it. Sure there is the South Square Market at 23rd and South, Trader Joe's and 22nd and Market, and Super Fresh and Whole Foods at 10th and South...but if you just want a few groceries to pick up for dinner on the way home from work, it's really the only option. But oh my goodness is it expensive. $7 for orange juice, $5 for a teeny block of cheddar, $6 for a box of oreos. It is out of control. I have never escaped this place without paying at least $17, and usually that's on top of a more thorough (and expensive), planned out grocery run earlier in the week. It's just no good. Having said that, I love the way it smells. You walk past and it's oh, so tempting. And they literally have EVERYTHING. I wanted ice cream cones in February last year. They had them. I needed poppyseed filling to make hamentashen. They were the only store around that had it. Every flavor of Ben and Jerry's? Check. Fat free ricotta? Yep. Bread from Metropolitan Bakery? Definitely. I mean, I have literally never not found what I have been looking for. Although I did just call from my desk at work to see if they had Girl Scout cookies...they do not. But price flaws aside, they work in a pinch, and let's be honest- the resentments are all stemming from some jealousy that we didn't think to open a grocery store there first, right? :)

text: Okay. Let me tell you this much...IF AND WHEN THIS PLACE IMPROVES ON THEIR SERVICE. IT WILL BE A 5 STAR RESTAURANT. text: Mama's House is a humble little gem tucked away in a strip mall on Pendleton Pike, but you won't be disappointed in the food. Come here with a big crowd and fire up the coal barbecue pit, conveniently located in the center of your table. text: My current benchmark for mussels is Monk's Cafe in Philadelphia, another Belgian Gastropub of sorts. The Belgian Dark Ale and a sour-style beer I had were spectacular. 2) Frites: Accompanying the mussels, these were excellent. Fried to crispness and rich color. 3) Cheese: I cannot remember the exact name, but it was a generous portion (almost the size of a deck of cards) of a hard, rich, buttery cheese that accompanied the sour ale perfectly. text: I found this place by accident as it isn't very noticible tucked away in the strip mall, frontlined by the dingy little Robin Hood restaurant. Anyway, I was going to make that my 3rd roll, but I was too full to order it haha. All I have to say is....I will DEFINITELY go back and even the kids liked the place. You can choose from many flavors both ordinary (cherry, lemon, grape) to exciting (rose, lavender). Everything else about the place is just as good. The atmosphere is cute, the service is helpful and friendly, and while the line can get very long there is almost always seating available. text: My buddy and I somehow got in for a 9PM reservation last night to enjoy their 4 course Sunday, $45 menu. We started with a hearty, rich lentil based soup with small chunks of veal in the stock. What was so memorable about this soup was that it was incredibly thick, rich, and smooth, with the soup almost coating the spoon -- a delicious way to start the meal. Second course was a choice between escargot, oxtail terrine, and foie gras. They had just run out of the oxtail, which worked out well as my friend wanted the escargot and I the foie gras. The escargot sat perfectly cooked with lima beans in a rich, salty sauce. My friend commented that it was the single best escargot presentation he's ever had. For me, I've never had better foie gras either. Buttery and soft, yet crispy on the outside, this paired incredibly with the kumquats and a small piece of syrupy bread. For mains, the choices were a pigs feet braise, scallops, hangar steak, or a branzino fillet special. I chose the branzino, perfectly seared over well cooked veggies. Very light yet very flavorful. My friend went with the hangar steak, which was cooked medium rare. The highlight, however, was the asparagus and hashbrown mix served as a side. This is classical french cooking at its best. Dessert was a choice of cranberry pie, creme brulee (sold out), chocolate roll, or ice cream and sorbet. My friend went with the ice cream and sorbet -- a scoop of slightly too sweet raspberry sorbet and a scoop of light and delicate pistachio ice cream. I went with the chocolate roll, which intertwined layers of soft white cake with perfect chocolate mousse. A garnish of whipped cream and a few berries completed a great dessert. I wasn't expecting a lot out of dessert here -- as a small byo, they don't have a pastry chef that I'm aware of -- but it was very well executed. Service was professional if a bit rushed. Charlotte, the co-owner, makes sure to stop by every table and greet customers -- her charm is only overshadowed by her husband's cooking. A great meal, and truly lived up to the hype!

text: I give Dock Street two stars, although we at least pick up a pizza here every month. Why do we keep coming back? Sheer desperation. Dock Street is the best pizza in the area. Hands down. It's not cheap, it's not unique, we always get the same thing (the Portabella and Gorgonzola number), and the atmosphere is crummy. But there's really no place else to get a decent pizza around here. If you do need a good pizza and are in West Philly, though, we'd recommend getting take-out. The space is big and looks as if it was originally intended to be industrial, but in a futile attempt to warm it up someone had amateur craft night and spattered their work all over the walls. The staff is, generally speaking, slow, and working too hard to affect how icily chic they are to serve you with any sensitivity or consideration. The beer is actually all right, but five bucks for beer brewed on the premises (which costs very little, despite the spiking cost of hops) and served in a tiny glass is just too much to bear. We hope never to have to eat in the restaurant itself again, although we'll certainly spend our hard-earned money on a palatable pizza, once in a while. That's the price one pays to live in West Philly, I guess.

I went in to buy a 12" inner tube for my stroller and hoped he would offer to fix the tire, something that takes 5-10 minutes. The store was empty when I got there. text: I went to El Tumi a couple weeks ago with some co-workers for lunch. I've never had Peruvian food before, so I can't claim to be a great expert, but I enjoyed my lunch. After being seated, we received corn chips and a magical green sauce. It was delicious, and my only complaint was the small serving. I asked for more, and we got another small serving. If my Googling is accurate, this sauce is "huacatay" and requires an imported herb, hence the rationing. I had a sandwich of fried sliced pork with sweet potato slices and marinated onions on a nice roll--slightly crusty on the outside, soft and tender on the inside. It was quite good. One of my companions had the ceviche, the other some sort of yellowish soup with noodles and chicken. I can't say much other than they both enjoyed their food. One also got the purple corn drink. I sampled, and it was quite good. The dining room is quite pleasant, and the service was friendly, though leisurely. All in all, a good place to try if you want something different.

text: We met some friends staying at the Royal Sonesta across the street. They wanted to check with their hotel concierge for recommendations. The concierge walked around from the desk, grabbed my friend's arm, and practically marched us over to Oceana Grill, which was across the street. The aggressive marketing (and what I can only assume are kickbacks to hotel staff) set a bad tone for the meal -- how good can a restaurant be if they have to try that hard? One couple in our group ordered an appetizer of fried eggplant that was tasty, although I recommend skipping the blend of ketchup and mayonnaise that they served as a sauce. (Ask if they have a marinara.) I ordered "Redfish Amer" ($18), which was pan-fried redfish smothered in a creamy crawfish sauce. I grew up on the gulf coast, where we used to catch our own redfish. I can only assume the redfish in my dinner (if it was indeed redfish) was farm-raised. At first bite, I thought it was catfish -- it tasted like the bottom of a lake! The crawfish sauce was bland almost to the point of being tasteless. It was like hollandaise with no lemon, with some chewy red bits of meat thrown in. Several people at our table ordered the "Taste of New Orleans" ($16), which was a trio of Crawfish Etoufee, Red Beans and Rice, and Jambalaya. The jambalaya had a pleasant spiciness, but the rice was a little gummy and the sausage was a little rubbery. This was the first time I've had jambalaya, and I would have to try it at a better restaurant before I passed final judgment. The etoufee was bland but passable. Is it possible that they used canned beans for the red beans and rice? I'm just not sure. On the plus side, we had a group of nine and we were seated immediately. We had some picky children eaters with us, but they had a kid's menu if you asked -- Chicken fingers or fried shrimp or fried cheese sticks (each served with fries) for $5. The mixed drinks were $6 and served in large schooners. The service, while not superb, was adequate - no complaints there. The prices, which seemed a little high at first blush, may not be too far out of line for a touristy restaurant just off Bourbon Street. Portions were large -- a couple could easily share an appetizer and one entree and fill up.
label: NEG

text: I attended a baby shower at Maurizio's in Cinnaminson* last Saturday and I have to say, it was quite nice. There were maybe two servers who worked a room of at least 50 women, and they did so with patience and haste. Bread baskets filled with shiny, hot garlic knots were placed at every table, and dressings for the starter salads were served on the side so everyone had control over how much and what kind. There were three options for lunch: chicken parm with spaghetti, a chicken panini with spinach and provolone and ravioli in tomato cream sauce with mozzarella. I went with the ravioli, which turned out to be the perfect size for an afternoon meal and quite delish. The paninis that my friends ordered were large enough to feed a linebacker (or a pregnant woman, take your pick), but my girls reported their selections to be on the bland side. Coffee was offered immediately after plates were cleared but before dessert, the way it should be. While I don't find myself dining out in this neck of the woods very often anymore, I would recommend the place for those who do, or as a decent venue alternative when you can't cram everyone into the living room. *I tried to change the address as this restaurant is not in Burlington, but it has not yet changed over. A friend ended up in Burlington when she looked up the restaurant and put it in her GPS... she was an hour late to the shower. Wah-wah.

text: This place is a hidden gem! After hearing about it from my boyfriend's Mexican friends (its now their favorite place to order), we have been back multiple times! The food is simple, fresh and addictive! And they deliver! The place is small, from the outside looks like a typical corner store. But in the back are a few tables and a counter for ordering. Everything is made to order, giving you time to wander around the store. Side Note: On my last visit, their produce looked better than anything I have seen recently in a supermarket! If I lived one that side of Broad St, I would shop there often. The food is worth the wait! Ive had the chorizo tacos and spicy pork w/ pineapple tacos. My BF has ordered the black corn & mushroom quesadilla and one of the extremely large Tortas. All are delicious, and even when your full, you want more! The side sauces make you wish they gave you something to dip into them. The only negatives: Parking is hard. This is South Philly, so you will need to circle for a spot or double park. If your local, its worth walking. If your a Gringa like me, you may have some trouble ordering over the phone due to the language barrier. Several of the items on the menu are similar if your not clear. Our last visit, our order was wrong, but we were happy to wait (the food IS good). This place is definitely worth a try for homemade food at great prices!

text: Please excuse the raunchiness I'm about to provide, but when you burp two hours after a meal, and you think to yourself... yummm... that is a sign of a mighty tasty dish. I went here on a Monday night... decent crowd. I loved the fact that there was virtually a TV, no exaggeration, EVERYWHERE I looked, with the Phills game on (though they lost my night was not ruined). I was seated by a pleasant host, and received great service all night! The atmosphere was dim, clean, and definitely comfortable. To start things off, with the suggestion of Blake F. (name drop for credibility), I and a bud ordered the sweet potato fries to split. They were nothing short of phenomenal. Their thicker than steak fry structure made the slightly sweet taters flavor beyond enjoyable, and the three dipping choices were all wonderful (a sweet-ish cinnamony creamy one, hint of a cayenne/ this tastes sorta like outbacks sauce for their bloomin' onion one, and a third that was citruslike and SPICY). From there I went with the vegetarian Mediterranean wrap, which was filled with humus, lettuce, tomato, and roasted pepper. It too was awesome. My friend went with the spicy Moroccan salmon, which was paired with grilled potatoes and a REALLY good red onion jam. Everything on his plate was thoroughly enjoyed as well. I cannot wait to go back. And side-note, the sweet potato fries are prob the only ones I'll ever eat post-fridge.

Cooked just right with a side of rice and a salad. ...again, this is one of my go-to joints. Low-key, decent prices, good service and tasty food keep me coming back.

text: There was an across-the-board mediocrity to the place that makes it better than the lower echelon of fast-food chains but not much higher. The first time I went I played it safe and got their $5 value meal. I guess I shouldn't have been surprised when I saw that the burger was more like a kids' burger. I learned my lesson and went for their two most premium burgers the next two times I was there. Unfortunately those burgers are on the dinky side as well, and I'm not exactly a fan of somewhat stale and crusty buns on my burgers. I felt like I was ripped off on my onion rings order given how many I got and what I paid for them. Their fries (which reminded me of Wendy's fries) are a better value. When it came to taste, everything I had was average at best, right down to the fry sauce. I didn't bother with their shakes. If you live right by or are coming down from Bogus Basin and starving, this place will do in a pinch. Otherwise there are better burger places to be had with a couple extra miles of driving. My experiences there were a lot like my experiences at Viking, another longstanding local burger joint whose appeal escapes me. I thought the food at Pac-Out was a little better (most notably with the fries), but not enough to give a higher rating than what I gave for Viking.

text: I was very excited when I was in Philly and realized I was a block away from McGillin's - the oldest bar in Philly. I had to check this place out. I was ready to go and made my way over. Walking up I was pumped with a back alley entrance, off the beaten path (at least to me), i thought i had found a great place. Then I walked into a karoke, crowded, loud, hard to get a beer, pushy people trapped in their college hayday. This was all on a Tuesday night... I don't know if this is a one off night or what but I took it as the norm. So I can say I have experienced McGillin's but I will look for another option next time I am in the neighborhood.

text: Rexall is . . . Rexall. There is nothing special about Rexall, sorry to say. I don't think it's going downhill. it's never really been that great. When I think of Rexall, I think of over priced food that is doused in fat and grease, I think of concrete in every direction, and I think of dirt. And yet, it continues to fill up for hockey games, concerts, trade shows, and other events. I guess when it's the only option, it's an appealing one. I find that the staff at Rexall are not very happy to be there either. I can't remember the last time I met a pleasant worker there. Whether it's good or bad, it's all we've got. Hopefully it won't always be that way though.
label: NEG

text: Perfect, perfect, perfect little restaurant. I brought my girlfriend here for her birthday and once again we had an excellent meal with no complaints. After the standard crusty italian bread with seasoned olive oil, we started with the grilled quail (a tiny delicious bird, on top of chopped vegetables) and the simple green salad, which frankly was one of the most amazing salads I've seen. It was this huge plate of bright green mixed greens, each one perfect as if they had all been hand picked - seriously, nothing wilted or brown on that plate at all. It was accented with candied almonds, green apple slices, and crumbled bleu cheese - delicious! Moving onto entrees, I had the magret of duck with hen of the woods mushrooms (absolutely perfect, the duck was cooked precisely medium rare, the mushrooms were succulent, the flavors were impeccable) and my girlfriend had the king of mackerel which she enjoyed immensely (but I'm pretty sure mine was better). The duck was a lot of food, actually - surprisingly so. We finished off by sharing the banana trifle, which was soooo good that it inspired us to go home and make a trifle cake the next day (not quite as good and certainly half as pretty, but tasty nonetheless). Probably one of our favorite restaurants in Philly. Make reservations well in advance, bring a bottle of wine, and bring plenty of cash because they don't take plastic.
label: POS

text: Minar Palace is at best, good, and at worst, inedible. I stop in from time to time due largely to it's proximity to my apartment, and the fact that new samosa sucks incredibly. I order chana masala, as it is one of only two vegan options. (the other being dal, which is consistently over salted.) It's usually ok, I do like the flavor, and I love the mint chutney with it. Also the cabbage salad. Today however, (and when i stopped in last week) the chana was some chick peas floating in flavored oil. You really couldnt even call it a sauce. Im not overly sensitive to oiliness, but this is seriously disgusting. My brother's samosas were burnt as well. And although theyve switched to actual dishes for dinner, their environmentally unfriendly plastic plate/cutlery predilection continues during the day. It's tacky and irresponsible. And speaking of tacky, what's with the mcdonalds style menu board up front?? They cant decide what vibe theyre going for. It's a weird juxtaposition, and I mean that in the worst way possible.
