text: Today I took a trip down memory lane(Drive Thru) today..back to one small patch of pleasure and relief that I experienced in the final miserable week of September 2005 in the aftermath of Katrina. I'd come back to close out the apartment of my then, soon to be fiancee, soon after that ex-fiancee. As I cruised the littered streets of Metairie in my Big Yellow 21' Hertz truck salvaging perfectly good throw aways(Like the $1900 refrigerator that the disposers had CLEANED that worked PERFECTLY!) there was little respite to be found. It was hot..it was bleak..it was sad..it was infuriating..and..did I forget to mention it was hot? I emptied the apartment all by myself after a few days of prepping in between my salvage runs. One of the neighbors said "You are in your element..like Mad Max" Pretty astute observation..I had started drawing plans for bomb shelters at about 12 years old. Shortly after that I had purchased a survivalist classic "Life After Doomsday" by Bruce D Clayton(a great book for the survivalist on your Christmas list). What I realized was that in that time after Katrina...we experienced the closest thing to apocalypse that anyone in the United States had endured in it's entire history. One thing that became pretty apparent..after the Fall(Society..Not Autumn)...restaurants are gonna be damn hard to find. That was the case after Katrina..in a time when most people had no kitchens, much less electricity or gas. Dining options tended to be limited to MREs, canned stuff.. or Red Cross meals. I had brought sandwich stuff in my 7 day ice chest with my precious ice all the way from Alabama..but Ohh for something fresh and hot... It was at THIS location of Lee's, one of the very first restaurants reopened that I found air conditioning..and hot food. The Menu was limited.. burgers..Fries..Not much else.. The wait was close to 30 minutes..but nobody cared..there was AIR CONDITIONING. I had ordered a Double Works..and when it came..and I bit in.. it was one of the most pleasant experiences of my life..sure it was because of the stark contrast from days of hard work in the heat and no other good hot food...but even in normal times Lee's burgers are much better than most chains. This brings me to today..I ordered the same thing but they had onion rings this time..I got the large.. When I sat down, that first bite took me back those 5 years to that bit of civilization on a bun that had given me such relief. It was juicy, it was hot, it was sloppy and it was good. What else can you expect from a burger cooked under onions? My mountain O onion rings(can I get a kiss?) were DAMN good also.. It may have taken the destruction of New Orleans and 5 years of nostalgia..but..this location earned this 5 star rating from me.
label: POS

text: I would never call this the best Mexican food in St. Louis. However, I keep coming back here. Why would I do that? The margaritas are delicious, cold, and when you buy them by the pitcher, they last forever and don't really cost that much. They have good live mariachi music on a fairly regular basis, and the patio in back is smoke free and lends itself to some great people watching...including the random shirtless (at least, I hope they are walking around just shirtless) that live next door in their very open apartments. The service at this place is stellar as well. Every waiter I have ever had has been incredibly attentive and makes sure that we have everything we need. They refill your chips if you are just there drinking, make sure your salsa is full as well, and make their rounds regularly, but not so much so that it is annoying and you want them to back off. The food is always hot and comes out very quickly as well. I have never waited more than 10 minutes for my food to arrive after ordering, even when the restaurant is packed. So, perhaps I come back for service, perhaps it is for the drinks, or perhaps it's because after said drinks I can walk to my friend Mary's and stay over without ever having to get in my car. Regardless, I enjoy coming here and although it's not the most stellar Mexican, it's still a solid dining experience.
label: POS

text: Was totally disappointed with my latest Franky & Johnny's experience. The door to the kitchen was open, and patrons could see into the kitchen area where food was being dropped on the floor, countertops were unclean, and servers didn't care. I had a crabclaw appetizer, which was listed as one of the specials. It came out fishy-smelling and cold, and I am unsure if this was what the "chef's" were aiming for. My date had an oyster salad. The lettuce was soggy and old. Even the crawfish, which is supposedly the restaurant's strong point, was a total disappointment. I have never been served so many dead crawfish. text: So, I went with a co-worker last week, and here's my take of the place: Pros: Clean Cutesy/Homey Neighborhood place Fast Service Cons: Californian conception of Southern food So-So Servers Tiny setting Needs pricing on online menu This neighborhood gem is not destination dining. There's no need to drive across town, stand in line, and wait for food you can experince better elsewhere for perhaps a few dollars less. Once I established that, it was easy to give a review. My co-worker and I sit down, and observe a server walk towards, us, then proceed to set a place at the empty table in front of us. no greeting, no 'someone will be right with you', nothing. We watched as his girlfriend sauntered in, (complete with a laptop, so that's revenue management lost during lunch rush at a 4-top while she nursed a latte),was served beverage and lunch before us (as we were there at least five minutes prior). The fried green tomatoes were deep-fried in some weird batter, and smothered in a remoulade sauce that seemed more like jacked-up mayo w/one sad shrimp atop each slice. My co-worker ordered the basic breakfast - lumberjack-sized portions, and straightforward. In fact, she couldn't finish the plate. I had their signature Shrimp and Grits. A hearty serving of well-made grits with a decent-sized amount of shrimp, only to be marred by the addition of rosemary. I like rosemary, but not in seafood and certainly not anywhere near my grits. This rendition is what I would expect if I were sitting in somewhere in the Bay Area, not in New Orleans. Naturally, the fastest thing that appeared at the table was our check. My ass out the door may have been even faster.
label: NEG

text: I feel for Percy Street. As a born and raised Texan I have visited the iconic Texas BBQ joints (Kreuz, Smitties, City market, etc.) and know how contentious a food BBQ is. No food draws so much skepticism. Combine this with being a little pricey and located in Phily and the stakes are high. The food: Brisket, good but quite smoky and a small portion. Sausage; I wanted a crispier case. Cornbread, stellar. German potatoe salad, spot on. Coleslaw, boring, tasted like store bought. Percys has an identity crisis. It wants to be original to the Texas style but it desires to be more upscale than the the Texas dives. And as they say, "You can't skin a hog two ways". Sadly, to charge upscale prices they should take a note from the classy BBQ restaurant in Austin Lamberts which respectfully plays with BBQ cuisine rather than replicating it.

The food isn't bad, (although I'm not sure what part of New Orleans they get their recipes from) and there is a limited bar. Seating is limited too, a few booths, a few tables and a few bar seats. You may also want to be prepared for the show to start late, because the sound check always seem to be happening at the time the show is supposed to start, but for $7 you can see a swingin' big band in Nashville on a Tuesday night.

text: This place gives farmers' markets a bad name. I was so excited to check this place out after just moving from the SF Bay Area. I was anxious to start buying all local and clean food here in downtown Nashville. The building is nice and the convenience of 7 days a week would be good if they actually were a true farmers market (non-profit and all local farms). Unfortunately, there is a lot of food sold here that isn't even local. Don't assume anything is local. Ask the vendors where it's from. We also couldn't find anything that was pesticide free. I'm not picky about whether something is certified organic, but would prefer to ingest (and send into the waterways) as little synthetic chemical dressing as possible. There were a few stands selling produce from California and Mexico. WTF? If you want to shop at an outdoor Kroger, you'll love it here. If you want a real farmers' market, go to Franklin. Your best bet for local produce in town is the Produce Place, Turnip Truck, or the Vandy farmers' market on Thursdays. Haven't checked out the East Nashville farmers' market yet, but that is likely a better bet too. Lame.

text: I've been to Silk City on 2 separate nights: once for the diner, and the other for the lounge. The diner night was on a Friday; nice crowd of people, and luckily we found 2 seats at the bar. Bartender was incredibly friendly, from the looks of it the rest of the staff seemed laid back and amicable. I got a glass of sangria which was pretty tasty and reasonably priced ($5). Whatever dipping sauce they are using for the calamari is kickass, better than just plain marina. I ran into my friend while I was there and he was there for the lounge. Mind you he is NOT a dancing guy (he went there for a girl) and he said he danced his butt off all night if that is any indication of how good the lounge is already. Plus, its free for everyone on Friday nights. I returned to the lounge on a Saturday to see what the infamous DJ Dee Jay was all about. He was definitely a lot of fun, mixing old school and new hits and keeping the crowd going. The people in the crowd were fun and even all the guys were dancing! Random other things: -There are 4 single bathrooms which wasn't too bad but I wonder how crowded it can get, especially since they are on the dance floor. -The music was a tad too loud; my ears were screaming by the time we left. -Oh n there's a coat check for $1 which comes in handy on those cold nights. Definitely check this place out if you're looking for an alternative of the skanky Olde-City and the pretentious Rittenhouse and seeking a cool, laid-back place thats a lot of fun. I'm coming back here for my graduation party for sure!

text: Cute Italian BYOB at a convenient location in Medford with plenty of parking. I'd say the other reviews have done a pretty good job painting the picture in terms of the atmosphere, so I'll limit mine to my opinion of the food. If you order the right thing, there aren't many better values in local dining, especially since you can bring your own bottle of wine. Yes, this does imply that the menu can be hit or miss here. But the hits are great enough to garner a 4-star review from me. Favorites: - The Garlic Knots: love those, sometimes ask for extra - Involtini Di Melenzane (Stuffed Eggplant): this appetizer you could make a meal of. They also offer it as an entree with pasta - but to me all that spaghetti in red sauce just gets in the way of my delicious stuffed eggplant. - Spaghetti Carbonara: If you REALLY want to try and kill yourself with a super heavy dish, try ordering the Carbonara with Gnocchi instead of spaghetti. I did it once and barely survived the experience, but it was so good. Proceed at your own risk. - Gnocchi w/ Vodka Sauce - Linguini w/ White Clam Sauce Not So Much: - Calamari Fritti: The fried calamari appetizer is the most disappointing thing on the menu for me. It's average at best; not good for an Italian spot like this. To qualify my opinion, it's one of my stupid little missions in life to find the best fried calamari out there. Whenever we go out to eat at a new restaurant and they have fried calamari, I order it. Had it from Italy to throughout New England to Arizona (where I had a very good Buffalo Calamari). It's average here. At best. - Vongole Casino: The Clams Casino were terrible, especially for the $8.99 price tag. - Crab Cakes: I'd ballpark these at below average. They're huge, I'll give them that, but if you are craving them you are much better off at a good seafood restaurant. They have a lot of dessert options, but with the portion sizes (one order of the Gnocchi w/ Vodka Sauce is enough for me to get 3 meals out of - and be full for all 3), you'll probably never dream of it unless you go in with the gameplan to eat conservatively and take home a massive doggy bag. Bonus - they do catering trays for parties at very reasonable prices. We did that for our Super Bowl party this year and it was SO worth it. Cut down on our work immensely. Again though - heed the portion sizes here. Yes, a tray of Pasta Tarantella for 5 will feed 5 adults ... if those 5 adults are intent on eating the entire tray and then passing out at the table. All in all, good place, good food, great value!
label: POS

text: I have a soft spot in my heart for Lambert Airport. It's not the biggest or the best or the fastest, as many reviewers have noted, but in a whole year of flights (2009 - 2010), it hasn't let me down once. It's reliable, it's simple, and it gets me to where I need to be. One of the best things about the airport is how you can Metrolink right into it, which I've done countless times. It sure beats shelling out the $40 cab fare or expensive parking, especially on a student budget. The security lines are never all too long (although you might want to save a bit more time for the A gates, which always seem to take longer to get to). Dean's fantastic review mentions how Southwest is going to be the biggest airline operating out of STL in 2010, which really isn't so bad -- it means there are a bunch of direct flights opening up (e.g., to Boston, New Orleans, and more), which makes travel out of the airport even more painless. The worst thing about Lambert? The creepy food court. It's depressing just sitting there.
label: POS

text: I stayed here for one night this past weekend and had a generally great time (once I got there). The only real negative that I had with this hotel was their reservation service. When I looked it up on Yelp, they detailed a special offer for Yelp users (15% off + Free WiFi + $10 Meal Voucher). I called in to inquire about the rate and mentioned the Yelp special and the woman I spoke to initially acknowledged the offer. I told her I would call her back after consulting my fellow travelers. When I called back, I spoke to a different reservations clerk who said that they had absolutely no idea what Yelp offer I was talking about and that they could not honor it. She said that she even went up to the front desk to inquire about it, but none of the hotel staff knew what it was. I tried to tell her how to get to the offer (it was even posted up on their website via a link through Yelp) but she didn't even bother to look it up. Though she was generally very polite, the fact that nobody in their reservations department (sans the one woman who mysteriously disappeared) knew about a special that their own hotel was promoting is ridiculous. It was also kind of embarrassing on my end, to be perceived as if I had "made up" a special offer. She said she would offer us the discounted rate but not the WiFi and voucher and we decided to take it anyway due to the price and reviews. However, when we arrived the next day to check in, our reservation had been lost. Luckily, the front desk was super helpful. Not only did she get us a room at the same rate, when I mentioned the Yelp special, she threw in both the free WiFi and meal vouchers without any trouble. Hotel Preston, this person pretty much redeemed you. After that our stay was smooth and flawless. The hotel's decor is full of 60's pop-art and has a vibrant personality. Even though it is an airport hotel, it looked like it belonged downtown. The room was clean and comfortable with high-quality amenities like LG flat-screen TVs and Aveda bath products and quirker ones like a pet fish companion and lava lamp (by request). Their dining room is equally quirky and the breakfast buffet (free for us with our vouchers) had all of the necessary staples. When we wanted to go downtown the front desk hailed us a shuttle service (run by the sunny and outgoing Leroy) which arrived within minutes. The reservation glitch aside, Hotel Preston proved to be a great example of Nashville's friendliness and hospitality.

text: Bottom line: come here for two hours with a bottle of wine or some beers, and eat your heart out for $40. Called on a Monday for a Wednesday night reservation. There was easily availability for two at 8pm. Parking was a cinch. It's byob so we brought a sixpack. (They chilled it in a buck of ice water on the floor. People next to us had a party of 7 and their champagne was chilled on the table.) There was seating for maybe 40 people inside, and a dozen or so outside. We went inside. It is tight, but you are not rubbing elbows with the next table - intimate and cozy, and nice lighting. Casual atmosphere; seemed good for dates and could handle groups of 6 or 8. There was crusty fresh bread and aioli butter and olive oil for the table. The server was perfectly attentive - not visiting too much, but always ready for our next request. He told us about the chef's background and education, the seasonal menu debuting that night, and the specials, and he made recommendations for my Turista courses. Dinner was a relaxing two hours by choice - we asked him to hold off in between courses while we talked and he was happy to do so. Each course was hot and delightful when it came out despite our request to hold. Antipasti: Mussels - white wine and butter, spicy. Delicious, creamy sauce. Perfect with the crusty bread and with just enough spice to warm it up. Fresh daily from Prince Edward Island, we were told. Good portion. Pasta: Lasagne with veal sweet breads, ground beef, chicken liver and a wonderful tomato sauce (full flavored and rich, like a bolognese that has simmered for 8 hours). Small portion, but rich. I could have been done eating after that, but thank god I didn't!! Secondi: Whole white fish, but I forget what kind. Barely breaded, then baked. (The menu says they won't debone). Crisp outside, moist and flaky, and probably great leftover with a nice ragout. My friend got the bistecca - perfectly medium rare steak with sopressata, extra sharp provolone, and a fried egg on top. A little rich and a bit salty from the provolone, but a flavor explosion and enough to fill you up if you are only ordering a la carte. Dessert: flourless chocolate torte. Yum. They also had espresso which sounded tempting, except there was no more room in my happy belly. I will certainly be back.

text: What is Peruvian food? That is the question that Husband and I had when we entered El Tumi yesterday. The answer? YUMMY! My first impression of El Tumi was that somebody with taste designed the interior. The restaurant is casual, but the decor is pleasing and understated, with some nice prints of Peruvian landscapes to remind you that this is NOT a Mexican restaurant. Even the wall colors lend to the nice cultural atmosphere. I like that they have managed to do this without plastering tourist posters all over the walls, like so many ethnic restaurants. The menu does a good job of explaining what everything is, and the waiter even brought out a drink sample for Husband. He went with the lunch special, Lomo con lentejas (basically Beef and Lentils), and I had the Pan con Lomo (Beef Sandwich). But before we got our dinners we received our complimentary... HUACATAY! (Cue music and light from heaven here.) I've never had this tasty little dip before, and oh, what I have been missing!! It's hard to describe except as Todd S. said, "a magical green sauce." I could have sworn there was avocado in it, but some research has proven otherwise. It is basically a silky smooth and spicy pesto made with huacatay leaves, which are native to Peru. At El Tumi they serve it in a very small little ramakin with a small bowl of corn chips. One dish SHOULD be enough for two people if, like husband and I, you lean way over the dish in a protective stance, hissing at each other if you think the other is taking more of their fair share. Another new thing we tried was the Chicha Morada, described on the menu as "Peruvian purple corn beverage, infused with cloves and cinnamon." It is quite tasty, and if you like Dr. Pepper, you'll like Chicha Morada. It goes incredibly well with the spicy HUACATAY (music and light again). So Husband and I both got Lomo dishes, which is basically strips of beef sauteed with red AND green onions (yum) and garlic and tomatoes. It's sort of like Peruvian fajitas. Mine came on a french roll for a sandwich, and Husband's came straight up with rice and lentils on the side. However it is served, it is delicious. The flavor is just right and the meat really tender. I wouldn't recommend it, though, if you don't like onions. There are two reasons I knocked off one star: 1) Husband's lunch special came with a salad, which was basically a plate of iceberg lettuce. This is a pet peeve for us both. Either make a salad or don't. Rabbit food is gross. 2) Although the prices were reasonable (we came in under $20 before tip), the serving sizes are very small. We weren't starving, so it worked out OK, but I wouldn't recommend that you come here with a big appetite. Think more along the lines of light lunch. Overall, I think Reno is very lucky to have a new ethnic cuisine that is so different and so delicious. If nothing else, you should come to try the HUACATAY (Music. Light.)

text: I've been here twice, odd, considering I don't live in Nevada. The first time I went, I think it was new. There was barely anyone in there, and I had the feeling that it was someone's pet project. It was done up all nice, with a mod-y vibe, with old photos, 60's films, and music. The staff were awful friendly like, and the cocktail list was small, but good. It felt a bit too nice, not alot of character, but something that I reckoned would come with time. That being said, it was a bar for locals in a town built on tourism and tacky casinos. Which was nice. The second time I went, it was as though every single person who lived in Reno had made it their local, and they were all there. Suits, hipsters, a bus full of Burners, a flash mob of Olivia-Newton-John-Physical-video-extras, 2 girls in garden party dresses following one another like a rather short trail of quails, squat builder types, and myself and my friend. We seemed to be on another plane of existence than everyone else there. From careful observation, the one uniting factor, the one thing that brings everyone together is the doorman. Everyone knows him, he is friendly with everyone. As we were leaving, yet another strange group were arriving, and i'm sure the hilarity was about to ensue. We were invited into a bus parked outside, for a cocktail. A cocktail bus outside of a bar. We declined, and hopped in a cab where the seats were reclined all the way back.

text: This was disappointing. A few months ago, we'd stopped in hoping for a table, but there was no room at the teeny tiny inn. I figured the food was good because of the turnout. And when our pleasant server recommended we order 3-4 dishes since the menu was designed as a small-plate offering, we did so. To make up for their size, small plates generally pack a punch of flavor, but these dishes were one-notes, if that. Out of eight dishes we ordered, three were good enough to mention: if you see pierogies, spinach salad, and panzanella on the menu it's safe to order them. Stay away from anything dubbed sofrito or bouillabaise (because apparently, at Elements, they are the same, watery, flavorless thing). And what was even more upsetting than the kitchen insulting my culinary intelligence is the owner pilfering my wallet. The prices here are on par with delicious, innovative, intricate plates you'll find at any respectable tapas house in the city. This place better check itself. I was heavily debating dessert; it could have meant redemption or the nail in the coffin. But I could no longer stand the mindless chatter of other patrons who bragged they've tried FOUR GRAS and the food of CHEF STEPHEN STARR. I had to get out of there. Coffin closed.

text: I love the selection of unique foods at TJs, but shopping at this particular store frequently proves to be a trying experience. The parking lot (especially since 40 reopened) is always packed and a nightmare to maneuver. The store is frequently crowded and popular items are out of stock. Also, it seems like whenever I find something I really love (like their banana waffles) they discontinue the product. My biggest problem with the store, however, is the staff. I know a lot of people enjoy the chummy atmosphere, but I do not. Call me a curmudgeon, I guess. When checking out I frequently have awkward and unprofessional interactions with the people ringing up my groceries. On one occasion, a young female employee looked at me and said, "Wow! You look exhausted! Are you OK?" I realize that, in her mind, she was being friendly and perhaps concerned, but that is not an appropriate comment to make to a complete stranger, let alone a paying customer. On another occasion I had forgotten my reusable bags at home. The older gentleman who rang up my groceries asked me if I wanted to buy some of TJ's (garish) bags and I declined. He then proceeded to give me a two minute lecture/guilt trip about how I shouldn't use THEIR disposable bags. Really? SERIOUSLY?! I came there to buy honey and eggs and now I'm getting a lecture on the environment? On another occasion the young man who checked out my groceries was so busy trying to chat me up that he neglected to place a few items in my bags. It wasn't until I got home and reviewed the receipt that I realized I had paid for about $10 worth of groceries which never made it out of the store. Highway 40 was closed at the time and I didn't feel like braving the traffic to go back. Although I really like TJ's products and their pricing, it's experiences like these that turn me off of this particular location.

text: I have to say, that a concept that intrigued millions of us into simplicity and modernism, has just shot us in the face. They have switched to no free plastic bags for your purchases---you can buy a reusable one for 59cents, or there is a bin at the front with used plastic.... I don't know---I like customer service, especially somewhere that is so large. What if a price happens to be wrong, or whatever? It's not like you can run to isle 7, you know? The "non-cashiers?" who were helping the hordes of customers trying to self-check-out seemed very, VERY annoyed at the system.... but at least they still had a job there. Honestly, I'd rather have the whole place online, and pay shipping charges if need be. But, that's not possible. text: Nan Zhou has been on my "to visit" list for months now, and did not disappoint. It's small and has brusque service that requires a lot of pointing and ordering by number, but the noodle soup, either handdrawn in the small open kitchen or fresh-shaved, is delicious, ridiculously cheap, and arrives at the table in 5 minutes. I was so eager to start slurping my vegetable and fried egg soup with handdrawn noodles, I forgot to take a photo until half the soup was safe in my tummy, but I think you'll still get the idea. The vegetarian soup costs less than $4, though I added an extra, entirely unneeded deep-fried egg, for an additional 50 cents. You can see the tangle of fresh noodles, which got even more delicious as they absorbed more of the soup broth, the deep-fried egg, and what remained of the generous heap of fresh cilantro. The broth is quite delicate, and I added two Tbs. of hot chili oil and soy sauce. Handdrawn noodles can be difficult to find, and I'd suggest ordering these instead of the thicker, very doughy shaved noodles. The menu can be a bit difficult to decipher, mostly because of poor English translation, and I wished for a vegetarian -friendly side dish. Overall, though, I was very pleased with the flavor of my soup, and its great value. The soup was so perfect on a blustery fall day, I somehow managed to finish the entire, huge, bowl!

text: Toppers- I wanted to love you. I had heard good things. But you were like a kiss on the cheek after a third date *sigh*. We waited a little bit for our drinks and then a little more for the first round of plates to come out. With tapas, the plates are usually just brought out as the kitchen finishes them...there is no real order to the madness and it's usually on the service is usually pretty quick. However with this meal things were a bit different. A few plates were brought out to start with. We then had to wait about 20 min or so for the next dishes to come out. Then it seemed even longer after that...about 30 minutes. Finally we were waiting for our last two courses and I kid you not this took about 1 1/2 hours to get the last course and dessert! Overall we were there from 8:15pm til 11:30pm! I don't know if they were having kitchen troubles or what but it was absolutely absurd how long it took. We even had to track down our waiter a few times to order more drinks because he was nowhere to be found. Some people at my table were almost ready to get up and leave near the end of the meal. The food was not fabulous but there were a few stand out items: the seasonal salad which had chickpeas, radicchio, cauliflower and potatoes in it (had a Mediterranean flare) and the empanadas with dates & bacon (very sweet, yet savory). Overall it isn't a bad deal for $30 a person for the amount of food you get. We ordered so much alochol to account for the time in between courses so that jacked up the bill, the food was so-so and the service was completely out of whack. text: Famous Barr's lunch room... Woolworth & Kresge's lunch counters ... the circa 1930's ambiance of the Parkmoor... uncomplicated, unsophisticated diners of our past. Recollections wandered through my mind last evening as I entered Cafe Manhattan once again. This compact affable neighborhood diner was packed at the tail end of dinner but loosened up quickly. Food selections cover four pages & offer comforting familiar favorites as well as a few surprises. Their soups, burgers & sandwiches are "old fashion tasty" with just enough grease & cheese to add flavor & the need for extra napkins. A classic chrome counter spans the north wall with spinning stools & soda fountain character. Desserts are simple & timeless; folks visit simply to indulge. (Happily I detected muted slurps & "spoon-stirring-inside-glass sounds" from a nearby couple.) Vinyl booths edge along floor to ceiling windows across the front & line the south wall. Fun reproductions of 50's & 60's memorabilia dot the walls. Folks in all age ranges visit regularly. Servers are young & friendly. One little guy sporting a plastic fireman's helmet sent his full glass of water soaring over the edge of his table. Patrons splashed at the next table took it in good humor & the staff quickly & kindly cleaned up the puddles. The only person a bit out of sorts was a young man, older than the rest, who worked behind the counter. Cafe Manhattan is a pleasant, small, Clayton corner eatery serving agreeable & soul-reassuring food. It is the kind of place to stop off after a day in Forest Park or taking in a matinee with the family. Hint: If you enjoy your meals quiet arrive in between peak hours & stay as long as you want.

text: Were I a Sorbet enthusiast, this place would be my 5-star wet dream. "Sorbet?" you ask, "I thought this was a frozen yogurt place??" Oh it is. Or, rather, that's how it promotes itself. Yes, even your 'normal' or 'plain' flavors like cake batter had this strange, tart, citrus (seemingly pineapple?) after-taste that overwhelmed the main flavor in such a way it was as though the yogurt should have been labeled "pineapple with cake batter leanings." The consistency is ok, but who can concentrate on consistency when the flavor is so far off? Who wants chocolate syrup, heath bar pieces or Oreos in something that tastes like a daiquiri? I went with a layer of cotton candy (at the time, it seemed the most UN-fruity tasting) with what I thought was heath bar shavings (turns out those were espresso chips), and on top of that was a layer of red velvet chocolate with bananas and little caramel chocolates. The red velvet tasted like raspberry sorbet and mixed with bananas and caramel chocolates the flavor was horrifying. I scraped out the entire top layer to try the one below... only to find it was even worse. I ended up throwing it all away it was so inedible. I know that you're thinking my poor flavor choices may have colored my opinion- and you're right. I agree they were awful. However, consider that I am a traditionalist. I actually LIKE vanilla and chocolate. What does it say about a place where the flavor that tastes most like traditional ice cream flavors is freaking cotton candy? And my confusion when it came to toppings was due to a lack of labels. But I'd say that's the least of your worries at Chill.

text: I am extremely EXTREMELY disappointed by my encounter with Dr. Murarka and the Compassion Vet Clinic. To begin, I set my appointment 2 weeks in advance to get my rabbit spayed. When I called the receptionist said that she would call be back in less than 10 minutes with more information. Over a half hour later, I dialed back because it was approaching the end of the business day. They said that they spay many rabbits so that it would not be a problem. Yesterday, the date of my appointment, I arrived at 6:00pm, my scheduled time. The clinic was closed. At 6:15 I get a phone call saying that they were running late and would arrive in 5-10 minutes. 25 minutes later, I call back and, sounding annoyed that I called back, he replied that he was stuck in traffic and offered no apologies for my inconvenience. At 7:30, the doctor arrived and, saying NOTHING at all to the two cars in the parking lot that had been waiting for a while, just walks into the clinic. I go in and the only words spoken to me were, "Fill out this form." After I did, I waited about 15 more minutes until I was led to the back. There, the doctor inspected my bunny and made a comment about the risk of this procedure due to the anesthesia. This did not concern me -- until he made another comment about the fact that he was warning me in advance so "if something happened, I can't blame him because he warned me" The way he phrased this comment raised red flags, so I asked him to elaborate. To which he responded, "We lose some." I asked what percentage and he hedged, not giving me a straight answer. After me repeating the question 3-4 times and getting evasive answers, he finally responds, "about 25%." Given how he avoided answering the question, I have no doubt that the percentage was higher. Spaying/Neutering is not a life/death procedure and a death rate of 25% is ludacris! I was aghast that, when I originally called to schedule the appointment and questioned if the doctor had the experience to spay rabbits, I was assured that he was an excellent doctor and was not told that over one-quarter of his rabbit patients have died! I can not comment on his ability to treat cats and dogs but, if you have a rabbit, stay away from this shady clinic!

text: I visited this legendary restaurant when my friends and I recently attended the New Orleans Jazz Festival '09. Neil Young was amazing, but Jaques-Imo's still ranks up there as one of the high-lights of the trip. I honestly thought I died and went to Creole Cuisine heaven. A friend who went to Tulane wrote me up a list of restaurants to check out, and Jaque-Imo's was one of those "must trys". My friends and I took a taxi to a remote area of New Orleans which seemed a bit sketchy, but once we arrived at our destination it was like we stumbled upon some outdoor patio party. Live music, oysters a la carte served right on the street, and a gallery we checked out as we waited for a table. The wait was long, but the food is well worth it. Plus there were plenty of friendly and colorful characters outside keeping us company. Once we went inside we went straight through the kitchen to a cozy and colorful back area. We were starving, and the food looked amazing (we did get a sneak preview as we walked through the kitchen), so we ordered right away. I ordered the alligator cheesecake, fried green tomatoes, and blackened red-fish, both which were incredible dishes. Were I not such a gentleman I would have cleaned the plate with my tongue. The sauces were amazing, and the food in general was angelic. On top of the incredible food the bar up front is lively and fun. They pour stiff drinks (if that's your thing), and there seems to always be a friendly local or two to chat about Jaque-Imo legends with you. I highly recommend you search out this out-of-the-way location if you're in New Orleans. I'm no local, but after spending my brief time in New Orleans this is easily my favorite restaurant in the Big Easy so far.

text: I am into coffee, and have been for over 20 years in a hard core way. I have pulled 10s of thousand of shots of espresso on commercial machines, drunk 1000s of gallons of French press brew, sampled coffee on five continents and 46 states of the Union. Blah Blah Blah. Even after all of this, Raging sage is my bean purveyor of choice ANYWHERE in the world. text: Cereality caused all kinds of buzz when in opened in 2004. Wow! everyone was saying. A restaurant devoted to cereal! The concept was designed by a couple of guys who know a whole lot about business and who thought of everything as far as restaurant design, sleek packaging and, generally, how to get young people excited about their product. And now, they're launching Cerealities near college campuses all over the country. I haven't been back there since the opening in 2004. To me, this project is just part of a greater evil we might call the "Starbucks Project" meant to make us forget what foods and drinks are really worth by blinding us with pleasant cafes and hip marketing campaigns. See, Cereality actually gives you what it claims: a bowl of cereal in a cafe environment. Now, as rational human beings, is that something we really need? And do we need to pay for that bowl the same thing we'd pay at a supermarket for an entire box?!?! Fine, I'm being negative. I can see how the charming, Chinese food-like take-out boxes are appealing, and I'm sure that cereal lovers will go gaga for the gigantic list of topping possibilities for their Frosted Flakes. But, really, is it too hard to pour your own bowl of cereal? Go out and buy a couple of nuts and berries to top it with, for God's sake!

The bachelor might have thought they were 100% though , lol. They provide you with a mask ( and repeatedly stress you will lose an eye if you lose it in the paintball shooting area ), a long sleeve shirt, gloves, and a gun for $30. We divded our group of 6 into 2 teams, waited 10 minutes or so for the other 2 groups to finish their rounds and then we went at it. For the next 3 hours, we had hella fun!! I slipped on my ass, ( the business warned you anyway how slippery it was) got shot everywhere, ( I still have quarter sized welts on my entire body, and shot my friends everywhere.....One of the final rounds the ref had the bachelor run to the other side without any gun, while 5 of us ruthlessly attacked without mercy. Our boy got jacked up. : ) You also can live out your Rambo 5 fantasy when the ref informs you that you are the only one left alive. At that point I removed myself from cover and unleashed the rest of my ammo on the other team. You can truly see how tough someone is or isn't ( I admit I let out a feeble " ooowwwww!!! upon being hit in the family jewels) here at Reno Indoor Paintball. All in all, for 3 hours of fun, all of us left tired, laughing, and out the door for only $50 a person. I am already excited to go back in September!

text: I gotta give the Factory some credit...it makes the Troc look like a classy venue. That, my friends, is some true wizardry. The Electric Factory is in many ways just like the Troc...except the negatives are far worse, and the positives do not exist. I can't imagine ever being anywhere near this shitbox if it weren't for a concert, yet the Troc at least is in a cool neighborhood. The security here will probably man-rape you whilst breathing from the mouth...a true feat. "Whats this...a pen?!?! In your uni-form?!?!" In the trash it goes. But...I like to write stuff down. "And STAB people!!!!" I am not making this up. Parking? Well, there is a lot that would satisfy about half of the staff on a slow night, otherwise, you get to pay an ever-shifting amount to park on what appears to be a public street/alley/lot/toxic dump around the venue. You get to polish your street cred, at least...toss the bum/security guard a few bucks when you park, and promise to toss even more when you get back so long as your car is still in one piece (and make sure you follow through...bums are like elephants when it comes to remembering things). Hey, it works. Ok, you make it inside. If the show skews more towards an "adult" audience, make sure you show up several hours early so you can get a good spot upstairs. Otherwise, hang out downstairs with the kids. The balcony gets very, very crowded for certain acts, the bar can't keep up, and the bouncers don't help (why, these are up-goin' stairs, not down-goin' stairs...can't you tell the difference?). Sound...sound??? Put a boombox inside of a heating duct and blast it...you have just been to a concert at the Electric Factory. It always, always sucks. Always. I saw the Mr. Show...show here, which had no music, and the sound still sucked. How does this happen? You simply need a mic that doesn't a-splode when spoken into. Didn't happen. It boggles the mind. A gang of stray cats could run a better venue. I truly hate this place and everything about it. I would normally not waste any time writing about it, but I figured I'd play a little game...I dropped a reference to the last band I ever saw (and will ever see) somewhere in my rantings...name them and you win scene points. Now, excuse me...I'm going to rent a helicopter just so I can pee on this dump.
